Trump vows the US will 'hit' Iran 'hard' after Tehran targeted US bases in Jordan
The US president, Donald Trump, has told Fox News’s chief foreign correspondent, Trey Yingst, that the US will respond to Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan overnight.
“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News. “There will be a response,” he added, after Jordan’s army confirmed it had intercepted eight missiles early this morning.
In response to the US assault on Larak Island late on Sunday, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.
In the interview with Fox News on Monday, Trump said all of the missiles were intercepted by American air defence systems, except one which was allowed to pass through the airspace because it was identified as not on course to hit anything “significant”, according to Yingst.
Trump was sending message to Iran with Kharg Island post, says Vance
US president Donald Trump was sending a message to Iran with his social media post about Kharg Island, vice-president JD Vance said on Monday.
“The president likes to switch it up on social media a little bit. He would be the first to say he doesn’t make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he’s sending a message to the Iranians,” Vance said when asked about Trump’s post.
Trump’s one-line social media post on Sunday was accompanied by an AI-generated video clip showing fake attacks by the US military.
A US official said on Monday the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes. An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable“.
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in an interview on Monday that the goal of US sanctions on Iran is “to create the conditions that they will want to come to the table” for negotiations.
As Bessent opened meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in Asheville on Monday, he said he wants to focus on ways to grow the global economy and rein in mounting debt.
But the event comes after hostilities renewed between the US and Iran, and as trade friction with Canada spiked following a breakdown in negotiations that led to escalating tariffs.
Bessent told the Associated Press in an interview on Sunday that he plans to turn up pressure on Iran by sanctioning another bank, part of what he is calling “Operation Economic Outcast.”
He said the administration is prepared to exact “financial violence if we have to.”
For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.
Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%.
As purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods. Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market.
According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages.
Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.” You can read more from our diplomatic editor, Patrick Wintour, here:
In a brief post to his Truth Social platform, Donald Trump claimed Iran is a “failed nation” with no navy, air force or currency. “IT IS DEAD!” he wrote, saying the only things Tehran have in its favour are a sympathetic US media, a “willingness to kill their protesters” and a “good line of bullshit”. Trump said the Iranian leadership is in “total disarray” and is “incapable” of properly representing the country.
It is true that Iran has suffered enormously because of the US-Israel war, with Iranians facing high food inflation and a depreciation of the nation’s currency, the rial, under pressure from US efforts to isolate Iran by threatening the country’s few remaining trade partners while blockading its main ports in the Persian Gulf and choking off oil exports.
Trump, frustrated at being unable to win an aerial victory over Iran, has regularly lashed out on social media against the regime, threatening the country with attacks that often do not materialise. He has emphatically denied reports in the American press that the US is suffering a munitions shortage and has vowed to seek “long term jail sentences” for officials who leak information about the military’s weapons stocks.
Trump vows the US will 'hit' Iran 'hard' after Tehran targeted US bases in Jordan
The US president, Donald Trump, has told Fox News’s chief foreign correspondent, Trey Yingst, that the US will respond to Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan overnight.
“We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News. “There will be a response,” he added, after Jordan’s army confirmed it had intercepted eight missiles early this morning.
In response to the US assault on Larak Island late on Sunday, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.
In the interview with Fox News on Monday, Trump said all of the missiles were intercepted by American air defence systems, except one which was allowed to pass through the airspace because it was identified as not on course to hit anything “significant”, according to Yingst.
Scott Bessent, US secretary of the treasury, has said that Tehran is taking Washington’s sanctions seriously, arguing that Iran is resorting to kinetic military responses only because it is losing economically.
Reuters reports Bessent added that the US will maintain its economic pressure on the country, claiming that Iran’s economy does not need to collapse, but rather, he said, the Iranian government needs to come to its senses.
US denies Iran's claim that oil tanker hit mines in strait of Hormuz
Reuters has a quick snap that US Central Command (Centcom) has denied claims made by Iran state TV and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that a ship had struck mines in the strait of Hormuz.
In a statement posted to social media, Centcom said “Iran’s claim that a supertanker passing through strait of hormuz struck two mines and was brought to a complete stop is false.”
The denial followed reports in state media earlier today that Iran had said an oil tanker caught fire in the strait after it hit two naval mines.
“A rogue supertanker attempting to pass through the illegal route south of the strait of Hormuz caught fire in massive fires after striking two naval mines and was brought to a complete stop,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in an earlier statement.
Israel signs $3.5bn defence export deal with Greece
Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece on Monday, the largest between the two countries, AP reports.
Israel’s defence ministry said the $3.5bn (€3bn / £2.6bn) export deal, dubbed Achilles Shield, is one of the country’s largest and includes a multilayered air defence system for Greece using Israeli technology.
The Greek defence ministry said in was part of “the greatest reform of its armed forces in its history”, as the Nato member looked to ramp up defence spending.
The deal was signed in Tel Aviv by Israeli defence ministry director general, Maj Gen Amir Baram, and Maj Gen Ioannis Bouras of Greece.

Gaza’s health ministry says at least 1,320 people have been killed by Israeli attacks since a ‘ceasefire’ was signed between Israel and Hamas last October.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by the US to end the war on Gaza.
Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said earlier this month that there can be no progress on the stalled Gaza ceasefire deal or an Israeli withdrawal from the territory until Hamas first disarms.
In its latest update, Gaza’s health ministry said that 73,456 people, mostly women and children, have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since October 2023, when Isreal launched its assault on the territory following the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

articles.title: ‘If We Need to Strike, We Will Strike’: Russian Lawmaker Calls for Nuclear Strike on Ukraine to Force Kyiv to Surrender
articles.body:
A senior Russian lawmaker has openly called for Moscow to use a nuclear weapon against Ukraine to force Kyiv to capitulate, as concerns grow over possible further Russian escalation.
Alexei Zhuravlev, a State Duma deputy and leader of the nationalist Rodina party, said Russia should use tactical nuclear weapons if necessary and dismissed any debate over whether Moscow should cross the nuclear threshold.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia must strike in such a way that the enemy understands that it must capitulate,” Zhuravlev said in a video address, posted on Telegram, on Sunday.
“There should not even be such a discussion. If necessary, we are obliged to use [tactical nuclear weapons]... If we need to strike, we will strike. And that is not up for discussion.”
Zhuravlev’s comments come amid renewed reporting about concerns inside the US and Europe over whether Russian President Vladimir Putin could escalate the war further.
Bloomberg previously reported, citing sources close to the Kremlin, that Putin was preparing for further escalation in Ukraine and could potentially consider tactical nuclear weapons as a last resort to avoid defeat.
There is no evidence that Putin has decided to use nuclear weapons, however.
CIA chief’s Moscow visit
The nuclear rhetoric follows CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s unexpected visit to Moscow on Aug. 25.
According to Axios sources, Ratcliffe sought to determine whether Putin could be persuaded to abandon further escalation and return to negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Kremlin Says Putin Sees ‘Absolutely No Point’ in Trump-Zelensky Peace Summit
The New York Times reported that Ratcliffe delivered a “grim assessment” of the Russian military and economy and urged Moscow to reach an agreement before its position deteriorates further.
Shortly after the visit, Russia conducted a test of a nuclear-capable missile capable of reaching the United States. The defense ministry did not disclose which missile was tested.
Bloomberg reported that there were no indications at the time that Putin was preparing to actually use nuclear weapons.
China warns Moscow
Any Russian nuclear strike would also risk a major confrontation with Moscow’s own partners.
China has strongly opposed the use of nuclear weapons in the war and has reportedly warned the Kremlin against taking such a step.

- 06:08 GMTOil prices rose in early trading in Asia following the exchange of strikes between US and Iranian forces. WTI futures grew by 2.47% to $85.46 per barrel, with Brent futures climbing by 2.71% to $90.49 per barrel.
- 05:55 GMTIran’s IRGC has said a supertanker which tried to traverse the Strait of Hormuz via the southern route, designated by the US, has “caught fire” after being hit by two naval mines. Passage through the waterway is only possible though the route overseen by Tehran, the IRGC stressed. “Shipping companies should not be deceived by the provocations of the child-killing American army and should not unnecessarily expose the property and lives of their ships’ crews to destruction,” the IRGC advised.
- 04:12 GMTIran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone over the Strait of Hormuz amid the renewed exchange of strikes between Tehran and Washington. IRGC air defenses hit the “long-range American MQ-9 drone,” causing it to crash into the waters of the Persian Gulf, Iranian media reported, citing a Guard statement. The US has yet to confirm the loss. The Washington Post reported earlier this month that the US military had lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reapers during the war with Iran, although not all were shot down. The aircraft can cost between $30 million and $50 million each, depending on its sensors and weapons.
- 03:30 GMTIran is “not looking for war” but will not “sit still in the face of any aggression,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in his first public comments since the US strike on Larak Island. “We will give a decisive response to the aggressors,” Pezeshkian said before departing for Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to attend a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit. “Instability and unrest in the region are not in the interest of any country and will challenge everyone,” he added, according to Fars news agency.

articles.title: MSPO-2026: 1,000 Participants From 40 Countries — What Ukraine Will Present
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense companies will present their developments at the MSPO international defense industry exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
A total of 29 Ukrainian manufacturers have announced their participation in MSPO-2026. Some will present their products at a joint Ukrainian stand supported by the Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry, while others will have separate exhibitions. Overall, the event will bring together 1,000 participants from 40 countries.
Targi Kielce organizes the 34th International Defense Industry Exhibition. Poland’s Ministry of National Defense is the main partner of MSPO-2026, while the country’s largest defense group, Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa (PGZ), is the strategic partner.
The exhibition is also held under the honorary patronage of Polish President Karol Nawrocki.
Canada will play a special role this year after receiving Lead Nation status. The Canadian national exhibition will bring together the country’s defense and technology companies and provide a platform for negotiations and B2B meetings. The Polish Armed Forces exhibition will also traditionally be held as part of MSPO, with this year’s edition focusing on innovation and artificial intelligence technologies.
Some companies are also preparing premieres of new developments. Some of these systems are already being used on the front line but will be presented to a broad international audience for the first time at MSPO.
For Ukraine’s defense industry, the exhibition in Kielce will be more than a venue for displaying products. Manufacturers expect to establish new contacts with European partners, discuss production localization, attract investment and explore potential contracts.
The participants include manufacturers that are members of the Militarnyi Alliance. They will demonstrate unmanned systems, drone interceptors, electronic warfare systems and unmanned ground vehicles.
UKRSPECSYSTEMS will have a presence at MSPO at two locations — its own stand and the NAUDI stand.
The association’s stand will feature the PD-2 and Shark reconnaissance unmanned systems.
At its own stand, UKRSPECSYSTEMS will present the Shark-M, the One Punch interceptor and several new systems whose names have not yet been disclosed ahead of the exhibition.
They will be presented to the public for the first time on September 8. The company said some of these developments are already operating on the front line, with their results appearing in situation reports, unit videos, and news reports.
Visitors will also be able to speak with UKRSPECSYSTEMS equipment operators from the 15th Separate Artillery Reconnaissance Brigade “Black Forest” and learn about its combat use.
“MSPO is the largest defense platform in Central and Eastern Europe, and those who make procurement decisions on NATO’s eastern flank come here. For the Ukrainian industry, this is the shortest route to these customers,” the company said.
UKRSPECSYSTEMS also sees the exhibition as a platform for discussing production localization, new orders, and potential investment under European programs.
Ukrainian Armor will present the Protector unmanned ground vehicle, as well as several drone versions equipped with warheads using explosively formed penetrators and fiber-optic control.
In addition to robotic systems and unmanned aircraft, the Ukrainian manufacturer will bring artillery ammunition, armored vehicles, mines, and mortars to Poland.
MSPO will traditionally serve as a platform for the company to present new developments. This year, Ukrainian Armor plans to present several new systems developed using real-world combat experience.
During the exhibition, the company will also hold a series of meetings with leading European and global arms manufacturers.
Ukrainian Armor views international exhibitions as a strategic platform for finding opportunities to develop and scale up production.
The company plans to seek foreign partners to integrate advanced Western technologies and to develop and jointly produce new weapons and military equipment.
At the same time, the company notes that it remains focused on supplying Ukraine’s Defense Forces, while new contracts and partnerships are intended to help strengthen the combat capabilities of Ukrainian troops.
Ukrainian company TAF Industries will present its defense technology ecosystem at three MSPO stands.
The Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry’s joint stand will feature the Kolibri 10 Advance UAV, the Kolibri 17 FR1 relay carrier, the TAF Kolibri-i10 interceptor, and the Kvazar A electronic warfare system.
The Teslia and Lehit L unmanned ground vehicles will be presented at the NAUDI association’s stand.
Meanwhile, TAF Industries’ own stand will feature a broader range of developments. The exhibition will include the Kolibri 10 Advance and Kolibri 13, the Kolibri 17 FR1 relay carrier, the Kolibri 15-O fiber-optic FPV drone, the Kolibri-i10 interceptor, the Kvazar A and Kvazar 3M electronic warfare systems, the Babka reconnaissance UAV, and the Lehit S UGV.
The company does not currently plan to sign new agreements directly during the exhibition. However, MSPO will take place after TAF Industries began cooperation with Poland’s defense industry.
TAF Industries said its presence at the exhibition is intended to highlight cooperation with Polish partners and demonstrate demand for Ukrainian defense technologies on the Polish market.
In June, the company signed a partnership agreement with Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa to localize drone production in Poland.
Ukrainian company Deviro will bring a new version of its M2R unmanned system to Kielce, featuring an updated camera.
The manufacturer will also present the Bulava V2, which has slightly larger dimensions, as well as a simulator using the company’s own software.
The company is not currently planning any separate premieres or agreements during MSPO.
Deviro said its main objectives at the exhibition are to present the latest product updates, establish contacts with potential partners, and explore opportunities for future cooperation.
Ptashka Drones will showcase the Ptashka 17-O-50 km system at MSPO, equipped with a digital daylight camera for long-distance missions.
Visitors will also see the updated Ptashka 2.0 manual counter-drone system.
The company’s main premiere will be the new Ptashka drone detector.
According to the manufacturer, the device analyzes video-signal parameters rather than signal strength alone. This is intended to reduce false detections and speed up FPV signal detection.
The detector automatically displays the intercepted video stream on its built-in screen, showing the active signal and frequencies. It simultaneously scans three frequency bands, is equipped with a 10,000 mAh battery, and supports wireless software updates via Wi-Fi.
Ptashka Drones is also negotiating possible cooperation with several international defense companies. The manufacturer plans to announce any signed contracts or memorandums separately.
The company views participation in MSPO as an opportunity to strengthen ties with the European defense industry, establish component supplies, attract investment, and present Ukrainian solutions in unmanned technologies and counter-drone systems.
Ukrainian manufacturers’ participation in MSPO shows that international exhibitions are becoming more than opportunities for defense companies to demonstrate new equipment.
Ukrainian manufacturers are bringing systems developed from modern warfare experience to Kielce while also seeking opportunities to scale up production with European partners.
At the same time, some of this cooperation is already moving from negotiations to concrete projects. One example is TAF Industries’ agreement with Polish defense group PGZ to localize drone production.
At the exhibition, Ukrainian companies will present both established systems and new developments in reconnaissance, FPV drones, enemy drone interception, electronic warfare, and unmanned ground systems.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1649: Russia keeps Kyiv under fire for a fourth day as Ukraine tests new interceptors and strikes back at Russian oil
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans. Kyiv is racing to scale new defences after Russia used more than 2,500 jet-powered drones in August alone.
Ukraine strikes Russia's second-largest oil refinery again in major overnight attack, also hitting airfield and drone launch site. The refinery has been targeted repeatedly during the full-scale war as Ukraine strikes infrastructure supporting Russia's military and economy.
Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies. Russia has launched nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 guided bombs and 31 missiles against Ukraine this week, while Kyiv faces repeated strikes and a shortage of critical air defence interceptors.
Ukrainian ground-robot maker has moved into air: Ratel's first strike drone flies 30 kilometres on Starlink link. The Ratel K1 carries two kilograms, the maker says.
"We have surprises for our neighbors": Ukraine's aviation commander says new aircraft developments are essentially finished and already in testing. Ukraine has already rebuilt what it flies. Its crews turned the 1970s-era Su-24 bomber into a launcher for SCALP cruise missiles.
Russia launches third attack on Ukraine's largest Danube port this month, during peak of wheat harvest. Five trucks loaded with grain were destroyed and three more damaged in the Izmail district.
Ukraine chooses three Western fighters to build its air force around. One of them can fly again from stretch of road in 15 to 20 minutes. The Air Force settled on them after weighing cost, logistics, and repair speed.
Fix for Ukraine's interceptors is radar seeker head, and American firm is selling one for $4,000, says president's tech adviser. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov says cloud and fog collapse interceptor hit rates, and a seeker head is the way out.
Four ground robots for one evacuation: Russia is targeting Ukraine's robotic medevac missions. Ground robots are helping evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions, but the systems themselves have come under intense Russian fire.
Ukrainian robot commander calls ground robots "Persian elephants." What army really needs are "Arabian steeds," he says. A "Khartia" robot commander says FPV drones and mines have collapsed the machines' lifespan.
Russia destroyed last of Kherson's heat and power equipment on 26 August. Ukraine's new defence minister arrived days later. Yevhenii Khmara met the regional governor days after glide bombs wrecked the city's power plant.
Ukraine has built twin-Kalashnikov turret for cheap ground robots. Security Service has already used one to destroy Russian ambushes. A Brave1 turret carries two AKs and went from idea to prototype in under six months.
Ukraine struck Tu-95 at base Russia launches its cruise missiles on Ukraine's civilians. Satellite image shows third of right wing gone. SBU Alpha struck the strategic bomber at Engels-2.
Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital's civilian supply chains. Russian jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck warehouses, businesses and logistics facilities around the capital, disrupting supplies while rescuers work under threat of further attacks.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine's intelligence: Russia is running its Nepal, Cuba, Kenya, and India recruitment scheme in Indonesia now. Ukraine's foreign intelligence says it holds documents on at least eight recruited Indonesian citizens.
Partisans say Russian recruiters in occupied Donetsk are taking drunk men from bars straight to enlistment offices. An ATESH agent inside the Dnepr grouping headquarters reports a new scheme.
Russians bought $300 million in body armor, thermal sights, and drone parts on Ozon marketplace Ukraine is bombing. Russians bought 157,700 body armour vests there.
International
After CIA head's visit to Moscow, Poland's PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months. Poland's prime minister says there are signals of serious Russian preparation.
Ukraine dismissed its defence minister in July. He is now advising NATO country on defence innovation. Guido Crozetto called the dismissed Ukrainian minister the day after Kyiv let him go.
From the Gripen sale to coast guard boats: Sweden sends 10 vessels to Ukraine. Ukraine's emergency service will use the boats for waterborne rescue work, including clearing mines from river beds. Stockholm's contributions to the US-led PURL programme now total $552 million.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture. More than 60,000 books were destroyed in a single warehouse strike near Kyiv this week, adding to losses that publishers say are becoming impossible to absorb.
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi says the country faces no threat of famine, but warns stores could see a narrower range of products.
Political and legal developments
What does Ukraine's new defence minister wear on his wrist? He did not mention it until reporter asked. Yevhenii Khmara's bracelet carries the names of fallen comrades, a US magazine reported.
"Territory that will allow us to export our energy resources to Europe": Russia's deputy Duma chairman calls for massed bombing of Ukrainian cities. Duma vice-speaker Pyotr Tolstoy said the aim is to demoralise civilians until they give up.

articles.title: China will stop Russia from going nuclear, Finland’s Stubb says
articles.body:
Alexander Stubb on his arrival for a dinner hosted on the occasion of the Summit of the Coalition of the Willing to Support Ukraine at the Elysee Presidential Palace in Paris on July 13, 2026. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
China has privately assured Finland that it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in an interview.
Speaking exclusively with Paul Ronzheimer of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Stubb was emphatic when asked whether Russia could resort to nuclear weapons, arguing that Beijing provides a powerful brake on Moscow escalating its war in Ukraine.
“I had the foreign minister of China visiting me this summer, and I raised the issue,” Stubb said. “And he said, we will never allow it to happen. And I think that’s a pretty good deterrence.”
Advertisement
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met Stubb in Helsinki on July 5, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and European security among the issues discussed. China remains one of Moscow’s most important economic and diplomatic partners.
Stubb also argued that Moscow benefits from keeping Europeans fixated on the prospect of nuclear escalation or a direct attack on NATO.
“Russia wants us Europeans to sit here and discuss: Will Russia escalate? Will Russia use nuclear weapons? Will Russia attack NATO and Europe?” the Finnish leader said.
His prescription was characteristically restrained: “Stay calm, stay cool, stay collected, stay vigilant. Don’t dramatize, prepare for the worst in order to avoid it.”
That measured tone is familiar from Stubb. In May, after a drone entered Finnish airspace near Helsinki and fighter jets were deployed, he insisted Finland was “not facing any direct military threat.”
In the interview, he similarly played down fears of an imminent Russian assault on NATO, describing Moscow’s attempts to probe the alliance as “more like teasing” than preparation for war. Russia’s troops remain tied down in Ukraine, he said, while NATO’s deterrence makes a direct attack highly unlikely.
Advertisement
But Stubb also argued that Europe is approaching the point when it should reopen direct political dialogue with Moscow — a notable call from the president of a country that shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia and joined NATO after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“I’m sure we are approaching the day when it would be useful for Europeans to be in more direct contact with Russia,” he said, “especially because we need to avoid misunderstanding.”
Europe is “not there yet,” Stubb stressed, with the immediate priority remaining support for Ukraine.
“You can’t sort of press mute. You have to open the discussion,” he added.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

articles.title: Russia’s 80-Missile Nuclear Battlecruiser Set to Return After Nearly 30 Years in Repair
articles.body:
- Category

Russia’s 80-Missile Nuclear Battlecruiser Set to Return After Nearly 30 Years in Repair
Russia’s nuclear-powered missile cruiser Admiral Nakhimov is nearing the end of trials after spending almost three decades undergoing repairs and modernization, potentially bringing an 80-cell missile platform back into active service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on August 30, the Project 1144 Orlan-class cruiser is completing factory and sea trials. Russian reports cited by the outlet indicate that state trials are expected to take place before the end of 2026, ahead of the ship’s planned return to the Russian Navy.
Admiral Nakhimov entered Soviet Navy service in 1988. The vessel was transferred to a repair facility in July 1997, although its overhaul was formally recorded as beginning in August 1999. If the cruiser returns to operational service as planned, it will have spent close to 30 years inactive, under repair, or undergoing modernization.
The prolonged program has also come at significant cost. Defense Express reported that current Russian estimates put the modernization bill at more than 200 billion rubles, equivalent to approximately $2.3 billion at current exchange rates. Previous estimates cited by the outlet suggested the total cost could have reached as much as $5 billion.
A major element of the modernization is the cruiser’s expanded missile armament. Admiral Nakhimov is equipped with 80 vertical launch cells designed to accommodate Kalibr cruise missiles, Oniks anti-ship missiles, and Zircon hypersonic missiles.
According to Defense Express, this configuration would make Admiral Nakhimov the most heavily armed surface combatant in the Russian Navy in terms of its offensive missile capacity.
The ship also retains nuclear propulsion, giving it long endurance without the need for conventional refueling. Admiral Nakhimov is one of Russia’s Project 1144 Orlan nuclear-powered cruisers, known in NATO terminology as the Kirov class.
Defense Express noted that the concentration of substantial weapons and resources aboard a single vessel has raised questions among military observers about the operational value and vulnerability of such large warships in modern warfare.
The modernization comes as the role of large surface warships is being reassessed amid the growing use of relatively inexpensive unmanned systems at sea. Ukraine has repeatedly demonstrated the ability of naval drones and long-range weapons to strike Russian naval assets, particularly in and around temporarily occupied Crimea.

articles.title: “If We Have to Strike, We Will”: Russian Lawmaker Urges Nuclear Attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
“If We Have to Strike, We Will”: Russian Lawmaker Urges Nuclear Attack on Ukraine
A Russian lawmaker has openly called for the use of tactical nuclear weapons against Ukraine to force Kyiv to surrender, declaring that Moscow should have no hesitation about launching such a strike if it considers one necessary, The Moscow Times reported on August 30.
Alexei Zhuravlev, a member of Russia’s State Duma and leader of the Rodina party, argued that Russian forces should strike Ukraine with enough force to compel capitulation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We need to strike in such a way that the enemy understands that it must capitulate,” Zhuravlev said.
He then dismissed debate over whether Russia should use tactical nuclear weapons.
“There are discussions: can we use tactical nuclear weapons or can we not? Listen, there shouldn’t even be such a discussion! If necessary, we are obliged to use them…If we need to strike, we will strike. And that is not up for discussion,” Zhuravlev said.
The remarks represent another explicit nuclear threat from within Russia’s political establishment as Moscow’s war of aggression against Ukraine continues.
Zhuravlev’s comments do not amount to an announcement of Russian government policy or evidence that Moscow is preparing a nuclear strike.
They come, however, shortly after Bloomberg reported that people close to the Kremlin believe Russian leader Vladimir Putin is preparing for further escalation in Ukraine as diplomatic efforts remain stalled.
According to that reporting, a growing number of Russian officials have begun discussing the possibility that Putin could eventually resort to tactical nuclear weapons as a last resort if Russia faced the prospect of defeat.
Bloomberg stressed that there were no indications that Russia was currently preparing to use a nuclear weapon in Ukraine.
Previously, Russia used its newest 9M723-2 ballistic missile, commonly referred to as the Iskander-1000, against Kyiv for the first time during a combined attack on the Ukrainian capital this summer.
Its most significant changes are a larger rocket motor and a correspondingly enlarged launcher. HUR says those modifications increase the missile’s maximum strike range to around 550 kilometers, compared with approximately 390 kilometers for the 9M723-1 variant.

articles.title: Middle East Live: US strikes Iran for first time in a month, Tehran retaliates
articles.body:
Middle East Live: Trump threatens to ‘hit Iran hard’ as strikes resume after month-long lull
President Donald Trump said Monday that the US would hit back against Iranian attacks on US targets in the Middle East, according to a Fox News reporter. The Iranian attacks were themselves a response to US strikes on an island in the Strait of Hormuz, the first flare-up in a month. Follow our live blog for the latest updates.
Bessent says goal of US sanctions is to get Iran to 'come to the table'
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in an interview on Monday that the goal of US sanctions on Iran is "to create the conditions that they will want to come to the table" for negotiations.
Lebanon urges Greece to help implement truce with Israel
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun asked Greece on Monday for support to help implement a ceasefire agreement with Israel and end Israeli attacks on his country, hours after Greece and Israel announced a multibillion arms deal.
The June 26 accord, brokered by the US, says both sides must cease hostilities and allow the Lebanese army to restore control over the entire country.
Beirut wants Israel to withdraw from all territory it has occupied in southern Lebanon. Israel first wants Lebanese militant group Hezbollah evacuated from the sector.
Greece has historically maintained cordial relations with Arab states while simultaneously developing strong military ties with Israel.
Senior Iranian source says latest hostilities with US are a 'limited' confrontation
Hostilities that flared overnight between the United States and Iran remain a "limited and contained confrontation", a senior Iranian source told Reuters on Monday, adding that Tehran was ready to deliver a harsh response if attacked again.
The source, who has direct knowledge of Iranian decision-making and declined to be named, said that conditions in the Strait of Hormuz "will become worse for vessels that violate" rules set by Tehran for passage through the waterway, adding that no target in the region was beyond Tehran's reach.
Trump says US will respond to Iranian attacks on US targets
President Donald Trump said Monday that the US will hit back against Iranian attacks on US targets in the Middle East, as the war flared after a prolonged pause, according to Fox News.
"We're going to hit them hard," Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who said he talked to Trump briefly.
"There will be a response," Trump said after Iranian attacks which were themselves a response to American strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.
US denies hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
The US military said on Monday that no ships had hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran's claim that a supertanker struck two mines in the area was false.
Iranian state TV, citing a statement by the Revolutionary Guards, had earlier reported that a supertanker caught fire and came to a complete halt after striking two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz.
US says Iran is lashing out amid economic pressure of sanctions
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that Iran is taking the US sanctions on it seriously and is lashing out now because it is losing economically.
"I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically," he told reporters at a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in North Carolina.
Relentless heat worsens Gaza's ongoing struggle to access water
In Gaza, securing drinking water is a relentless daily struggle. The war with Israel has destroyed critical water and sanitation infrastructure, and as temperatures soar, the extreme heat is escalating an already severe shortage into a deadly humanitarian crisis.
Two and a half years of war have damaged or destroyed nearly 90% of Gaza’s water and sanitation infrastructure, according to UNICEF.
Iran state media says US attack on island in Strait of Hormuz killed two people
The US attack on Iran's Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz killed two people and wounded several others, Iranian state media reported.
"During the attack on Larak Island late Sunday, two people were martyred and several others were injured. The injured in the incident are receiving medical services and their treatment is ongoing," said the official IRNA news agency, quoting Hossein Amir Teymouri, governor of nearby Qeshm Island, without specifying whether the victims were soldiers or civilians.
Iran's Pezeshkian says Tehran still seeking negotiated solution to conflict with US
Tehran still seeks a negotiated solution to its conflict with the United States, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, according to semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Pezeshkian told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, that continued war was in no one's interest and that dialogue and cooperation were the way to resolve existing problems.
Oil prices rise as US launches fresh attacks on Iran
Oil prices were trading nearly 2 percent higher on Monday after the US attacked Iran's Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz and drew retaliation from Tehran.
Brent crude futures climbed $1.77, or 2 percent, to $89.87 a barrel by 0733 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $84.85, up $1.45, or 1.74 percent.
US President Donald Trump also claimed in a brief social media post on Sunday that Iran's energy hub of Kharg Island was being "blown to smithereens", but there was no evidence that the island was under attack and the post, accompanied by an AI-generated clip, contained no further details.
Iran denied the attack on the island, adding that oil operations continued.
Israel signs three-billion-euro arms export deal with Greece
Israel's defence ministry announced it had signed a deal with Athens worth approximately three billion euros to set up an "Achilles Shield" aerial defence system for Greece.
"Under the deal, Israel will build Greece a comprehensive, multi-layered air defence array, drawing entirely on Israeli-made systems and on the extensive operational experience Israel's defence establishment has gained during the war," the ministry said in a statement, adding that "this is the largest defence export deal in the history of Israel-Greece relations, and one of the largest in the history of the State of Israel".
UAE presidential adviser says Iran's policy of targeting Gulf states has failed
The policy of targeting Gulf Arab states and Jordan has failed, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said in a post on X on Monday.
"A state of neither war nor peace cannot be a sustainable solution," Gargash said, adding realistic political solutions should begin with de-escalation and the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
UAE denies claim Iran targeted base hosting US forces
The United Arab Emirates denied claims that Tehran targeted a base housing US personnel with missiles, after announcing it had intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters.
"Media reports regarding a missile attack on Al Minhad Air Base are baseless," the Emirati defence ministry said in a statement on X.
Earlier on Monday, Iran had said it targeted the base using "dozens of attack drones".
Iran denies US attack on Kharg Island, calls Trump's post 'laughable', Nournews reports
Oil operations at Iran's Kharg Island have not stopped, National Iranian Oil Company CEO Hamid Bovard said, according to Nournews. Bovard reportedly denied the key oil hub was being destroyed, as US President Donald Trump had earlier claimed in a social media post.
"Trump's tweets are laughable and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate," Nournews cited him as saying, adding that the island, from which 90 percent of Iranian oil exports originate, had been bombed repeatedly by US and Israeli forces in the past, but oil workers had not allowed operations to stop "even for a moment".
Contractors were currently rebuilding and modernising storage tanks and jetties, he added.
UAE says it dealt with a drone coming from Iran over its waters
The United Arab Emirates said it had dealt with a drone over its territorial waters coming from Iran, after Tehran claimed an attack on a US base in the Gulf country.
"The Ministry of Defence announced that the UAE Air Force responded to a UAV detected over the country's territorial waters, approaching from Iran," the ministry said in a statement on X.
Supertanker hits mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say
A supertanker caught fire and was brought to a complete halt after being struck by two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz, Iran state TV reported, citing a statement by the Revolutionary Guards.
The Guards said the tanker had been attempting to pass through the waterway illegally. It did not identify the vessel or provide information about its crew.
The Guards warned that other ships violating its security rules would face the same fate and said compliance with its regulations for passage through the Strait of Hormuz was mandatory.
Iran says it struck US bases in Jordan used to support Larak attack
Iran's armed forces struck US military bases in Jordan in response to a US attack on Larak Island, the Iranian foreign ministry said in a statement.
The ministry said the US bases in Jordan had been used to launch and support the attack on Larak that killed and wounded members of Iran's armed forces and civilians.
It said Iran would respond decisively to further military aggression and stressed that the US and parties supporting its actions bore full responsibility for any escalation.
Iran’s army says it attacked UAE’s Al Minhad Air Base with drones, state TV reports
Iran's army said it attacked the United Arab Emirates' Al Minhad Air Base with drones, Iranian state TV reported, citing a statement from the army.
The army said the attack targeted locations where US forces and helicopters were stationed at the base.
It said the attack was in response to the killing of Iran's Revolutionary Guards and Iranian civilians on Larak Island.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they shot down a US drone over Strait of Hormuz
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz with air defence missiles, causing it to crash into Gulf waters, the Mehr news agency reported on Monday, citing an IRGC statement.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Why the Baltics are pushing back against new fears of a Russian attack
articles.body:
Officials across NATO’s eastern flank say there is no evidence of an imminent Russian attack, even as they strengthen their defences and warn that Moscow’s campaign of sabotage and provocations against Europe is intensifying.
Nearly a week after CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow fuelled fears that Russia could be preparing to test NATO, European officials are pushing back against suggestions that a conventional attack might be imminent.
From Finland and Romania to the Baltic states, governments say there is no evidence Moscow is preparing for a direct confrontation with NATO – even as they continue strengthening their defences and warn of a growing Russian threat.
Officials across NATO’s eastern flank argue that preparing for Russian aggression is not the same as expecting it.
John Hardie, deputy director of the Russia Program at the US-based Foundation for Defence of Democracies, told Euronews that Ratcliffe may have been delivering several messages in Moscow.
“My own view is that a conventional Russian military attack against a NATO member remains highly unlikely, especially while the Ukraine war continues,” Hardie said. "However, even while that scenario remains unlikely overall, there are reasons to see the risk ticking up a bit."
“The Iran war has reduced US readiness, while the Trump administration has sowed doubt regarding US political will to defend Europe. In recent months, we've seen intrusions into NATO airspace that could have been intended to probe our response.”
Hardie also said US officials may also be worried about what Putin could do if he feels “frustrated or cornered” in Ukraine, although he saw a second round of Russian mobilisation as a more likely response.
No imminent attack, but better be ready
Hardie’s assessment broadly mirrors what European leaders are saying publicly.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb dismissed predictions that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO country within the next few years.
“If anyone has a crystal ball like that – that’s great. I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” Stubb told Germany’s Bild newspaper over the weekend, adding that the intelligence available to him supported his assessment.
“It makes no sense for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance.”
Nonetheless, Finland is strengthening its defences along its 1,340-kilometre border with Russia, while Sweden has granted a request from Helsinki to send Gripen fighter jets and a naval vessel to support Finland’s territorial surveillance along the border.
Finnish officials see no contradiction: greater military preparedness is intended to deter Russia and guard against drones, airspace violations and other forms of escalation, not brace for an impending attack.
Romania has offered a similar assessment. Defence Minister Radu Miruță told Romanian broadcaster Digi24 on Sunday that Bucharest and its allies were constantly sharing intelligence, with “no indication” that Russia intended to attack a NATO member.
“I don’t think Russia has any intention to attack a NATO member country,” Miruță said.
Romania shares a 614-kilometre border with Ukraine and has repeatedly seen Russian drones cross into its territory.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was more explicit still, saying in a statement on X that the country's military threat level had not changed and the risk of a direct Russian invasion remained low.
Latvia nevertheless remains on heightened alert for cyber attacks, sabotage, provocations and drones, while strengthening its eastern border alongside NATO allies.
“Readiness for a possible threat is not the same as an immediate threat,” Kulbergs said. “These two things must not be confused.”
Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia are among NATO’s biggest military spenders relative to the size of their economies.
When ‘hybrid’ warfare is already war
Poland has struck a more cautious tone.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said after a briefing from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte this weekend that “the escalation from Russia’s side is progressing”.
“We cannot rule out provocations from Russia against one of NATO’s members,” Tusk said. “The next six months will be decisive, and we must be prepared as Poland and NATO for various scenarios.”
His warning points to another dimension of Europe’s threat assessment: while a conventional attack may not be imminent, Russian aggression is already taking other forms.
European governments have accused Moscow of cyber attacks, sabotage and other hostile operations across the continent, while Russian aircraft and drones have repeatedly violated NATO airspace.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna argued on X that calling activities like these “hybrid warfare” understates the threat.
Responding to comments by Estonia’s foreign intelligence chief Kaupo Rosin, Tsahkna wrote: “Enough with the euphemisms. Putin’s campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe is not ‘hybrid warfare’. It is state-sponsored terrorism. Call it what it is.”
Hardie also said such Russian actions were already taking place.
“As for aggressive acts below the threshold of open war, such as arson against European defence plants, those are already occurring and have been for years now, but to limited strategic effect,” he told Euronews.
“Moscow does have options to escalate in this area, but doing so is unlikely to achieve much greater impact and could perversely produce blowback.”

articles.title: The Trump-shaped problems awaiting Andy Burnham, ranked
articles.body:
LONDON — Andy Burnham spent most of his first 42 days as prime minister in his comfort zone, talking about jobs, living costs, homelessness and shifting power out of London.
Now he’s got to look beyond his own borders. As parliament returns from its six-week summer break on Tuesday, Britain’s new leader faces a towering in-tray of decisions that will affect his relations overseas, especially with Donald Trump.
British officials are preparing for the prospect of his first face-to-face meeting with the U.S. president in late September after Burnham confirmed his intention to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Downing Street is privately exploring the possibility that he visits the White House on the same trip, depending on Trump’s availability.
Advertisement
Burnham has played down the jeopardy, but he also promised to “say what I feel.” He has the advantage of having seen his predecessor Keir Starmer try to please Trump, only to be hectored relentlessly on Truth Social. Like Italy’s Giorgia Meloni or Canada’s Mark Carney, Burnham may sense a political advantage in not kissing the ring.
A visit will still tie him up in diplomacy, however; tricky for a man who wants to keep his focus at home rather than engaging in the geopolitical wrangling for which voters gave Starmer little credit. It will also come days before his first Labour conference as leader, where some of his party faithful oppose oil and gas drilling and want him to take a harder line against Israeli settlements.
POLITICO runs through a few of the Trump-shaped headaches awaiting Burnham, informed by conversations with more than a dozen U.K. government political aides, civil servants and ministers who were all granted anonymity to speak frankly.
Oil and gas drilling
The U.K. is inching closer to a politically fraught decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in two of the North Sea’s last major untapped fields.
An oil rig is seen through the mist on the Cromarty Firth on the north-east coast of Scotland on April 24, 2026. | Andy Buchanan/AFP via Getty Images
The Jackdaw gas field received initial approval in 2022, while the Rosebank oil field was green-lit in 2023. Further consultation due to a legal tussle over their environmental impacts ended in mid-August and Whitehall and industry officials expect a final decision in September. Jackdaw operator Adura has claimed gas could start flowing from Oct. 1.
Burnham — who pledged to give voters “breathing space” on the cost of living, yet is watching unrest in the Middle East push up energy bills — has spent his summer dropping positive hints about the projects, painting North Sea drilling as a “bridge to a renewable future.” He indicated similarly to Trump, who has repeatedly urged Britain to get drilling.
Advertisement
Yet the Green Party surged in opinion polls earlier this year and almost three quarters of England is in drought, after a summer that is on track to be the U.K.’s hottest on record.
A person with knowledge of the planning said the North Sea decision, which will be taken on a quasi-judicial basis by Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, is not expected this week. (One senior figure close to Burnham insisted the timing was “definitely not” tied to the optics of the dry summer, despite some MPs suspecting as such.)
When it does come, the U.S. president is likely to see it as a test of Britain’s priorities. One U.K. official said senior figures in Trump’s administration “really don’t understand” the hesitancy.
Trump Danger Rating: 4/5
Defense spending
Burnham’s new finance minister John Healey quit as Starmer’s defense secretary to demand that military spending accelerates to 3 percent of GDP by 2030 (on the road to hit a Trump-pleasing 3.5 percent by 2035).
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey plays a game of table tennis on a visit to Kiln Park Holiday Centre on August 27, 2026 in Tenby. | Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
Now he has the job of chancellor, Healey has refused to make that guarantee — and will leave the issue dangling well into next year. Healey will not set a target date for reaching 3 percent in his Oct. 28 budget, a British government official confirmed, and will instead name it as part of a cross-government spending review in 2027.
Advertisement
Conservative opponents seized on Healey’s indecision Friday, arguing he “is backtracking on the very pledge which sealed the fate of the last PM.” Whether Trump will choose to single out Britain is another matter; the president has taken a fairly equal-opportunities approach to berating NATO allies over their spending and many other nations rank below the U.K.
Healey is attending this week’s meeting of G20 finance ministers in the U.S., which could prove an early test of whether the issue is cutting through.
Trump Danger Rating: 3/5
Israeli settlements
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has promised a “comprehensive” U.K. response to Israel’s E1 settlement in the West Bank, risking a confrontation with the U.S. administration.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband listens as he meets with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Department of State in Washington on August 5, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
Two officials said Miliband is expected to make a statement to parliament in the next two weeks on the E1 project, which he has branded “unacceptable and destructive.” One senior Labour figure said they expected him to announce sanctions on Israeli settlements, though the Foreign Office has declined to comment on any future action. Miliband is separately due at regular questions in parliament on Tuesday.
His intervention will be fresh for two audiences: UNGA and then the party conference in Liverpool, at which grassroots members call for Labour to go further.
Advertisement
One minister said Burnham would want to “put his stamp” on foreign affairs due to the political salience of the Middle East. The senior Labour figure quoted above argued Miliband should wait six weeks until Knesset elections on Oct. 27, but one of two U.K. officials quoted above said: “They don’t want to go into Labour conference with this hanging around.”
A hostile reaction from Israel is inevitable, but it’s less certain how Trump will respond. The U.K. has consistently gone further than the U.S.; Starmer used UNGA last year to recognize a Palestinian state.
Israeli soldiers arrive at the scene where Israeli settlers occupy a Palestinian building under construction in the village of Qusra, south of the city of Nablus on August 29, 2026. | Jaafar Ashtiyeh/AFP via Getty Images
Burnham picked Ukraine for his first foreign trip, saying it “particularly” affected his intention to travel to UNGA, and will meet French President Emmanuel Macron in London this week. The prime minister is considering a meeting of European and other non-U.S. leaders in the “Coalition of the Willing” to coincide with the New York summit.
The new PM is not trying to be a global fixer like Starmer but he faces the same challenges. Burnham said he wants to help solve Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors, many of which are being hoovered up by the conflict between the U.S. and Iran.
Advertisement
Britain has little to fear about Trump’s rhetoric or actions against the U.K. itself, but the president’s actions in both volatile conflicts will have knock-on effects for Britain’s economy. One person who works on U.K. foreign policy said civil servants believe “the Ukraine trip was a bit of an awakening” for Burnham, while a U.K. official claimed Burnham’s team “appear a little blindsided” by the scale of the Iran conflict’s impact.
Some Whitehall officials had low expectations that Burnham would attend UNGA — Conservative PM Rishi Sunak skipped the summit in 2023 — until he told reporters last Monday that he was “likely” to go. At that moment the intensity of planning ramped up, said two Whitehall officials.
Supporters and members of the British Indian Ocean territory Chagos Archipelago hold placards and the territory’s flag outside the Houses of Parliament in London on January 7, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images
The story of both wars has been one of Britain and its allies forming coalitions to nudge the U.S. to a more favorable position, with only mixed success and, as yet, no resolution. Britain’s position is not entirely comfortable in the meantime; Burnham has continued a policy (agreed under Starmer) of allowing the U.S. to use British bases to launch “defensive” strikes on Iran.
Trump Danger Rating: 4/5
Chagos Islands
Burnham has inherited a controversial deal, agreed under Starmer, to hand the sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius — while leasing back a U.K.-U.S. joint military base on the Indian Ocean archipelago.
Three U.K. government officials said the deal itself — negotiated and backed personally by No. 10 national security adviser Jonathan Powell — is unlikely to change to appease Trump, leaving it in limbo unless the president changes his mind. “If there were easy additional baubles to provide, they would have been found by now,” said one of the three officials.
Yet this hold-up is causing tension with Mauritius, which was due a windfall in the deal and could press the U.K. to move at UNGA. It also affects wider diplomatic relations since the deal is backed by India, whose trade deal with Britain took effect a few weeks ago.
Trump Danger Rating: 2/5
Tech and trade
Burnham has inherited a complex web of deals that Starmer’s government secured (and in some cases, later un-secured) with the U.S.
These include the “economic prosperity deal” announced in May 2025, which secured lower tariffs for the U.K. than some other countries, including on steel and cars. But elements which had been due for negotiation at a later date remain in the ether. Those include the implementation of a U.K.-U.S. deal on pharmaceutical trade, which has implications for NHS spending on drugs (Britain agreed to spend more in order to get the deal over the line).
Less advanced is the “tech prosperity deal” that both sides hailed in 2025 but was then paused by the U.S. administration. Talks over nuclear fusion energy have resumed while separate tracks on AI and quantum co-operation remain stalled.
Advertisement
One U.K. official said talks could continue at an official level with little involvement from Burnham and Trump. “There is more to do” on both the trade deal, which is “imperfect but better than anyone else’s,” they said, while the tech prosperity deal gave a framework to build on. They added: “It’s a different phase of the relationship. It’s less shuttling over to Washington all the time … it’s not the same sort of theater, needing to be in the Oval constantly, in the way that Starmer had to be.”
One stumbling block: the U.K.’s digital services tax, which has drawn Trump’s repeated ire and raised more than £1 billion last year, much of it from U.S. tech firms. A spokesperson for Burnham’s government said “we remain open to discussing U.S. concerns,” but the U.K. has reiterated its commitment to the tax until a multilateral solution can be found.
Another stumbling block: Burnham wants closer ties with the EU ahead of a summit between Brussels and London this fall. British alignment with EU food standards has previously caused tension with the U.S. administration.
Trump Danger Rating: 3/5
Miliband on the world stage
A wild card in all this is Burnham’s pick for foreign secretary: Ed Miliband.
An outspoken former Labour leader who missed his shot at becoming prime minister in 2015, Miliband had coveted Healey’s job of chancellor. Instead he is set to use the foreign office to press Britain’s economic case on the world stage. That inevitably includes his long-held support of net zero, which rankles some in the U.S. administration.
Advertisement
He has personally taken the U.K.’s seat on the World Bank board, instead of a junior minister, and officials believe he would likely attend New York Climate Week (at the same time as UNGA), along with the COP31 climate summit in November. Trump has a habit of deciding individual politicians are beyond the pale. So far, though, the relationship appears to be functioning well enough; he met U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 90 minutes of talks in early August in Washington D.C.
Trump Danger Rating: 2/5
Reparations
One summit looms in November without the U.S.: the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), presided over by King Charles III and attended by the U.K. alongside 55 other countries, most of them former colonies.
The location of Antigua and Barbuda means calls for reparations for the slave trade — which dominated the last CHOGM in Samoa — will inevitably come up.
If Burnham were to attend, it would test how a PM who forged his politics campaigning for justice — including for victims of the 1989 Hillsborough stadium crush, and patients given infected blood products in the U.K. — responds to a call that the U.K. government has long said it cannot afford.
It’s not such an issue for Trump, though. The U.S. president might barely notice the summit is happening.

articles.title: U.S. Strikes Iran in First Military Action in a Month
articles.body:
U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, according to the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), marking the first publicly confirmed strike on Iran in weeks.
CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed in a statement to TIME the strikes on the launchers on Larak Island, adding that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the strait.
Last week, U.S. forces finished clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
“U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” Hawkins added.
Iran attacks US bases in Jordan
Axios later reported, citing a U.S. official, that Iran launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan in retaliation for the strikes. Jordan’s armed forces said it intercepted eight missiles that entered the country’s airspace early Monday morning.
Iranian state news agency IRNA carried a statement from the Revolutionary Guards issued soon after the U.S. strikes saying that Iran will respond to the attacks on Larak Island “with punishment for the aggressor”.
In a statement, CENTCOM rebuffed the Revolutionary Guards’ claims, describing the Sunday attack as “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat” to the strait.
Before the Sunday strikes, the last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, announcing a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including command centers, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defense sites.
On Aug. 1, President Donald Trump said that he agreed to “hold off” strikes in Iran at the request of the U.S.’s regional allies in the Middle East.
How the U.S.-Iran war began
The strikes mark the latest escalation in the war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched a wave of attacks across Iran. Trump described the operation as a “massive and ongoing” campaign intended to eliminate what he called imminent threats from the Iranian regime and openly encouraged Iranians to overthrow their government.
The attacks came after U.S.-Iranian negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program failed to produce an agreement and amid the Iranian government’s deadly crackdown on nationwide protests. Trump had accused Iran of rebuilding its nuclear capabilities following U.S. and Israeli strikes on three major Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025. Iran has consistently denied seeking a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening salvo of the Feb. 28 campaign. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at Israel, U.S. military bases and other sites across the Middle East, widening the conflict throughout the region.
The war also led Iran to militarize and largely close the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy transit routes, through which about a fifth of global oil production typically passed before the hostilities.
A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports was lifted under a June agreement, but Trump reimposed it after that deal and its accompanying cease-fire fell apart.

articles.title: Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans
articles.body:
Ukraine has four potential interceptor systems that could shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on 30 August, according to Suspilne.
Russia has sharply increased its use of the faster drones against Ukrainian cities, causing major damage to civilian infrastructure and many civilian casualties. The attacks are putting near-unprecedented strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
All four interceptor systems have undergone field testing, Khmara said. Ukraine now aims to bring them to the required level as quickly as possible and scale production to thousands of units.
“The search for countermeasures against jet-powered drones continues,” Khmara told journalists, according to Suspilne. “There are already four potential interceptors that can shoot down jet-powered ‘Shaheds.’ Field tests have already been conducted on them.”
Russia is rapidly expanding Geran attacks
Russia's Gerans are jet-powered adaptations of the Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones that Russia has produced domestically throughout the full-scale war. The faster Geran variants give Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect and engage them.
Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said Russia used more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans against Ukraine in August, up from about 1,500 in July.
He also said the drones are being launched against Ukraine almost directly from Russian factories, highlighting the rapid expansion of their production and use.
Zelenskyy calls for faster production
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made countering the Gerans a priority as Russia sustains repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities.
At a 28 August meeting of Ukraine’s military leadership, Zelenskyy said the country needed to maximize domestic weapons production, with the immediate focus on defending against jet-powered Gerans and increasing Ukraine’s own long-range strikes against Russia.
“[The] main thing is our defense against jet-powered ‘Shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said in his evening address.
He said Russia had adopted a tactic of keeping Kyiv and other cities under repeated air raid alerts, with Gerans reaching the capital as well as cities including Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.
Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies
“All our means of countering [them] are already being used,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine needs a significant acceleration in production of interceptors specifically designed for the jet-powered drones.
Khmara said the four potential interceptors are now at the field-testing stage, with the next step being to bring them into production at a scale of thousands of units.
For Ukraine, that scale is critical. The country must defend a large territory against increasingly large Russian drone barrages while also preserving limited air-defense resources for ballistic and other missiles that require more advanced interceptors.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Four Interceptors to Counter Jet-Powered Geran Drones
articles.body:
Ukraine has conducted field tests of four interceptor drones designed to counter jet-powered Geran drones.
LB reported on this, citing Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
“The search for ways to counter jet-powered drones is ongoing. There are already four potential interceptors that can shoot down jet-powered Shaheds,” the Minister shared.
According to him, the immediate task is to bring these solutions to the required level as quickly as possible and scale up production to thousands of units.
Recently, it was reported that production of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type kamikaze drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, had surpassed production of Geran-2 strike drones equipped with conventional internal-combustion engines.
This was likely achieved by redirecting part of Russia’s production capacity to manufacturing jet-powered drones.
A substantial and gradual increase in Russia’s use of jet-powered drones began to be recorded in early 2026. By April, 15–20% of the Shaheds Russia launched were equipped with jet engines.
As of early June, Russian forces had launched 1,400 jet-powered UAVs, compared with only 180 such cases recorded by Ukraine’s Defense Forces throughout 2025.
However, since the first weeks of summer, the Defense Forces have recorded a significant increase in Russia’s use of jet-powered Shaheds, substantially increasing the burden on Ukrainian air defense units and aviation.
It was recently reported that the jet-powered Alexa Spatium interceptor had been accepted into service with Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones are among the newest members of this Russian family. Despite sharing the same designation, their designs differ substantially.
The Geran-4 builds on the concept of the Geran-3 jet-powered drone. Its fuselage is optimized for higher-speed flight, and the drone has a more powerful engine.
The drone has a wingspan of about 3 meters and a length of 3.5 meters, matching the previous version’s dimensions. At the same time, its maximum takeoff weight has increased from 350 to 450 kilograms.
The Geran-4 is equipped with a Chinese turbojet engine producing 160 kgf of thrust, twice that of the Chinese Telefly JT80 engine installed on the Geran-3. This has increased its cruising speed from 280-330 to 350-500 km/h and its range from 600 to 850 kilometers.
The drone can fly at altitudes ranging from 100 to 5,000 meters, with an endurance of about 2.5 hours. Its warhead weighs at least 50 kilograms.
The Geran-5 has a fundamentally different design. Its developers abandoned the aerodynamic configuration characteristic of earlier models.
The fuselage shape makes the new aircraft resemble a cruise missile more than a Shahed-type drone with a delta wing. The drone is equipped with a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A jet engine producing 200 kgf of thrust.
The Geran-5 carries a 90-kilogram warhead, while its stated strike range is about 1,000 kilometers.

articles.title: Iran, US trade strikes for 1st time in month to reignite Mideast war
articles.body:
Iran struck U.S. military targets in the Middle East Monday after American attacks targeted its territory for first time in a month, escalating a war that has roiled the region.
Tehran's powerful Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said they had responded to Sunday's American attack by striking two U.S. air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing "heavy damage."
Jordan's army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
Tehran also claimed it targeted U.S. military personnel at an air base in the United Arab Emirates and shot down a U.S. drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
The flurry of attacks came after the United States said Sunday it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the small island of Larak in the strategic shipping lane.
Washington said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from placing more sea mines in the strait, days after the U.S. announced it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
"U.S. forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz," the U.S. military's Central Command wrote on X.
Iran's Guards said the U.S. strikes resulted in "casualties" and that their subsequent attack on Jordan was "in response to the U.S.-Zionist aerial aggression."
The Iranian Foreign Ministry condemned the U.S. attacks on Larak and justified the Jordan strikes as "legitimate defense."
"We are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors," added Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in a statement quoted by state TV.
Pezeshkian was speaking before traveling to Kyrgyzstan for a summit of a bloc that seeks to counter influence from the West, along with Russia's President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping.
The exchange of fire between the United States and Iran came shortly after their war hit its six-month mark and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
In recent weeks, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has prioritized "economic warfare" over military strikes.
Tehran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic sea lane through which one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the U.S. and Israel triggered the war with strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
"Last week, CENTCOM completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes," said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for U.S. Central Command.
"U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway," he said.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators, including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war.
While a cease-fire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding toward a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming, and Washington has since declared "economic warfare" against Tehran.
A U.S. naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran during a shortfall in domestic production.
The April cease-fire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks – mainly around the Strait of Hormuz – have dimmed prospects for a final peace agreement.
The last U.S. strike on Iran before Sunday came on July 29 in response to "an attempted surprise attack on U.S. forces" in the region, the U.S. military said. Earlier in July, CENTCOM attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights.
Throughout the war, Iran has fought back by striking U.S. facilities and allies in the Gulf region, hitting targets in Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others.
Its closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused pain around the world in the form of price hikes and shortages of fertilizer and energy.
Both main crude oil contracts rose at least 2% Monday.
The war is also deeply unpopular with the U.S. public, with midterm elections looming in November that could overturn Republican control of Congress.
In a statement on Friday, U.S. Senator Jack Reed criticised Trump over the war.
"Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved," said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
"Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly."

articles.title: FT: Musk willing to allow Starlink to be used in Russia, but needs Trump's decision
articles.body:
FT: Musk willing to allow Starlink to be used in Russia, but needs Trump's decision
Billionaire Elon Musk has told former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov that he is willing to allow Ukraine to use Starlink systems beyond its borders but is awaiting a political decision.
Source: Financial Times, with reference to its own sources
Details: The FT's sources state that Musk had previously told Fedorov he was willing to allow Ukraine to use drones equipped with Starlink systems beyond its borders to strike Russian targets. However, according to these sources, Musk told Ukraine that this is a political decision that must be taken by the White House.
Fedorov declined to comment on his conversations with Musk.
Fedorov also stated that Ukraine's intensification of its long-range strikes against Russia is the most realistic way to force Russian leader Vladimir Putin to stop the war, but this requires additional investment in the weapons used for such strikes.
Background: During closed-door negotiations at the White House on 28 July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked for Ukraine to be granted permission to use the Starlink system on Russian territory to strike ballistic missile launchers.

articles.title: Russia Attacks Ukraine With Nearly 1,500 Drones in Four Days, Including 800 Jet-Powered UAVs
articles.body:
