Russia Attacks Ukraine With Nearly 1,500 Drones in Four Days, Including 800 Jet-Powered UAVs
Russia has launched nearly 1,500 drones of various types against Ukraine over the past four days, including around 800 jet-powered UAVs, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his evening address on August 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy, Russia’s current aerial attack tactics are aimed at exhausting Ukraine and its population through sustained waves of drone strikes.
“Our warriors shoot down a significant share of them. There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in these four days alone—around 800 of them jet-powered. The most difficult task is intercepting the jet-powered ones. Now, it is mainly our combat aircraft that protect against them,” the president stated.
Ukraine currently relies primarily on combat aircraft to counter such drones, according to Zelenskyy. At the same time, the country is working to expand the use of specialized interceptor drones as a less resource-intensive means of combating Russian UAVs.
Four Ukrainian companies have already developed interceptor systems designed for the task, Zelenskyy said, adding that one of the designs is currently demonstrating the strongest results.
The president called on Ukraine’s Defense Ministry and the military to expand the country’s capabilities as quickly as possible to intercept all types of Russian drones.
Zelenskyy also set a target for Ukraine’s air defenses to achieve an interception rate of more than 90% against Russian drones this fall, as Moscow continues to intensify its use of unmanned systems in attacks across the country.
The scale of the threat was evident during another large-scale Russian aerial assault on August 29, when Moscow combined ballistic and anti-ship missiles with waves of attack drones, including jet-powered UAVs.
During the overnight attack, Russian forces launched an Oniks anti-ship missile, an Iskander-M ballistic missile, and 267 attack drones across Ukraine.

Russia’s Defense Ministry says it is preparing large-scale strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities in response to Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure
Russia’s Defense Ministry said on its Telegram channel that, “in accordance with instructions received,” it has begun preparing massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities.

articles.title: US military attacked IRGC rocket launchers in Iran, senior official confirms
articles.body:
A senior U.S. official said Sunday evening that the U.S. military struck two Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rocket launchers on Larak Island. 
“The two launchers were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the Strait of Hormuz,” the official told Reuters and other news outlets. “Our forces have completed clearing mines from international shipping lanes, are closely monitoring the area and are prepared to defend the free flow of commerce through the strait.”
Iran’s Fars news agency reported that an explosion was heard near Larak Island in the strait.
The Tasnim news agency reported that according to "Preliminary, unofficial reports" two people were killed and two others were injured in the American attack.  
Shortly after the attack, the Revolutionary Guards threatened that "the enemy's terrorist act of aggression on Larak Island will be met with a response, and the aggressor will be punished."
"The American-Zionist enemy, once again driven by desperation in solving its internal problems and reducing its credibility among regional countries, seeks to revive its nefarious role and justify public opinion. In a blatant act of aggression, it attacked Larak Island, resulting in the martyrdom and injury of several of our soldiers and fellow citizens," the IRGC also said in a statement.
The Washington Post reported Sunday that senior U.S. military commanders had warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that large-scale operations against Iran could not be sustained over time, and that continuing to concentrate forces in the Middle East could impair the U.S. military’s ability to deal with threats elsewhere in the world, including defending the United States itself.
According to officials familiar with the classified assessment prepared for Hegseth, the warnings were delivered to the defense secretary by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, as well as commanders of U.S. forces responsible for Europe, Asia and Latin America. They were included in the August 14 edition of the “Secretary of Defense Orders Book,” a classified document detailing the availability of U.S. ships, aircraft, troops and weapons systems around the world that the Pentagon uses in making force-deployment decisions.
The strike in the strait came after about six months of fighting with Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump pressures Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept Washington’s terms for ending the conflict. Trump continues to make clear that all options remain on the table, including renewed strikes, and U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, has for months kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in case the president orders further military action.
According to the Post, some of the forces deployed to the Middle East have already been ordered to remain in the region through September, while others are expected to stay into 2027. The Air Force is also preparing for a prolonged presence: According to two officials who saw the document, many of the units sent to the Middle East for bombing missions and round-the-clock operations are expected to remain in the region into 2027.
The possibility that the deployments could be extended again prompted several senior commanders to voice explicit objections. The commanders of U.S. European Command, Indo-Pacific Command and Southern Command, along with the Navy’s top officer, submitted what the Pentagon calls a “non-concur” — meaning they oppose the defense secretary’s decision to extend the allocation of their forces to the campaign, though they would carry out the order if it remains in effect.

articles.title: EU preparations for State Duma election provocations, plans to null results — SVR
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Brussels has tasked Russia’s non-systemic opposition with staging provocations at polling stations in Russia and abroad, the press bureau of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said.
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) and the European Parliament are preparing statements refusing to recognize the results of Russia’s elections, it said.
TASS has compiled the SVR’s key statements.
EU plans to destabilize Russia
Western countries are actively preparing for elections in Russia, while the EU is implementing a large-scale strategy to destabilize the country. "According to the data coming to the SVR, the EU and leading European countries are implementing a large-scale strategy to destabilize the situation in Russia on the eve of the single day of voting this September."
Representatives of European security services discuss "plans to organize cyber-attacks on the elections infrastructure" in Russia during visits to Ukraine.
The West has mobilized "all the ‘weapons’ from the arsenal of anti-Russian aggression" to destabilize the country ahead of the elections.
Sabotage, provocations
Europeans aim to disrupt the normal electoral process in Russia and discredit the voting results. "European so-called advocates of lawfulness and democracy have set a twofold task for themselves: interfere with the normal electoral process and discredit the results of the expression of will on all levels of the electoral campaign."
Brussels has tasked Russia’s non-systemic opposition with staging provocations at polling stations in Russia and abroad. "During the recent events in Vilnius and Berlin the European buriers of democracy have set before the non-systemic opposition tasks on digging up dirt on members of systemic political parties, as well as staging provocations at polling stations within the Russian Federation and abroad."
The West has encouraged the Kiev regime to intensify sabotage and terrorist attacks on facilities in Russia. "On the margins of the July 13, 2026 Coalition of the Willing summit in Paris on creation of a new European missile defense system, the Europeans oriented the Kiev regime towards intensification of sabotage and terrorist attacks and strikes on facilities both in the liberated Russian territories and in the depth of Russia."
Plans not to recognize results
The West has tasked foreign-based non-systemic opposition groups with spreading claims about the "illegitimacy and unlawfulness" of elections in Russia. "Promulgation of assertions about ‘illegitimacy and unlawfulness’ of the voting - that hasn’t even taken place yet - has been assigned to foreign-based structures of the Russian non-systemic opposition."
PACE and the European Parliament are preparing statements refusing to recognize election results in Russia. "According to available information, upon completion of the electoral cycle, PACE and the European Parliament are preparing to release a statement on the non-recognition of the election results in Russia due to the ‘gross violations during their preparation and conduct.’"
Moscow’s response
Neither Kiev, Russophobic political emigres nor totalitarian-liberal Western circles will prevent Russia from holding State Duma elections. "Neither Ukraine, with the corrupt, ‘long overdue’ regime in power, nor Russophobic ‘political emigres’ torn away from the native soil, nor the totalitarian liberal Western circles standing behind them will prevent Russian citizens from making their choice."
Russia will repulse both external aggressors and attempts to undermine the country from within. "Russia is capable of repulsing the aggressors, not only on the external front, but also their hopeless attempts to sabotage our country from within."
Russian position
Russia’s adversaries are trying to intimidate Russians and disrupt the September elections, but the Kiev regime’s efforts are doomed to fail, Russian President Vladimir Putin said in an interview with Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin.
The Russian Foreign Ministry has urged Russians living abroad to remain vigilant and not yield to provocations ahead of State Duma elections.
Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a briefing that there remained a "high probability" that Russia’s adversaries abroad would stage extremist and protest actions to discredit the State Duma elections.
Voting in State Duma elections in unfriendly countries could be accompanied by various provocations and attempts to discredit the electoral process, Russian Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova said.
Extremist organizations and foreign agents are preparing to conduct fake voter polls abroad, near Russian embassies, on September 20 in order to claim in Western media that State Duma elections were rigged even before they end, Vasily Piskaryov, chairman of the State Duma commission investigating foreign interference in Russia’s internal affairs, said.
State Duma elections
Elections to the ninth State Duma will take place in Russia in the fall of 2026.
Voting will take place from September 18 to 20.
Residents of Donbass and Novorossiya will take part in State Duma elections for the first time.
Elections to legislative assemblies will be held in 39 regions, while senior regional officials will be elected in seven regions by direct vote and in three others by regional parliaments.
About 23,000 seats will be filled in total.

FT: SpaceX head Elon Musk willing to let Ukraine use Starlink to strike Russia
Billionaire Elon Musk is willing to let Ukraine use drones equipped with Starlink outside Ukraine’s own territory to strike targets inside Russia, according to Financial Times sources, who said he made the remark during a conversation with former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

articles.title: Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
articles.body:
Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has suddenly – and rather unexpectedly – become an adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. The news caught many conservative military analysts off guard. Why would Italy want him, and what does Rome hope to gain? Let’s try to make sense of the move without getting carried away.
A manager in khaki, not a marshal
It should be obvious that Fedorov is no military genius, nor does he possess any particular talent as a battlefield commander. That is simply not who he is. He was never a career officer, and he never made his name drawing thick red arrows across maps of future operations. First and foremost, Mikhail Fedorov is an effective IT executive – and a knowledgeable chief customer for the entire defense industry.
His path to that role began as the top digital strategist for Vladimir Zelensky’s presidential campaign, where he built an online campaign network and bet heavily on internet marketing. From there, he went on to create Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and roll out the Diia digital ecosystem, which changed everyday life across the country. In 2026, Fedorov took over the Defense Ministry amid an urgent need to impose order and bring sweeping digitalization to the armed forces. The timing, it seems, could hardly have been better.
Several major changes in the Ukrainian military were introduced with Fedorov’s involvement:
- Drone procurement for military units was radically overhauled through the launch of a dedicated marketplace designed to minimize red tape. It was a highly unconventional move that significantly shortened the path from manufacturer to frontline unit while opening up a market for many small and relatively young companies. After drones, the same digital approach began spreading to other parts of the defense industry.
- Agile management methods were effectively brought into military life, breaking down long-established systems of multistage approval and allowing new ideas to be tested quickly under real battlefield conditions – directly in the trenches.
- The military opened its doors to software developed by civilian companies. The emphasis shifted toward finding new and unconventional solutions that could be deployed quickly and deliver results immediately, rather than waiting for lengthy testing reports and reviews by specialized military institutes.
Of course, Fedorov’s role in these changes should not be overstated. Many of the initiatives that reshaped the Ukrainian military began before he arrived at the Defense Ministry. What he brought was a fresh, digital perspective that helped cut some corners and speed up the adoption of new ideas.
There were no combat operations or battlefield triumphs involved. He was a digital-solutions manager who put on a military uniform – focused exclusively on digital systems and a project-based approach to reform. And naturally the process was not without its rough edges. Digitalization remains the only clear success he can point to.
Why Rome wants the “Ukraine playbook”
Perhaps that is precisely what Rome needs: not military victories or battlefield credentials, but a fresh, modern approach. That, presumably, is where Italy is placing its hopes. Modern European militaries, including Italy’s, are weighed down by bureaucracy. Decisions on the procurement of new weapons systems and software take years. By the time they are finally approved, technology has already moved on, leaving armed forces to adopt systems that were obsolete before they ever entered service.
Fedorov may well be useful to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto as a new battering ram against his own conservative military establishment. Rome wants to borrow Ukraine’s experience of rapidly digitalizing military logistics and integrating unmanned systems in real time.
To understand exactly which processes Fedorov may seek to adapt for the Italian military, one need only look inside his “digital briefcase.” It contains no secret missile technology – only commercial software and civilian IT solutions adapted to the needs of a defense ministry.
The Italian military is eager to introduce new digital battle-management systems that combine geospatial tools with hundreds of information sources and a distributed network of users, extending from the General Staff all the way to a frontline commander’s tablet in the trenches. Italy is also naturally interested in digitalizing weapons and military-equipment procurement – and even more so in applying artificial intelligence to military command and control.
It is difficult to judge the results, but on paper Fedorov’s résumé looks highly impressive: experience introducing cutting-edge digital solutions in Europe’s only army currently fighting a major war. That is certainly one way to present it – and why be shy when listing your strengths on a résumé?
What Rome is really buying
A modern army increasingly resembles an IT corporation. Rome does not need Fedorov’s advice on how to defend its coastline or plan an armored offensive. It needs his ability to turn the military into a functioning digital platform.
But let’s take an honest look at the former defense minister’s record. Yes, there was digitalization and digital transformation. It may still be too early to assess the final results, but there have been no major successes on the battlefield – and that, one would think, is what an army is ultimately for and how its performance should be measured.
Then there is the less flattering part of the picture: the image of a petulant child who could not find common ground with career officers and began playing political games in the middle of an ongoing war to increase his own value back home. That hardly seems consistent with the image of a gifted digital manager. Wars, after all, are not won through digitalization alone, but through the coordinated action of different branches and types of forces.
It will be fascinating to see what Fedorov ‘achieves’ in his new job – and whether the spirit of Silicon Valley can take root in the austere offices of the Italian Defense Ministry.
As for the man with the polished résumé and the reputation of a ‘digitalization expert’, a position like this – especially in Rome – offers a splendid opportunity to make a graceful exit from Kiev and trade Ukraine’s brutal political reality for the warm, easygoing comforts of Europe.

articles.title: Japan seeks record $56B defense budget amid military buildup
articles.body:
Mucahithan Avcioglu
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
Japan’s Defense Ministry requested a record budget of about 8.9 trillion yen ($56 billion) for fiscal year 2027 as the government prepares to unveil a new military buildup plan later this year.
The request, covering the fiscal year beginning next April, is 0.9% higher than the current year’s initial budget, according to figures released Monday.
The ministry identified unmanned platforms, artificial intelligence, long-range strike capabilities, integrated air and missile defenses, space and cybersecurity among its spending priorities.
The proposal includes $1.8 billion for 17 MQ-9B SeaGuardian unmanned aircraft intended to strengthen maritime surveillance, particularly in the Pacific.
Some $1 billion was also requested for hypersonic missiles and associated ground equipment. Funding was sought for additional missiles capable of striking targets at long range as Japan works to strengthen its deterrence and counterattack capabilities.
The ministry said it aims to expand the use of unmanned systems for surveillance, targeting and attack missions while reducing risks to personnel and achieving cost advantages.
AI would meanwhile be integrated into military data collection and analysis to accelerate target selection, battlefield visualization and operational decision-making.
The proposal also includes measures to improve pay, food, housing, and working conditions for Self-Defense Forces personnel as Japan struggles to recruit and retain service members.
The headline figure could rise significantly because the ministry left costs unspecified for around 160 projects that may be affected by revisions to Japan’s three key security documents later this year. Additional funding will be considered during final budget negotiations.
The documents comprise the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program.
Japan’s current five-year program, adopted in 2022, envisioned about $269 billion in defense spending through fiscal 2027.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has pledged to accelerate the country’s military buildup amid increased Chinese military activity around Japan and expanding defense cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
Japan’s defense-related expenditure reached roughly $68.8 billion or 1.9% of gross domestic product in the previous fiscal year when spending by agencies such as the coast guard was included.
The overall budget requests for fiscal 2027 are also expected to reach a record 143 trillion yen ($890 billion), according to Kyodo News.
Debt-servicing costs are projected to hit an all-time high of 36.6 trillion yen ($230 billion) as rising interest rates increase the cost of government borrowing.
The government also received requests exceeding 10 trillion yen ($63 billion) for a new investment category covering areas such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors, robotics and national security.
The Finance Ministry will review the requests before drafting the budget for Cabinet approval by the end of the year.

articles.title: US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak island amid strait of Hormuz tensions
articles.body:
The US has reverted to military attacks on Iran for the first time in a month, firing missiles and drones at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, prompting the Iranian military to attack US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.
US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday after it detected the Iranians planning to fire fresh mines into the strait. Last week Donald Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies.
Iranian state TV later reported that a tanker had caught fire after hitting two naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. It did not identify the vessel or provide information about its crew.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that other ships violating its rules would face the same fate and said compliance with its regulations for passage through the strait was mandatory.
The last known US strikes on Iran were in late July, but there has been little sign of hard diplomatic progress apart from claims that Oman and Iran had reached agreement on a single permitted navigation route through the strait. Iran has set preconditions before the agreed route is opened, and the US has not stated its position on the route.
The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with a US attack on Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”
The IRGC said the US attack killed or wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with “punishment” from Tehran, Iranian state media reported. At least two Iranians were killed and two injured, initial reports said. One IRGC navy officer was announced killed.
The Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash into Gulf waters.
In response to the US attack, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.
On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far. The UAE ministry of defence said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters.
The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters without fear of Iranian reprisals is heavily contested.
Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8mbpd.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time.
A G20 finance ministers meeting in the US is likely to lead to a clash over US demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by the US. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact.
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is attending a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Kyrgyzstan where he will hold talks with Chinese officials.
China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign, and Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete Chinese investment to reduce the scale of the economic chaos inside Iran.

articles.title: Russia Turns to Harder-to-Intercept Jet Drones as Use Against Ukraine Jumps Fivefold
articles.body:

Russia Turns to Harder-to-Intercept Jet Drones as Use Against Ukraine Jumps Fivefold
Russian forces significantly increased their use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine in July, launching five times as many as in June, according to Yurii Ihnat, head of communications for Ukraine’s Air Force Command.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking on Ukrainian television on August 31, Ihnat said July marked a sharp increase in the deployment of jet-powered UAVs, alongside growing Russian use of the Banderoľ system.
“In July, five times more jet-powered UAVs were used than in June. That was the month when the use of these drones, as well as Banderoľ systems, increased significantly,” Ihnat said.
The Banderoľ has been variously classified as a loitering munition, missile, or drone, Ihnat noted. Its flight characteristics are approaching those of a cruise missile, with the system capable of traveling at approximately 600 kilometers per hour.
According to Ihnat, Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered drones after recognizing that they are considerably more difficult for Ukrainian forces to intercept using conventional air defense methods.
Countering the faster UAVs requires short-range surface-to-air missile systems as well as aviation platforms, including fighter aircraft equipped with air-to-air missiles, he said.
The increased deployment is being supported by Russia’s expanding production capacity. Ihnat said Moscow has established mass production of jet-powered drones, allowing the systems to be deployed almost immediately after leaving production lines.
The scale of their deployment has continued to grow. Over a recent four-day period, Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones of various types against Ukraine, including approximately 800 jet-powered UAVs, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on August 30.
According to Zelenskyy, the sustained waves of drone attacks are part of a Russian strategy aimed at exhausting Ukraine and its population.

articles.title: Someone placed funeral wreaths near defense companies in Lithuania and Czechia
articles.body:
In Lithuania, a photograph of a company executive with a black mourning ribbon was placed next to funeral wreaths, and similar objects turned up near a Czech defense company, Delfi reported on 30 August. Law enforcement officials are investigating whether the two incidents are connected.
Russia is trying to obstruct the defense assistance that NATO countries provide to Ukraine. To this end, Russia uses various forms of intimidation: exerting political pressure, carrying out cyberattacks, and recruiting people to conduct sabotage against foreign defense companies. Russia is suspected of using a new form of psychological pressure against the executives of companies that supply aid to Ukraine: through the use of elements symbolically associated with death.
Wreaths outside a Vilnius drone maker, and a suspect in custody
In Vilnius, funeral wreaths were left near the offices of RSI Europe, a company that manufactures unmanned systems and supplies Ukraine with FPV drones and remote detonation systems. Next to the wreaths, unknown individuals placed a photograph of company head Tomas Milašauskas, tied with a black mourning ribbon. Milašauskas is alive and well.
"We are not afraid. This is ordinary intimidation, a provocation, the usual methods of Russians' work. Our reaction is absolutely normal—we continue to work, we do not react and do not get distracted, because their goal is to distract our attention and direct it where it should not go," Milašauskas told LNK Žinios, as relayed by Delfi.
Milašauskas said that this was the first time RSI Europe had faced such a provocation. But the company had previously faced attempts to interfere with its operations, including cyberattacks.
A similar incident occurred in Czechia at almost the same time. Funeral wreaths also appeared near the offices of Czech defense group CSG, which makes ammunition and military equipment. A photograph of CSG executive director David Chour was placed nearby, Delfi reported.
Lithuanian police have already detained one suspect and launched a pre-trial investigation. National Crisis Management Centre head Vilmantas Vitkauskas said he believed the monitoring and the measures taken after earlier talks with defense firms made the detention possible. The detainee is a Ukrainian citizen, LNK's sources said. Preliminary information suggests that he may have been hired to deliver the wreaths, while the person who ordered them may have been a Belarusian citizen.
“This is probably only the beginning”
Lithuanian officials are treating the use of mourning symbols against defense companies as a possible provocation linked to Russian intelligence, after warning the sector to expect such attempts. Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Lithuanian parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, said:
"I think that such cases may become more frequent—and they have already become more frequent. This is probably only the beginning," he said.
He said the warnings are serious enough to require particular vigilance, although security at infrastructure facilities in the country has already been strengthened.
The Lithuanian authorities are also paying particular attention to the fact that photographs and videos of the wreaths quickly spread on social media and Telegram channels following the incidents. Posts accompanying the material promoted claims that NATO is allegedly fighting Russia with Ukraine’s hands, while European companies assisting Kyiv are supposedly making money from the war. Lithuanian officials consider this information component characteristic of information operations by Russian intelligence services.

articles.title: American nuke sub skips post-shakedown due to availability
articles.body:
The US Navy has declared the Virginia-class attack submarine USS Massachusetts ready for fleet tasking after completing shakedown trials, waiving the boat’s planned post-shakedown availability because of its material condition and combat readiness.
The U.S. Navy announced the decision on 17 August, saying the submarine had completed extensive testing and evaluation following delivery and would move directly into fleet availability rather than entering the maintenance period normally associated with a newly commissioned submarine.
USS Massachusetts, hull number SSN 798, was delivered by Newport News Shipbuilding on 21 November 2025 following sea trials and commissioned in Boston on 28 March 2026.
The Navy said the decision to waive the post-shakedown availability was based on the condition of the submarine during trials and the requirement to make the boat available for operational tasking.
Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle said in the U.S. Navy release: “USS Massachusetts is ready to fight, and that is exactly where we need her, in the hands of our Sailors and available to the Fleet.”
He added: “Waiving this availability reflects the exceptional condition of the ship and our determination to deliver combat-ready capability faster. It also allows our shipbuilding workforce to focus its talent and capacity where we need it most, building the next generation of submarines our nation requires.”
A post-shakedown availability normally follows the initial period of operations for a new warship or submarine, allowing the Navy and shipbuilder to address defects identified during trials, complete outstanding work and incorporate alterations before the vessel enters routine fleet service. In the case of Massachusetts, the Navy said the submarine met and exceeded the construction and safety standards required during its trials and subsequent shakedown period.
Vice Admiral Rob Gaucher, Director of Submarine Programs, said the decision represented a deliberate departure from the normal process. He said: “Waiving a submarine’s post-shakedown availability is an example of driving efficiency, innovation and speed in shipbuilding.”
Gaucher added: “While it is a calculated risk, we do it without ever compromising the safety of our sailors or the quality of our submarines. By getting this boat into the fight we can continue to maintain an absolute advantage in the undersea domain.”
USS Massachusetts is the seventh Block IV Virginia-class submarine. It was constructed under the long-running teaming arrangement between General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding. The Block IV boats incorporate design and maintenance changes intended to reduce major maintenance periods over their service lives and increase the amount of time available for deployments compared with earlier members of the class. Virginia-class submarines are nuclear-powered fast attack boats designed for anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, strike operations, intelligence collection and special operations support.
Vice Admiral Rick Seif, Commander, Submarine Forces, said in the release: “Massachusetts brings unmatched stealth and lethality to the undersea battle force.”He added: “This decision will immediately add combat readiness and capacity to ensure our nation’s ability to dominate and maintain undersea superiority.”
The U.S. Navy’s decision also avoids placing another newly delivered submarine into a shipyard availability at a time when the US submarine industrial base is supporting construction of additional Virginia-class boats alongside Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines and maintenance of the existing fleet.
USS Massachusetts is the fifth US Navy vessel to carry the name and entered service as the latest addition to the Navy’s fast-attack submarine force. With the shakedown period complete and the planned post-shakedown availability waived, the submarine is now available for operational tasking by the fleet.

articles.title: Iran fires ballistic missiles at US bases in Jordan
articles.body:
Iran said Monday it launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. bases in Jordan in retaliation for an American strike on Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking a new escalation in the months-long conflict between Washington and Tehran.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said ballistic missiles targeted U.S. forces at the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
Jordan’s armed forces said Monday they intercepted eight missiles that entered Jordanian airspace, state television reported.
The launches followed reports Sunday that Iran was attacking U.S. forces stationed in Jordan. Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst, citing a U.S. source, said there had been no significant impact and that nearly all incoming missiles had been intercepted at that point.
The Revolutionary Guards said Monday’s missile attack was retaliation for a U.S. strike Sunday on Larak Island, a strategically located Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.
A senior U.S. official said the American military struck two IRGC rocket launchers on the island that were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the Strait of Hormuz. The official said U.S. forces had finished clearing mines from international shipping lanes and were prepared to protect commercial navigation through the strategic waterway.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported preliminary, unofficial figures of two people killed and two wounded in the U.S. strike. Shortly afterward, the Revolutionary Guards vowed that the attack would be met with a response and that the United States would be punished.
The confrontation comes after about six months of fighting with Iran as President Donald Trump presses Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept U.S. terms for ending the conflict. U.S. Central Command has kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in the region for months amid the possibility of further military action.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Infrastructure Across Occupied Ukraine, Takes Out Pantsir-S1
articles.body:

Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Infrastructure Across Occupied Ukraine, Takes Out Pantsir-S1
Ukrainian forces struck a series of Russian military targets on August 29 and overnight into August 30, hitting drone infrastructure, command posts, logistics and ammunition depots, and a radar station, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 30.
Among the targets was a drone storage facility belonging to Russia’s Rubicon unmanned systems unit in temporarily occupied Khartsyzk in the Donetsk region.

Ukrainian forces also hit a Russian UAV command post near Chumatske in the Donetsk region, targeting infrastructure used to coordinate drone operations on the battlefield.
Additional Russian command posts were struck in temporarily occupied Sukhodolsk in the Luhansk region.
The operation also targeted several logistics facilities supporting Russian forces. Ukrainian strikes hit supply depots in Berdyanske and Hirnyk in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region, as well as another facility near Krasnosilske in occupied Crimea.
An ammunition depot in temporarily occupied Kadiivka in the Luhansk region was also hit.
Beyond temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian radar station near Pavlychi in Russia’s Bryansk region.
The General Staff separately announced a confirmed result from an earlier operation. After analyzing additional intelligence, the Ukrainian military confirmed that a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense gun-missile system was destroyed near Kletnya in the Bryansk region on August 27.
The Pantsir-S1 is designed to provide short-range protection for military installations and other high-value assets against aircraft, missiles, and drones.
Previously, Ukrainian forces struck several Russian military targets in temporarily occupied Crimea, as well as command posts and equipment concentrations in the Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk regions.
Near Olenivka in Crimea, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Nebo-SV radar station, equipment associated with a P-18 radar, and a mobile communications system.

articles.title: A Russian State Duma deputy called for the use of nuclear weapons against Ukraine
articles.body:
A Russian State Duma deputy called for the use of nuclear weapons against Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Aleksey Zhuravlyov called for the use of tactical nuclear weapons against Ukraine to force its capitulation. There are no signs of preparations for a strike.
Russian State Duma deputy and leader of the Rodina party Alexei Zhuravlyov called for the use of tactical nuclear weapons against Ukraine to force it to capitulate. The Moscow Times reports this, citing a statement by the Russian parliamentarian, writes UNN.
Details
According to Zhuravlyov, there should allegedly be no discussion in Russia at all about the possibility of using tactical nuclear weapons.
If necessary, we are obliged to use them. If we have to strike, we will strike. And this is not up for discussion
There are currently no signs of preparations for a nuclear strike
Earlier, Bloomberg, citing sources close to the Kremlin, reported that Vladimir Putin might view tactical nuclear weapons as a last resort in the event of a sharp deterioration in Russia’s position. At the same time, the outlet emphasized that there were no signs of Moscow preparing to use them.
Russia’s partners also oppose such a scenario. In particular, according to media reports, China warned the Kremlin against using nuclear weapons.
Zhuravlyov’s statement came amid new reports of attempts by the United States to persuade Moscow to abandon further escalation and return to negotiations on ending the hostilities.

articles.title: US, Iran exchange fire in flare-up; Bessent signals more sanctions
articles.body:
Iran still wants negotiated end to war, President says after exchanges of fire
- Iran seeks a negotiated end to its conflict with the US despite recent exchanges of fire, with President Pezeshkian emphasising dialogue and cooperation to avoid further war.
- US forces struck Iranian launchers on Larak Island, prompting Iranian retaliatory attacks on US bases in Jordan and reports of drone incidents near the UAE.
- Economic sanctions continue to pressure Iran, with the US planning weekly secondary sanctions and the EU supporting ongoing efforts to curb Iran's regional influence and nuclear programme.
AI generated
DUBAI – Iran is still seeking a negotiated solution to its conflict with the US, President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Aug 31, a day after the two countries resumed hostilities for the first time since late July, driving oil prices up more than 3.5 per cent.
Pezeshkian’s comments also came after US President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated video clip that he said showed Iran’s oil hub Kharg Island being destroyed.
There was no evidence of any such attack, and a US official said on Aug 31 that the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes. An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable”.
US forces on Aug 30 struck two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak Island, some 660km east of Kharg, a US official said, prompting Iran to strike two US bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
Two people were killed, and others were injured in the attack on Larak Island, Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted the local governor as saying on Aug 31.
The return to hostilities followed weeks in which Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Tehran and its business partners with costly economic sanctions, shifting away from military options. Diplomacy remains in stalemate.
Pezeshkian, speaking to India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of a regional security meeting in Kyrgyzstan, accused the US of failing to fulfil its commitments under past agreements.
“Nevertheless, we are still trying to achieve an agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is in no one’s interest, neither ours, nor the region’s, nor humanity’s,” Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted him as saying.
“We believe the solution to the existing issues is dialogue and cooperation and that every capacity must be used to prevent the spread of insecurity and conflict.”
‘Blown to smithereens’
Earlier, Trump had annoyed Iran by posting on his Truth Social platform the AI-generated video clip with the message: “Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT.”
Reuters confirmed that the video clip showing dramatic explosions was most likely synthetically generated, using software that detects AI-manipulated imagery.
The White House and the US Defense Department did not respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours.
Kharg handled 90 per cent of Iran’s oil exports before the US and Israeli launched attacks on Iran on Feb 28, sparking a war that would severely disrupt its energy trade and put huge pressure on the economy.
“Trump’s tweets are laughable, and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate,” said Hamid Bovard, chief executive of government-run National Iranian Oil, on Aug 31.
Oil operations had not stopped, and workers were busy repairing previous damage and modernising facilities, Bovard said in comments cited by Nournews, a semi-official outlet close to Iran’s top security body.
Iran vows to respond to any attacks
A US official said forces had attacked the Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Aug 30 after “Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz”.
Larak is a small island in the strait near the strategic Iranian port of Bandar Abbas. The Strait of Hormuz, which normally handles a fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments, has been effectively blocked since the start of the war.
In a statement, the US Central Command said it took “limited, precise” action against minelaying forces of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards that posed an “imminent threat” in the strait. It gave no details.
As well as attacking the US bases in Jordan, Iran’s army said it had also struck the Al Minhad airbase in the United Arab Emirates early on Aug 31. However, the UAE’s defence ministry dismissed that report as false.
The UAE Defence Ministry later said its air force engaged a drone that had come from Iran over its territorial waters. It provided no further details, including whether it was shot down.
The Jordan strikes targeted US bases used to launch and support the attack on Larak, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said.
The Revolutionary Guards used air defence missiles to shoot down a US drone that crashed in Gulf waters, the Mehr news agency said on Aug 31, citing a statement from the elite force.
A supertanker caught fire and was brought to a complete halt after being struck by two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz, Iran state TV said, citing a Guards’ statement.
Piling economic pressure on Iran
Trump has yet to achieve the objectives he set out at the start of the war: dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme, curbing its ability to attack regional rivals and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Aug 30 new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
The European Union said on Aug 31 it would continue to work with the US and others to maintain economic pressure on Iran.
The Guards said the supertanker on fire after being hit by mines had been attempting to pass through the waterway illegally, but gave no details of the vessel or crew, according to a statement cited by state television.
Last week, Trump said all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait and Iran had been warned that any vessel placing new mines would be destroyed.
Iran denied Trump’s assertion. REUTERS

articles.title: Fired Ukrainian minister offers to help build America’s drone army— for Patriot missiles in return
articles.body:
Ukraine's former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov has offered to help the United States build a fleet of attack drones if Washington sends Ukraine the Patriot interceptor missiles it needs to get through winter, he told the Financial Times. The idea is Fedorov's own proposal, not a deal, and he holds no government post that would let him negotiate one for Kyiv. He is in Washington mainly to raise American money for a fund that would both invest in Ukrainian defense-tech companies and build new ones of its own.
Over the past year, Ukraine's partners have shifted from handing over weapons off their shelves to funding and co-producing Ukrainian-designed drones and missiles, inside and outside the country.
What the fund would do
Fedorov used his working trip to Washington to line up venture funds, entrepreneurs and tech companies as backers, Suspilne reported. The fund would not simply invest in existing Ukrainian defense-tech firms, he wrote; it would also create new companies around the technologies the front line needs most. He set out three targets: battlefield robots to replace soldiers in the most dangerous positions, jet-powered interceptor drones to bring down Russia's faster new attack drones, and cheap missiles that use artificial intelligence. He did not say what his own role would be, or whether he would profit. He said the next step is to assemble a team and launch the first projects.
The Fedorov protesters lost. But they backed a man for what he built, not what he promised—and that may be new in Ukraine.
The interceptors behind the offer
Fedorov framed the drone help as a straight swap.
"I'm ready to make that trade," he told the FT.
Ukraine is running low on interceptor missiles for its Patriot batteries, one of the few air-defense systems able to reliably stop Russia's ballistic missiles. Fedorov declined to say whether he would meet anyone from the Trump administration.
Ukraine's ex-minister turns open critic
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Fedorov on 15 July, after six months in the job. Fedorov said a feud with Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, who he says blocked his reforms, drove the split, Zelenskyy removed Syrskyi on 21 July as protests spread. in an interview with Reuters published on 25 August.
"it looks as though we're gradually, slowly losing," he said in an interview with Reuters.

articles.title: Ukrainian strike kills two civilians in Russian border region
articles.body:
Ukrainian strike kills two civilians in Russian border region
Two civilians, including a teenager, were killed and several others were injured in a Ukrainian strike on the Russian city of Belgorod, acting regional governor Aleksandr Shuvaev said on Sunday.
The missile attack struck a commercial facility, causing the roof of one building to collapse and triggering fires at seven warehouses, including a sorting center and delivery hub belonging to the online marketplace Ozon. Firefighters, rescuers, and other emergency personnel continued working at the scene as of Sunday evening.
“A man and a 16-year-old boy were killed,” Shuvaev wrote on Telegram, expressing condolences and urging residents to remain vigilant. “I know that at a time of such a grievous loss, no words can ease the sorrow of relatives and loved ones,” he said, adding that “all Belgorod residents share your pain.”
According to Shuvaev, 16 people were injured, including nine children. Twelve of the wounded were hospitalized, with five – including one teenager – listed in serious condition.
In recent months, Kiev has intensified its drone and missile attacks on retail warehouses and other civilian infrastructure in regions bordering Ukraine and deeper inside Russia. Earlier on Sunday, Shuvaev said Belgorod Region alone had been attacked 138 times over the preceding 24 hours.
On the same day, four Ukrainian UAVs struck the non-operational Duvannaya coal mine in the Lugansk People’s Republic, causing part of an administrative building to collapse and killing a female lamp-room attendant. The attack occurred on Miners’ Day, an annual holiday honoring workers in the coal-rich region.
Between August 17 and 23, Ukrainian attacks killed 46 civilians, including five children, and injured 364 others across Russia, according to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik. He said Ukrainian forces fired at least 7,462 munitions at civilian targets during that period. Belgorod, Kherson, and Zaporozhye regions, along with the Lugansk and Donetsk People’s Republics, recorded the highest civilian casualty figures.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure as indiscriminate terrorist attacks and vowed to carry out “systematic and consistent strikes” on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities. It has maintained that Russian forces never deliberately target civilians.
On Saturday, Russian forces struck several military-related sites in Kiev and its suburbs, including a facility storing components for Ukraine’s long-range Flamingo cruise missiles.
The strike triggered secondary detonations that severely damaged the surrounding area and killed 37 people, forcing Vladimir Zelensky to admit that a military depot containing drones and ammunition had been located near residential buildings. Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky called the repetition of “the same mistakes” “criminal negligence.”
Placing military targets in densely populated civilian areas is strictly prohibited under international law and is considered a form of using non-combatants as human shields. Following a similar incident in early July, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials pledged to end the practice.

articles.title: Kremlin Says Putin Sees ‘Absolutely No Point’ in Trump-Zelensky Peace Summit
articles.body:
The Kremlin on Monday poured cold water on the prospect of a three-way peace summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, saying there is “absolutely no point” in such a meeting without a deal ready to be signed.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said any meeting between the three leaders would only make sense if it were held to formally seal agreements ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“You know the position of our head of state well: such a meeting is possible only to fix agreements,” Peskov said, adding that a settlement would be a “very complex process” involving numerous details.
He also accused Kyiv of refusing to pursue what Moscow calls a “real settlement” of the war.
Peskov’s comments came after reports that CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral summit during a secret Aug. 25 visit to Moscow.
Sources cited by Axios reported that Ratcliffe raised the possibility of bringing Trump, Putin and Zelensky together.
Trump first floated the idea of a trilateral summit in August 2025, saying preparations were underway and suggesting it could happen within two weeks. More than a year later, the meeting has yet to take place.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Trump personally sent Ratcliffe to Moscow without informing some of his closest aides and military commanders beforehand.
Ukraine and Israel Draw Closer as Israeli Elections Loom
During the visit, Ratcliffe met with Russia’s top security officials, including SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin and FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov.
Axios sources said the CIA director sought to determine whether Russia’s security chiefs could persuade Putin to return to negotiations.
The New York Times reported that Ratcliffe delivered Bortnikov a “bleak assessment” of the Russian military and economy and urged Moscow to strike a deal before its position deteriorated further.
Yet the Kremlin’s latest message suggests Putin remains far from ready to compromise.
After Ratcliffe’s visit, Ukrainian Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov said US-mediated talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations could take place in September.
Kyiv, however, remains skeptical of Moscow’s intentions.
Budanov’s deputy, Pavlo Palisa, said Putin had ordered Russia’s military to prepare several scenarios for an offensive in northern Ukraine, including possible advances toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin continues to demand that Ukraine surrender the remaining Ukrainian-held parts of Donbas, where Kyiv’s forces control roughly 20% of the territory.

articles.title: The President of Finland does not believe in Russia's attack on NATO and rules out a nuclear strike on Ukraine
articles.body:
The President of Finland does not believe in Russia's attack on NATO and rules out a nuclear strike on Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Alexander Stubb said that he sees no evidence of Russia preparing to attack NATO. He also doubts that there will be a nuclear strike on Ukraine.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he sees no evidence of a possible Russian attack on NATO, and also expressed doubt that Moscow would use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. BILD reports, writes UNN.
I do not believe that Russia will ever want to attack the world's most powerful military alliance — NATO
He commented on Germany's warning that Russia could be capable of attacking NATO territory by 2029, noting that he sees "neither evidence nor facts" supporting such a scenario.
According to Stubb, NATO has a powerful deterrent based on conventional forces, missiles, and nuclear weapons.
There is no point for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance
The President of Finland also expressed doubt about the possibility of a Russian nuclear strike on Ukraine. According to him, he raised the issue during a conversation with China's foreign minister, who said that China "would never allow this to happen."
At the same time, Stubb emphasized that Europe must be prepared for the worst-case scenario in order to prevent it.

articles.title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says it struck 2 US airbases in Jordan with ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Tarek Chouiref
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said early Monday that it had struck two US airbases in Jordan with ballistic missiles in retaliation for a US strike on Iran’s Larak Island.
The IRGC said its Aerospace Force targeted the King Hussein and Azraq airbases in a combined missile-and-drone operation.
It said the strikes hit technical and maintenance infrastructure as well as areas where fighter jets were stationed, claiming “heavy damage.”
The guard warned that any further attack would be met with an even stronger response.
Earlier Sunday, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island, marking the first strikes on Iranian territory since late July, a US official told Axios.
The operation targeted systems allegedly being prepared to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said several fighters and civilians were killed and injured in the attack and vowed to respond.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency said preliminary information suggested the attack was carried out by drones.
Tensions between Tehran and Washington have remained high since the war began with strikes on Iran in late February. Although a framework deal was signed in June through Pakistani and Qatari mediation, in July the US began a two-week bombing campaign and reimposed a naval blockade after differences over navigation in the strait.

articles.title: Israel, Greece seal €3B ‘Achilles Shield’ defense deal
articles.body:
Israel agreed to build a multilayered air-defense network for Greece in a new €3 billion defense deal published on Monday.
“This is the largest defense export deal in the history of Israel-Greece relations, and one of the largest in the history of the State of Israel,” Israel’s Defense Ministry wrote in a statement.
The “Achilles Shield” deal represents the largest defense export agreement in the history of relations between the two countries, combining David’s Sling, BARAK MX and SPYDER interceptors with Israeli-made radars and a national command system designed to counter ballistic missiles, aircraft and drones.
Advertisement
Greece put the deal’s total value at €3.035 billion, adding that 19 Greek companies are already involved, accounting for more than €750 million of the program, with plans to build a domestic production base capable of exporting equipment. Defense Minister Nikos Dendias said Greece would become “the first country in the European Union to adopt a similar system.”
The deal caps a fast-deepening security partnership between the two countries.
In January, Greece and Israel agreed to expand cooperation on drone and underwater-vehicle swarms, cyber threats, military exercises and defense technology. The push feeds into Greece’s “Agenda 2030,” a sweeping military overhaul aimed at modernizing the armed forces and building more weapons at home.
Athens is going further than some other European buyers of Israeli air defenses. Germany bought the Arrow 3 system in 2023 and Finland acquired David’s Sling in 2024. Greece says it will be the first EU country to stitch several Israeli platforms together into a single national shield against ballistic missiles, aircraft and drones.

articles.title: US Trains Polish Special Forces to Operate in High-Drone-Activity Zones, Drawing on Ukraine War Experience
articles.body:
In Germany, Polish special forces are taking part in military exercises designed to teach them how to operate in areas where they could easily be detected by drones.
The Associated Press reports that the U.S. military developed the training program based on lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.
The special forces are practicing how to move through a 3,000-square-kilometer area controlled by a simulated enemy and how to carry out simulated strikes on key targets using drones.
According to the exercise scenario, the Polish troops must secretly move through the positions of U.S. soldiers playing the role of the enemy.
The U.S. troops also monitor reports from local residents to the police, which could help them detect and locate the Polish team.
The special forces must then travel about 100 kilometers across Germany to reach another training area in Grafenwöhr, where they are tasked with destroying a simulated target.
During the mission, the troops must avoid detection not only by military personnel but also by civilians. To do so, they move through villages and farms, where surveillance cameras are also in operation.
The U.S. military plans to conduct these exercises several times a year and expects special forces from more NATO countries to take part.
Meanwhile, the U.S. approach to developing counter-drone capabilities remains unclear.
Shortly before these exercises, the U.S. Army shut down a specialized unit in Europe that focused on studying warfare involving drones.
Despite this, the United States has been systematically studying the use of drones in Russia’s war against Ukraine for several years.
This work is carried out both by specialized units and by combat formations, which receive new drones and counter-drone systems to test during military exercises.
One of the key initiatives is the Transforming in Contact (TiC) program, under which the U.S. Army delivers new technologies directly to combat units for testing during deployments and training.
The 3rd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division tested new drones, electronic warfare systems, command-and-control systems, and mobile platforms while deployed in Europe.
The brigade fielded more than 150 unmanned systems of various types, designed for a range of different missions.
Another initiative is the JIATF 401, a U.S. military interagency task force responsible for countering unmanned aircraft systems. Its main mission is to rapidly integrate advanced counter-drone technologies into military units.
JIATF 401 personnel are also studying the experience of Ukraine and European countries, where the widespread use of drones has become a routine part of modern warfare.

articles.title: US trains Polish special forces using lessons from Ukraine's war against Russia – AP
articles.body:
US trains Polish special forces using lessons from Ukraine's war against Russia – AP
US forces have begun training Polish special forces in Germany using exercises designed to "simulate many of the challenges" of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: Associated Press
Details: Polish special forces are taking part in exercises designed only a few months ago which simulate breaking through enemy lines, travelling for miles through hostile territory and using drones to strike a key enemy target.
Associated Press noted that the exercises, initially developed by US Army Green Berets for American special operations units, began on Friday 28 August and incorporate and simulate many of the challenges faced by Ukrainian forces in the war against Russia.
"We're using lessons learned from Ukraine," a US Army Green Beret officer attached to the training facility said. "All of those effects that we're seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome – we're doing our best to replicate."
The exercises highlight efforts by some US military units to study the latest methods of drone warfare, which Ukraine has pioneered during more than four years of fighting to repel the full-scale invasion launched by Russia. They also demonstrate how the US, its NATO allies and Ukraine are working together to prepare for the possibility of further Russian aggression in the coming years, even as US President Donald Trump's administration has warned of troop reductions in Europe.
During the exercises in Germany, a senior soldier told AP that similar training is planned to take place several times a year.
A participant and officer involved in the exercises told AP that they expect most, if not all, NATO countries to be interested in sending troops to take part.
The exercise scenario lasts several days and takes place across a vast 3,000-square-kilometre training area in the Bavarian countryside.
The Polish special forces are expected to sneak past a US Army airborne infantry unit whose soldiers will play the role of the enemy. The US airborne unit will parachute into a restricted training area at the Hohenfels base and establish itself on the line of contact.
If the Polish troops manage to get past the US forces, they must head north, travelling about 100 km through the German countryside to another training area in Grafenwöhr, where they are expected to destroy a simulated target.
German farms and villages, private and government-operated cameras and a densely populated town lie along the route. These not only create obstacles but also increase the likelihood of the Polish troops being spotted.
A senior serviceman told AP that during earlier stages of the exercises, the Green Berets removed their uniforms "so they can blend in", adding that "blend in also means don't get seen by civilians".
AP added that local German civilians are largely unaware of the exercises and provide a useful test of how effectively special forces can blend into the local population. If they fail, reports of suspicious individuals made to the police will be passed to the military, which will use them to pinpoint the group's location.
The US Army will also use its own drones to search for the Polish units.
If they are detected, "now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you", a US soldier said.
The US Army could either send a military police unit with dogs to search for the Polish special forces or deploy additional drones to the area. In previous versions of the exercise, the US Army had more than 100 drones at its disposal, the soldier said.
As part of the exercises, servicemen may be "captured or killed".
AP noted that while the exercises demonstrate the use of drones and NATO teamwork, there have recently been differing views within military circles about the importance of cooperation and the value of drones.
Trump has caused confusion among NATO allies by repeatedly changing his position on possible reductions in the number of US troops stationed in Europe, while his administration has begun a review of US military forces to determine its next steps. Last week, the US Army's top military commander also disbanded a unit specialising in drone warfare.
Quote from AP: "But overall, there is growing interest in tapping Ukraine for its expertise on modern warfare and, specifically, drones."
Details: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Ukraine was helping five countries in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf counter Iranian drone attacks carried out during the US war against Iran. Those seeking assistance included both the US and European countries.
Meanwhile, the number of mysterious drone incursions across Europe has increased, including this month, when two drones were spotted over a German military base and a drone carrying explosives was discovered at one of Germany's key cargo airports.
Background:
- During the Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, Ukrainian drone operators from the Nemesis unit – the 412th Brigade of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces – quickly detected and simulated strikes on vehicles belonging to a US mechanised brigade, demonstrating their superiority in the use of drones.
