articles.title: Trump vows 'retaliation' after first US-Iran strikes in a month
articles.body:
• Iran and the US have exchanged strikes for the first time in more than a month, causing oil prices to rise more than two percent.
• The US military said it struck Iranian launchers on Larak Island, claiming they were preparing to launch naval mines into the Strait of Hormuz.
• Iran said it responded by attacking US bases in Jordan and an airbase in the UAE. Abu Dhabi denied the Al Minhad airbase had been targeted.
• Iran's president Masoud Pezeshkian said that his country "never welcomes war" but accused the US of "not fulfilling its commitments" during a meeting with his Indian counterpart.
• Israel has killed at least three Palestinians in Gaza after striking a vehicle in Gaza City.
• Israeli authorities have announced a new illegal settlement southeast of Nablus in the occupied West Bank.
US doubles down on Iran sanctions as G20 finance talks begin
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed Monday to persist with economic pressure on Iran, saying a turning point could be near as G20 finance leaders opened talks clouded by war and trade tensions.
"We are going to continue exerting pressure, and we've had very good discussions here already," Bessent told reporters before starting meetings with Group of 20 finance ministers and central bank governors.
He said a turning point in this US pressure campaign could come "within weeks or months," adding that Iran's economy need not collapse in the Middle East war to achieve this.
President Donald Trump's administration is working to rally G20 partners to ramp up economic pressure on Iran during the talks in Asheville, North Carolina, through Tuesday - amid a renewed exchange of fire with Tehran.
Iraq hands 15-year jail term to kidnapper of US journalist
Iraq's judiciary has sentenced a man to 15 years in prison for the kidnapping of American journalist Shelly Kittleson, who was abducted earlier this year by a powerful Iran-backed group, a judicial source said Monday.
At the height of the Middle East war, on 31 March, Kataeb Hezbollah kidnapped Kittleson in Baghdad, holding her for several days before setting her free just hours before the United States and Iran agreed to a ceasefire.
Iraqi authorities arrested one member of the group at the time.
Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "hard" after the two foes traded fire for the first time in over a month.
"We're going to hit them hard," Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. "There will be a response."
The United States said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the key shipping lane.
Iran responded by with missile and drone attacks aimed at Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, saying they targeted US forces there, but President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday called for dialogue.
Israel kills three Palestinians in new Gaza strike
Three Palestinians were killed on Monday evening in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City, Palestinian news agency WAFA reports.
A medical source at Al-Shifa Hospital said that three bodies arrived at the hospital following the strike, which reportedly targeted a vehicle in the southern Tel Al-Hawa suburb.
Rescue workers arrive following an Israeli strike in Gaza City, 31 August 2026. [Getty]
Israeli authorities have established a new illegal settlement named "Noa" southeast of Jenin in the north of the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian news agency WAFA.
Several government ministers and Knesset members attended a ceremony to unveil the new settlement, which is close to other settlements which have been illegally built on Palestinian land.
Settlement construction has accelerated at its fastest pace in history under the current far-right Israeli government, which observers have warned is marching closer towards a de facto annexation of the occupied West Bank.
Crude prices rise above $90 per barrel on US-Iran strikes
Oil prices jumped more than two percent Monday, with the Brent international benchmark rising above $90 a barrel after a fresh flare-up in the US-Iran war.
The move came after the United States said it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the Strait of Hormuz, its first strikes on the country in a month.
The attack prompted Tehran to retaliate by hitting US military targets in Jordan.
President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States would hit back against Iranian attacks on US targets in the Middle East, according to Fox News.
The exchange came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
Oil storage tanks at a refinery in Houston, Texas. [Getty]

articles.title: ‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villages
articles.body:
It is a day and a half since a Russian jet-powered drone smashed into an ammunition dump in Myla, a village 15 miles outside central Kyiv. Volodymyr, 61, a security guard, leads visitors from his family’s badly damaged home, its roof blown off, back windows shattered, through the garden towards the impact site 300 metres away.
The garden, like so many in Ukraine’s villages and suburbs, is a sizeable allotment. But today the greenhouse is shattered, a vegetable patch is blackened and crisp underfoot. Several metres of grapevine have been destroyed. Even so, Volodymyr finds two surviving bunches to hand to the Guardian.
It is a remarkable moment of generosity, though his family now has no electricity and no water after Thursday night’s extended bombing. The death toll rose by one on Sunday, to 38, and four more people are still missing in an episode that has swiftly raised questions about why ammunition was stored so close to people’s homes.
In the yard before the garden, Vira, 65, knows who is at fault. “Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” she says. She and her son Serhii hid for hours in a small bunker by the side of the house waiting out what witnesses said were 30 or 50 explosions that went on for about six hours after the initial strike at 8pm.
Serhii says they had no idea ammunition was stored in their village. “I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there.” Now the family is presented with a cleanup that will be costly and difficult while starting with next to nothing. He is charging his phone from a car battery via a converter. It is all the power they have.
A missile shell from a Grad rocket launcher was found on their property once the explosions subsided, Serhii adds, as well as “several mines and cluster munitions”. They have been removed by the cleanup team, although a burnt-out box of bullets, freshly discovered in another part of the semi-collapsed ceiling, has not and sits by the front door awaiting a further collection.
Volodymyr’s tour continues out back. A grass line, effectively a track, has been marked out through the wood beyond the garden, between blackened patches where fires burned. There is smouldering, even flames in places, more bullets and boxes of bullets, then, on the right, unmistakably, a detonated anti-tank mine.
Finally, the woods open out, revealing a warehouse site, large parts of which are bombed out, an open area of destruction. A sulphurous smell endures, and periodically explosions can be heard, though they may be controlled detonations. Clear-up work by the emergency services is in the process of being halted at lunchtime because there is another drone threat above.
Volodymyr was on guard duty at a lumber yard close to the ammunition store on the night of the bombing. He survived the initial strike unscathed, and headed back home promptly, but feels a guard’s need to return. “I’ve been coming back and forth for two days to see these ashes,” he says.
Thirty of the dead were from a care home close to the ammunition store, the location of which is now subject of a criminal inquiry by Ukraine’s intelligence service. But it is not the first attack of its kind in recent weeks. There have been other Russian bombings of poorly placed ammunition dumps, as Moscow aggressively targets warehouse sites at a time when Ukraine is doing similar.
The fact this has happened recently in Ukraine is not lost on Liudmyla, whose adult daughter was in the house a couple of doors down when the Shahed drone hit. The home is also heavily damaged, windows facing the warehouse blown in, and Liudmyla recalls that a similar incident happened in early July, on the edge of Kyiv.
“Look at what’s going on here. Everything’s smashed to bits right here. Vyshneve [the scene of the previous incident, nine miles south-east] wasn’t enough for them, and there was more somewhere else too. No, they’ve dumped all this right by people’s vegetable gardens, right on their doorsteps,” she says, warning that munitions are still strewn around, not yet cleared up.
Nine people were killed after a munitions store was hit at Vyshneve, and 280 homes damaged. Two people have been detained on suspicion of allowing weapons to be stored in an inappropriate place after the episode, but as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Saturday, similar has happened again.
It is a dismal repetition at a time when Kyiv is already coming under increased attack from Moscow, the harm to civilians from attacks on food stores and logistics warehouses increasing. When Liudmyla is pressed to say who is at fault for the deaths and destruction at Myla, she offers a double answer.
“Putin! Who else? And those who set up the depot here.”

articles.title: Iran, US trade fire in first exchange for a month
articles.body:
Iran attacked U.S. military targets in the Middle East on Aug. 31 in retaliation for American strikes on an island in the Strait of Hormuz, the first exchange of fire for a month in a war that has engulfed the region.
Six months into the conflict, the two sides remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic strait shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
The United States had signaled a pivot to economic pressure in place of military action, but on Aug. 30 said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the small island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the strategic shipping lane.
Tehran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of its military, said they responded by striking two U.S. air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage.”
Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
Iran also claimed it targeted U.S. personnel at an air base in the United Arab Emirates and shot down an American drone over Hormuz.
The exchange of fire between the United States and Iran came at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
In recent weeks, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump had prioritized “economic warfare” over military action.
But the militaries of the two sides remain vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran having blocked the passage of commercial ships since the war began.
The strikes came as the Washington Post reported that a recent Pentagon assessment warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that sustaining the current pace of military operations against Iran could weaken the U.S. ability to respond to threats in other regions and defend the homeland.
Commanders overseeing operations in Latin America, Europe and Asia have had aircraft, ships and other resources redirected to support the six-month-long war with Iran, which shows no clear signs of ending.

articles.title: The battle Ukraine claims it won could expose its entire front
articles.body:
The battle Ukraine claims it won could expose its entire front
Last week, Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky, along with the new Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) Mikhail Drapaty, visited a section of the front line in Dnepropetrovsk region. Zelensky stated that this year, the AFU has almost completely regained control of Dnepropetrovsk Region, with only about 10 square kilometers of territory remaining under Russian control.
What is the logic behind this PR campaign? Did the AFU really make progress in this direction? What were the real goals of the Ukrainian operation, and to what extent have they been achieved? We explore all this below.
Strategic hub
The southern sector is the most strategically important part of the 1,500-kilometer-long front. On one end it borders the Dnieper River, while the other end stretches northeast to Pokrovsk, where, as it is generally considered, the central sector of the front begins.
In 2023, Ukraine’s only strategic offensive took place in this area. The AFU’s aim was to reach the sea and cut off the land corridor to the Crimea by means of two decisive blows. If successful, this operation would have radically worsened the situation for the Russian army and, according to Kiev’s plans, changed the course of the conflict. Even though the 2023 offensive failed, this section of the front did not become less important for the AFU. In the spring of 2026, with the aim of cutting off supply routes to the Crimea, the AFU launched a middle strike campaign, particularly targeting the highway located 50-70 km from the front line. These attempts have so far proven unsuccessful.
For Russia, the southern sector of the front is extremely important for three reasons. Firstly, as the front is pushed further north, Ukrainian middle strikes become less effective. Secondly, the capture of the city of Orekhov will pave the way for an advance toward Zaporozhye, a regional center with a pre-war population of over 700,000 and one of the largest industrial cities remaining under Kiev’s control.
Thirdly and most importantly, an advance north from Zaporozhye will allow the Russian army to approach the central sector of the front from the rear, either encircling it or at least significantly disrupting its supply lines.
Last year brought troubling news for the AFU in the southern sector of the front as the defense near the city of Gulaipole collapsed. At the time, all forces were pulled for the defense of Pokrovsk and Mirnograd, while several areas in the south were left with no one to defend them. As a result of the successful campaign of Russia’s East Group of Forces to identify and destroy drone crews, the AFU were forced to abandon approximately 300 square kilometers between the Yanchur and Gaichur rivers without fighting. To restore the front, then Commander-in-Chief Syrsky was forced to curtail the counteroffensive near Pokrovsk and essentially abandon the encircled garrison in neighboring Mirnograd.
Syrsky’s last gasp
This situation determined the priorities of the 2026 spring-summer campaign for the AFU: the aim was to restore the southern front at all costs, eliminate the threat to Zaporozhye, and push Russian forces as far east and south as possible to relieve strategic pressure on the central sector of the front.
We don’t have any information from the Ukrainian General Staff, so we can only assess the operation’s goals based on indirect evidence. Apparently, the AFU planned two auxiliary strikes in the Stepnogorsk and Uspenovka area to cut off the pincers of the Russian army, which threatened to close in around Orekhov. The main strike, however, was to be directed at Velikaya Novoselka. If it had been successful, the entire defense system of the East Group of Forces from Gulipole to the junction with the Center Group of Forces near Pokrovsk would have collapsed and the Russian army would have been pushed back 30-40 kilometers.
The AFU’s attacks began in the spring and were accompanied by an unprecedented media campaign. The operation was labeled a second counteroffensive, Ukrainian authorities claimed dozens of “liberated” settlements and hundreds of square kilometers of reclaimed territory, and once-respected Western publications churned out articles about a turning point on the front, a heroic Ukrainian offensive that would change the course of the war, and other such nonsense.
However, by mid-summer, news about the AFU’s success on the southern front became less frequent and after Syrsky’s removal, disappeared completely. Instead, news surfaced about the plight of Ukrainian storm troops which, advancing through the gray zone, got stuck there for weeks and even months. It was reported that due to disruptions in aerial deliveries, the soldiers hid in stashes, lacked food, and were forced to drink their own urine.
On August 12, Zelensky officially summed up the results of the operation. According to his claims, 745 square kilometers of territory had been liberated and Ukraine regained control over 26 settlements located in Dnepropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Zaporozhye regions.
Online victory over Russians
This information was immediately refuted, both by Ukrainian sources (e.g., by Yuriy Butusov, Konstantin Mashovets, and a Ukrainian soldier with the call sign ‘Muchnoy’) and Western media (for example, well-known German journalist Julian Röpcke). But most importantly, the overwhelming majority of these settlements had recent photo and video evidence of the presence of Russian assault troops. Some were even located in the rear of the Russian army and well beyond the recognized gray zone.
The discrepancy in cartographic data provided by the Ukrainian and Russian sides is noteworthy. The Russian front line is primarily marked using very conservative methodology: photo and video references. According to certain data, the situation on the ground deviates even more significantly in favor of the Russian Armed Forces.
So what really happened? Then Commander-in-Chief of the AFU Syrsky and the Ukrainian General Staff attempted to adopt the Russian army’s advanced assault tactics, i.e., infiltration by small infantry groups. With drones dominating the battlefield around the clock, such assault duos stealthily penetrate the gray zone and attempt to reach enemy strongholds.
Simultaneously, these strongholds are identified by aerial reconnaissance and destroyed by air and artillery strikes.
On the map, this looks like tentacles that penetrate deep into the enemy’s defenses, gradually creating a numerical superiority in one area or another and forcing the enemy to move FPV drone launch points further back. As a result of this painstaking work, the gray zone gradually turns red, i.e, comes under the control of the Russian army.
Due to the Russian army’s advantage in aviation and artillery and particularly since the initiative lies with the attacking side, this situation is very unpleasant for the AFU. Often, situations occur where no infantry or drones remain in a particular section of the front.
As a result of this tactic of semi-encirclement, replicated to a various extent across the entire front, Russian assault groups have been able to penetrate Ukrainian defenses and form a sort of noose around the AFU’s strongholds.
The AFU’s assault duos
The Ukrainian Armed Forces attempted to adopt the Russian strategy. Assault regiments were formed that reported directly to the commander-in-chief and were supposed to become the main striking force of the Ukrainian army. However, as we know, things did not go according to plan.
The tactics described above do not bring immediate results. The attrition of the enemy’s defenses and the formation of semi-encirclements take weeks, sometimes months, and only in the final stage does quantity begin to translate into quality: the weakened defense begins to collapse, and the enemy is forced to pull reserves from other sectors of the front, which in turn, results in a crisis.
The spring-summer campaign of 2026 demonstrated that the AFU are incapable of advancing in any given sector for more than a couple of weeks. The arrows on the first map could have become reality if the Ukrainian offensive had been a) simultaneous, b) continuous, and c) supported by superior forces and resources. Then, and only then, would the assault duos be able to act as a vanguard, a kind of landing force, gradually followed by the main forces. Only under these conditions would the accomplishment of the tactical objective (i.e., taking hold of a particular defensive line) contribute to the strategic objective – i.e, the preemptive exhaustion of the enemy along the entire front or along a long section of it.
Since the AFU possessed none of these capabilities, the assault troops found themselves isolated and ultimately abandoned to their fate in the gray zone. Instead of being the vanguard of the offensive, they became its sole component and therefore were doomed.
What were the real results of the operation? After all, as we’ve seen, its goal was not to liberate a certain number of villages or square kilometers. The goal was to shift the strategic situation in favor of the AFU at a critically important section of the front and to secure Zaporozhye and their own rear.
None of this was accomplished. However, Syrsky did achieve one thing: he slowed the Russian army’s advance in this sector and apparently delayed the decisive events around Zaporozhye.
What’s next?
The new commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, Mikhail Drapaty, has been tasked with holding the Slaviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration, the last stronghold of the AFU in Donbass, at any cost. Two new army groups are being created for this purpose, and the Ukrainian army’s assault units are (once again) being consolidated into the ‘commander-in-chief’s reserve’.
However, rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic won’t solve the AFU’s main problems: a shortage of personnel and the near absence of aviation and artillery. Shifting the main efforts to Donbass could lead to the crumbling of the AFU’s southern front, which is what happened last year.
The front is already unstable. As of late August, Russia’s Dnepr and East Group of Forces are advancing in seven sectors – something that Syrsky’s assault troops could only dream of. Street battles continue in Orekhovo, the AFU’s main defensive hub in the south.
In previous years, the Russian army achieved its greatest success in October-December, since towards the end of the year the quantity of assault operations finally translated into quality.
We’ll see what happens this time.

articles.title: Missile strike hits Belgorod, reportedly damaging Ozon facility and power plant
articles.body:
Smoke rises over Belgorod, Russia, following a reported missile strike on Aug. 30, 2026. (Exilenova+ / Telegram)
Russia's Belgorod came under a missile attack on Aug. 30, with a logistics facility housing an Ozon sorting center and delivery hub damaged in the strike, according to Russian officials and the company.
The attack comes as Ukraine continues targeting Russian military and logistics infrastructure that supports Moscow's war effort.
Acting Belgorod Oblast Governor Alexander Shuvaev claimed that two people were killed and 16 others injured in the attack.
Ozon confirmed that its sorting center and delivery hub in Belgorod had been hit.
A fire broke out at the facility but was later contained, Ozon said. The company suspended deliveries and the acceptance of customer orders and goods from sellers in Belgorod and the surrounding region while it reorganizes its logistics routes.
OSINT Telegram channel Exilenova reported that the attack also damaged the Belgorod thermal power plant. It also reported a strike near the city's television tower.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claims nor claims made by Russian officials.
Anna Fratsyvir is an assistant opinion editor at the Kyiv Independent, with a background in broadcast journalism and international affairs. Previously, she worked as a news editor at the Kyiv Independent, and as a TV journalist at Ukraine’s public broadcaster Suspilne, covering global politics and international developments. Anna holds a Bachelor's degree in International Communications from Taras Shevchenko National University and is currently an MA candidate in International Relations at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS).
The Financial Times reported on Aug. 30 that Elon Musk was open to Ukraine using Starlink-equipped drones to strike targets in Russia, but said the decision would ultimately be a political one requiring approval from the White House.
The two leaders' meeting took place in a "friendly and constructive atmosphere" and focused on bilateral Russian-Chinese ties, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
Emergency services remain at the scene, while law enforcement agencies are working to determine the circumstances and cause of the explosion, the National Police said.
Sverdlovsk Oblast Governor Denis Pasler confirmed that the strike occurred near a logistics center but did not identify the company that owns the facility.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov wrote that the rising risk of hostile incidents could lead to an armed confrontation with potential "catastrophic consequences."
At around 8:10 p.m. local time on Aug. 28, a Russian drone struck a facility in the village of Myla, about 5 kilometers (3 miles) west of Kyiv along the Kyiv-Chop highway. The attack sparked a large fire, followed by ammunition detonations, the Prosecutor General's Office reported.
Romania's Defense Minister Radu Miruta also argued that the Russia-Ukraine war has reached a new stage, marked by stagnation along the front line where Russian forces are unable to advance.
Democratic U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal urged his colleagues in the House of Representatives to approve long-awaited sweeping Russia sanctions legislation in an interview with CBS News on Aug. 30, as the House prepares to reconvene on Aug. 31.

articles.title: Russian strikes on warehouses leave Kyiv shops empty and destroy 12m school books ahead of new term
articles.body:
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday it is preparing “massive strikes” on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Russian forces relentlessly battered Kyiv and cities in the region around the Ukrainian capital for a fifth straight day on Monday, leaving some supermarket shelves bare after repeated strikes on warehouses as Ukraine reels from attacks with jet-powered drones.
Russia has intensified its aerial attacks in recent months, more than four years after it launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour.
Almost constant air raid alerts in the Kyiv region in recent days have severely disrupted daily routines. Two major attacks in July killed almost 50 civilians and a strike on Saturday killed at least 38 people.
Meanwhile, an overnight strike on a printing press on the edge of the Ukrainian capital destroyed around 12 million textbooks ahead of the start of the new school year.
Classes were due to resume at Ukrainian schools on Tuesday, but it was unclear whether parents would send their children. Schools have air raid shelters, and classes can also be held online.
Earlier this month, a Russian strike on a warehouse in northeastern Kharkiv destroyed 8 million books, the publishing house said, slamming it as an attack on Ukrainian culture.
It is not the first time Russia has struck a major publishing centre, drawing accusations from Kyiv that Moscow was specifically targeting them.
"The enemy is trying to burn out our education and culture," the publisher, Ranok, said.
But Ukraine has also tried to make Russian civilians feel the burden of war by hammering major online retailers and oil facilities.
The attacks have brought shortages for ordinary Russians, though its strikes have not been as deadly for civilians.
Ukraine builds technology to counter jet-powered drones
A pall of black smoke drifted over Kyiv on Monday morning. In Brovary and Boryspil, cities in the Kyiv region, the aerial attacks struck several warehouses and four people were wounded, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy conceded on social media that Ukraine is struggling to counter fast-flying jet-propelled drones that Russia is increasingly deploying.
Between Thursday and Sunday, Russia fired almost 1,500 drones at Ukraine and around 800 of them were jet-powered, Zelenskyy said.
Combat aircraft are currently trying to stop the jet-powered versions while Ukraine looks to develop more effective technology.
“Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology,” Zelenskyy said. He didn't elaborate.
Kyiv official says Ukrainians won't go hungry
Repeated Russian strikes on food distribution centres and retail hubs have disrupted Ukrainian logistics, leaving some supermarket shelves bare and fuelling public concern about shortages.
Those fears prompted Zelenskyy adviser Serhii Beskrestnov to say on social media on Monday that Ukraine will not go hungry.
He urged the public not to give in to rumours, disinformation or panic, saying producers and retailers are currently restructuring supply chains.
He added that European countries would be ready to fill any food supply shortfall, if necessary.
At the same time, Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to leave civilians cold and without running water in the approaching winter.
Russian forces launched what officials said was a massive overnight drone attack on Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, which borders Russia, where an energy facility was damaged, according to Viacheslav Chaus, head of the regional military administration.
He did not provide details of the damage.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday it is preparing “massive strikes” on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Russia overnight shot down 239 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea, the Defence Ministry in Moscow said Monday.
A Ukrainian missile attack on Sunday evening on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people, acting regional Governor Alexander Shuvayev said.

articles.title: Cornered by Stalemate, Putin Prepares to Escalate the War in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Cornered by Stalemate, Putin Prepares to Escalate the War in Ukraine
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s refusal to back down in Ukraine is rooted in the survival instincts of Russia’s “gangster politics,” The Economist reported on August 30.
The report noted that the cornered leader is now planning to escalate the war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His predatory worldview was recently on display during an August 29 meeting with university students in Moscow, where Putin bizarrely claimed that orcas eat polar bears to illustrate “the food chain” and justify the war.
While factually inaccurate, The Economist noted that the remark provided a window into the mindset of a leader facing a strategic dead-end. With the Russian army stalemated and suffering tens of thousands of casualties each month, and Ukrainian drone strikes inflicting visible damage on Russian infrastructure, Putin is seeking a new way to escalate his way out of the crisis.
Western intelligence agencies are increasingly anxious about his next moves. The Economist highlighted several recent indicators of this growing alarm: CIA Director John Ratcliffe unexpectedly flew to Moscow on August 25, Finland requested Swedish military assistance to monitor its border for incursions, Romania destroyed a Russian naval drone targeting a drilling platform, and authorities in Germany and Slovakia foiled suspected sabotage plots linked to Moscow.
Putin himself has ended his long silence regarding Ukraine’s successful drone campaign against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, including warehouses belonging to the e-commerce giant Wildberries. In an August 22 address, he accused Ukraine of opening a “Pandora’s box” and promised severe retaliation.
Earlier that same day, he dismissed any notion of peace negotiations, vowing to his political party that the military operation would move “only forward.”
Sources close to the Kremlin told The Economist that after weeks of deliberation over the summer, Putin appears to have formally chosen the path of escalation. Waning public tolerance for the war is becoming an increasing concern; independent polling from the Levada Centre shows 57% of Russians now describe the situation as “tense,” citing the rising death toll, mobilization fears, and a lack of a future.
The mood among the Russian elite is even more pessimistic. Insiders cited by The Economist reveal a growing consensus that the nearly five-year war is a failure because of the sheer amount of time wasted, regardless of the outcome. However, the criminal logic guiding Putin’s regime dictates that he can never show weakness.
A failure to achieve even his minimum goal of capturing the entire Donbas region could put his life in physical danger. “They will hang me,” he reportedly confessed to cronies earlier in the war, The Economist wrote.
While the exact shape of the impending escalation remains unclear, The Economist suggests Russia will likely intensify hybrid warfare and sabotage operations targeting European supply routes to Ukraine. On the battlefield, Russian sources indicate Putin is prepared to throw an additional 300,000 to 400,000 men into the fight.
Rather than announcing a highly unpopular new mobilization wave, the Kremlin is expected to rely on localized coercion by regional governments to fill the ranks. Ultimately, these escalatory measures are designed to project strength and ensure regime survival, even as they guarantee further instability and suffering.
Russia’s manpower crisis is further underscored by Western intelligence estimates indicating Moscow is losing roughly 6,000 more troops each month than it can recruit. Despite enlisting about 1,000 personnel daily, the Kremlin remains unable to cover battlefield casualties, driving Russian forces to intensify long-range missile strikes against Ukraine’s civilians instead.

articles.title: Poland Joins US Drone-Warfare Drills Built on Ukraine’s Battlefield Lessons
articles.body:
Polish special forces are taking part in US-led drills focused on drone warfare as Poland seeks to bolster its capabilities in the event of a potential confrontation with Moscow.
The multiday exercises, which began Friday, are taking place at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center near the town of Hohenfels in southern Germany, the US Army’s main combat training center in Europe.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The exercise was initially developed for the Green Berets, the US Army’s special forces and was designed around Ukraine’s battlefield experience in its war with Russia.
This is the first time a NATO ally such as Poland has taken part in the training.
During the drills, Polish forces will operate under a scenario in which they must covertly bypass enemy positions, travel about 100 kilometers through German countryside controlled by a simulated adversary, and use a drone to strike an important target, according to an exclusive report by The Associated Press (AP).
The reported route runs from Hohenfels toward the Grafenwöhr Training Area, a major US Army and NATO training site near the town of Grafenwöhr in Bavaria, southern Germany.
‘Lessons’ from Ukraine
According to the report, the exercise is planned to take place several times a year and may eventually include military personnel from most or all 32 NATO countries.
“We’re using lessons learned from Ukraine,” a US special forces officer told AP.
Kremlin Says Putin Sees ‘Absolutely No Point’ in Trump-Zelensky Peace Summit
“All of those effects that we’re seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome — we’re doing our best to replicate,” he added.

articles.title: Russia plans to control drones from two-seater Su-57D fighter jet
articles.body:
Russia plans to control drones from two-seater Su-57D fighter jet
Russia has outlined the tasks for which it plans to use the two-seater variant of the Su-57D fighter jet, a prototype of which is currently undergoing flight tests.
Source: Russian state corporation Rostec
Details: Russia claims that the aircraft made its first flight in May 2026.
Rostec has identified two main tasks for the new modification. The first involves using the aircraft for training to practise special flight modes which, the company claims, cannot be replicated on ground-based simulators.
The second task involves testing technologies that Russia classifies as sixth-generation. The developers intend the second cockpit to enable the Su-57D to serve as an airborne control station for unmanned systems.
Mikhail Strelets, Director of the Sukhoi Design Bureau, said this capability is important for controlling the S-70 Okhotnik drone, as well as drone swarms and groups, when the main pilot's attention is focused on carrying out the primary combat mission.
In addition, representatives of Russia's United Aircraft Corporation said that the two-seater Su-57D is planned to be used to test so-called combat artificial intelligence technologies that the corporation's specialists are currently developing.
However, Russia has not provided any test results confirming the Su-57D's claimed capabilities for controlling drones or employing artificial intelligence technologies.
According to Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), the S-70 Okhotnik ("Hunter") is a Russian reconnaissance and strike UAV. Its stated maximum take-off weight is 25 tonnes, its range is 6,000 km, and its maximum speed is 1,400 km/h.
Background: Previously, DIU revealed details of a new Russian cruise missile developed for the Su-57 fighter jet.

articles.title: Poland intercepts Russian spy plane over Baltic Sea again
articles.body:
- Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, 30 kilometers north of Łeba.
- Poland's defense minister said the aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, in at least the third such intercept reported this year.
Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) north of Łeba on Poland’s coast, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
“Russia has once again tested our deterrence and air defense systems,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote. “Before noon, 30 km north of Łeba, our fighters intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft. There was no violation of our airspace over the Baltic.”
The aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, according to the minister. Monday’s intercept was at least the third publicly reported Il-20 intercept by Polish fighters over the Baltic Sea this year, following similar incidents in March, May and July.
The Il-20, known by NATO as the “Coot-A,” is a Soviet-designed signals and electronic reconnaissance aircraft derived from the Il-18 airliner. Russia regularly flies the aircraft over the Baltic Sea to collect electronic and communications intelligence, and the flights have become a recurring trigger for NATO quick reaction alert sorties in the region.
In several previous intercepts this year, Polish officials said the Il-20 was operating without a filed flight plan and with its transponder switched off. In March, Poland’s Operational Command of the Armed Forces said one such intercept marked the aircraft’s ninth reconnaissance mission of the year in the region, describing the pattern as a sustained Russian intelligence-gathering effort rather than an isolated event.
Poland has used both MiG-29 and F-16 fighters to carry out Il-20 intercepts over the Baltic this year. The MiG-29, a Soviet-designed aircraft, remains in a shrinking quick reaction alert role as Poland phases in newer F-16 and FA-50 fighters, with some retired Polish MiG-29s transferred to Ukraine.
Kosiniak-Kamysz has previously described the Il-20 flights as deliberate provocations intended to test Polish and NATO air defense response times, radar coverage and command-and-control coordination along the alliance’s eastern flank.

articles.title: Roketsan Conducts First Ground Launch of ÇAKIR Cruise Missile
articles.body:
Roketsan has conducted the first publicly disclosed launch tests of the ÇAKIR cruise missile from a mobile ground-based launcher against land and sea targets.
Roketsan published footage of the launches on its X account.
Roketsan said two missiles were launched in two separate tests, and both hit their respective targets. The company did not disclose the launch ranges, target types or detailed configuration of the launcher.
In 2024, the company conducted launch tests of the ÇAKIR missile from a Bayraktar Akıncı UAV. At the time, the missile struck a surface target at a range of 100 kilometers.
Roketsan unveiled the ÇAKIR family of subsonic cruise missiles in March 2022 as a modular system designed for use from air, naval and ground platforms.
The ÇAKIR cruise missile was developed with a modular architecture that allows it to be adapted for different missions.
In its press release, Roketsan said the missile would be produced in anti-ship, anti-radiation and strike cruise missile variants.
The missile weighs approximately 275 kilograms, rising to 330 kilograms when equipped with a solid-fuel booster for launches from ground platforms. The warhead weighs 70 kilograms.
The stated range of the ÇAKIR exceeds 150 kilometers. Its baseline guidance system combines inertial navigation, jam-resistant satellite navigation and an altimeter. Different versions can be equipped with various types of seeker.
The missile is also equipped with a two-way data link that allows target information to be updated in flight, a decision to be made on conducting a second attack, and the mission to be canceled.
The missile is designed to use terrain masking to approach targets covertly or fly at low altitude over the sea. Roketsan has also stated that multiple missiles can be used in coordinated attacks.
According to Naval News, in July 2023, the CEO of Roketsan said an export agreement for the ÇAKIR had been signed before the missile entered service with the Turkish military but did not identify the customer. Two publicly known customers for the system are Qatar and Indonesia.
Earlier, in late March, Turkey’s SOM-J air-launched cruise missile, developed specifically for the F-35, successfully completed flight testing and entered serial production.

articles.title: Senator Elizabeth Warren calls Trump ‘the most corrupt president ever in American history’
articles.body:
Senator Elizabeth Warren calls Trump ‘the most corrupt president ever in American history’
TEHRAN — US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has delivered a scathing critique of President Donald Trump, labeling him "the most corrupt president ever in American history" and accusing major energy corporations aligned with his administration of reaping vast financial gains from the military conflict against Iran.
Speaking at an election campaign rally for a junior senator from Massachusetts, Warren emphasized that oil executives who poured millions into political campaigns are now extracting massive corporate windfall earnings as energy costs skyrocket for ordinary working families. She pointed out that the single fastest path to relieving energy burdens on everyday citizens is to halt military operations in the region immediately, declaring that ending the campaign in Iran would instantly lower fuel prices at home. “So the question becomes: What do we do about that? When Donald Trump starts a war with Iran and his oil buddies, who gave him a million dollars for his campaign—when they start making profits like crazy, then our job is to call it out and fight back. That’s what we do,” Warren told the roaring crowd during her address. “You want to lower the price of gasoline? End the war in Iran. Just end it,” she added, directly challenging the White House's foreign policy rationale.
The senator's blunt assessment comes alongside recent official financial disclosure filings showing that Trump continues to hold and actively trade stock portfolios in major natural gas and petroleum giants. While White House spokespersons maintain that these portfolio movements operate independently of presidential oversight, political analysts and watchdog organizations highlight the undeniable conflict of interest in overseeing a massive military operation while maintaining tens of millions of dollars in personal equity tied directly to energy conglomerates that profit from wartime market volatility.
Financial data analyzed by congressional committees reveals that major US oil corporations—including ExxonMobil and Chevron—have seen their quarterly earnings multiply dramatically since the outbreak of hostilities, with corporate profits topping tens of billions of dollars and driving executive net worth to historic highs. Senate Joint Economic Committee reports indicate that Trump's personal energy portfolio alone has surged in value by over $15 million during the conflict, growing by an average of nearly 40 percent since the beginning of the year. Inside the US Congress, a steadily growing coalition of anti-war lawmakers and progressive representatives has voiced fierce opposition to the administration's aggressive policy in West Asia, strongly condemning the unprovoked and illegal nature of the military actions.
Opponents in Capitol Hill argue that the executive branch deliberately bypassed constitutional war powers requirements to embark on a disastrous military campaign that severely jeopardizes international stability, harms America's standing on the global stage, and serves narrow corporate interests over the welfare of the American public. Members of Congress are demanding an immediate cessation of offensive military funding and an end to weapon transfers, asserting that hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars currently being spent on overseas military interventions must instead be redirected toward fixing crumbling domestic infrastructure, expanding healthcare access, and alleviating the severe economic burdens faced by working families at home.
The broader international crisis stems from the joint military operations initiated by US and Israeli forces against Iran on February 28, targeting military sites and civil infrastructure, including residential area. Iranian defense forces responded under international frameworks of self-defense as recognized by Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, deploying advanced missile capabilities and maritime operational measures to neutralize hostile targets, protect territorial integrity, and assert strict defensive control over critical strategic transit corridors such as the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has repeatedly affirmed its right to defend its territory against foreign hostility, maintaining that regional security must be governed by regional nations without imperialist interference.
Six months into the military campaign, the US armed forces face operational constraints, highlighted by the rapid depletion of critical precision-guided munition stockpiles, Patriot interceptors, and complex air defense systems. US defense industrial supply chains continue to struggle under severe structural bottlenecks and material shortages, rendering the rapid replenishment of key military hardware functionally impossible in the short term. At the same time, the broader American domestic economy suffers from persistent inflation, soaring pump prices, rising shipping fees, and expanding public debt, leaving working-class citizens to bear the financial costs of an overextended foreign policy. Public dissatisfaction across major cities continues to surge as critics point out the glaring contrast between unlimited funding for foreign military actions and the neglected needs of the domestic population.

articles.title: The US built itself a Russo-Ukrainian drone-war drill—Poland is the first ally in
articles.body:
US Army Green Berets have begun training Poland's special forces to move and strike on the kind of drone-saturated ground Ukraine fights on, the Associated Press reported. No ally besides the US had taken on the drone-heavy drill until now, and US instructors built it only months ago from Ukraine's battlefield lessons.
Ukraine has turned from an aid recipient into a source of tactics, feeding allies the counter-drone methods and strike tactics it forged against Russia's invasion. NATO is still behind: an alliance war game in February exposed how badly its own forces fare against drone warfare of that kind.
Bavaria plays the part of Russia
The drill spans a 1,100-square-mile (3,000 km²) stretch of Bavarian countryside around the US Army's Hohenfels training center, an hour southeast of Nuremberg. Polish commandos must slip past a US airborne unit playing the enemy, then move about 60 miles (100 km) north to Grafenwoehr and blow up a mock target.
In earlier runs, Green Berets removed their uniforms to blend in, a senior enlisted soldier familiar with the scenario said. He and a Green Beret officer at the training complex spoke anonymously, under a US policy against naming special forces personnel.
"This is supposed to be Russia and you're going to stand out in Russia," he said.
Farms, villages, cameras, and a populous city line the route. German civilians, largely unaware of the exercise, become the test: any tip they phone to police can help the military pinpoint the team. Once a team is spotted, "now you have the entire Russian arsenal coming at you," the soldier said. The US side can send military police with dogs or direct more drones to the area, and had more than 100 available in earlier runs.
Allies want Ukraine's lessons—the US Army is stepping back
A Green Beret officer said the drill tries to replicate "all of those effects that we're seeing either Russia or Ukraine having to overcome." Ukraine pioneered this kind of drone warfare across four and a half years of fighting Russia. Its combat experience has been entering NATO training elsewhere in Poland, and its drone crews recently outmatched a US brigade in another German drill. The exercise has run just twice before, both this year with US teams, and the officer said he expects most, if not all, of NATO's 32 members to show interest in trying it.
The wider US message on drones has been mixed, AP said. On 20 August, the Army's acting chief of staff ordered a Europe-based drone unit back to infantry duty. US President Donald Trump has also wavered on cutting troop levels in Europe, and his administration launched a force review.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Ukraine was already helping five Middle East and Gulf states counter Iranian drones fired during the US-Israeli war on Iran, and that US and European governments had asked for help too, AP reported.

articles.title: Ukraine Knocks Out Two Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense Systems in Back-to-Back Strikes
articles.body:

Ukraine Knocks Out Two Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense Systems in Back-to-Back Strikes
Ukrainian forces destroyed two Russian Pantsir-S1 short-range air defense systems in separate strikes in temporarily occupied Crimea and Russia’s Krasnodar region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The first Pantsir-S1 was destroyed near the temporarily occupied city of Kerch on August 29, while the second was hit a day later near a military airfield in Yeysk, Krasnodar region, according to the open-source channel Dossier Shpiona, which published images showing the destroyed systems.
OSINT project CyberBoroshno reported that Russian forces had positioned a decoy near the Pantsir-S1 in Yeysk. The presence of the decoy did not prevent the operational system from being identified and struck.
The Pantsir-S1 is a Russian self-propelled short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery system designed to protect military and other critical facilities against aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones.
The system combines two twin-barrel 30 mm 2A38M automatic cannons with up to 12 surface-to-air missiles. Its cannons can engage targets at ranges of up to approximately 4 kilometers (2.5 miles), while its missiles can reach targets at distances of up to 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) and altitudes of up to 15 kilometers (9.3 miles).
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck multiple Russian military targets, including a radar station and an S-400 command vehicle in the Bryansk region, a communications hub in Belgorod, a drone command post near Huliaipole, and logistics depots in temporarily occupied Crimea, Luhansk region, and Russia’s Kursk region, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 31.

articles.title: Budanov's political honeymoon is over
articles.body:
Budanov's political honeymoon is over
President's Office Head Kyrylo Budanov works in his office on April 18, 2026 in Kyiv, Ukraine. (Julia Weber/Babel.ua/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
President's Office Head Kyrylo Budanov had something rare in Ukrainian politics: a reputation largely untouched by scandals.
A career military officer, he is best known for running Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) and overseeing a number of formidable operations during Russia's full-scale war. Under his leadership, the agency came to be regarded as one of Ukraine's most competent institutions.
Nine months after switching a military post for political office, Budanov became mired in controversy.
The corruption
Budanov's name has surfaced in recordings as part of a sprawling corruption case, Hromadske news outlet reported on Aug. 26, citing court documents. The case centers on Budanov's former deputy, Iryna Mudra, who was charged last week with corporate raiding and money laundering.
The case is linked to the ongoing investigation into Energoatom, the state nuclear-power monopoly. In the new revelations, Mudra says that the illegal proceedings she was undertaking were ordered by her "boss."
Mudra's boss is Budanov.
The recordings repeatedly refer to a "Kyrylo Oleksiyovich" — Budanov's first name and patronymic. At a court hearing on Aug. 25, a lawyer for Sense Bank's chief executive, one of the suspects, cited an exchange where a man bearing Budanov's name was discussing illegal activity.
Transcripts submitted by prosecutors explicitly identify the speaker as Budanov, according to Hromadske.
Other conversations are more pointed. Mudra and the former lawmaker Maksym Mykytas allegedly discussed a request from Timur Mindich, a suspect in the Energoatom case and a close associate of the president, to take control of Sense Bank's cash flows. "Mindich approached Kyrylo," Mudra allegedly said, adding that there were "serious money flows" to be controlled.
Mudra and Mykytas are accused of laundering Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) through Sense Bank to pay bail for another high-ranking official implicated in the scheme.
The case is complicated, with revelations in November, May, and now August adding meat to the biggest corruption scandal of President Volodymyr Zelensky's tenure.
Anti-corruption agencies haven't pointed at Budanov, and he has not been charged.
Budanov joined the President's Office in January, replacing Andriy Yermak, who was ousted months prior amid the same corruption scandal and charged with money laundering.
In some ways, Budanov was seen as Yermak's opposite. Officials and lawmakers who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said the former intelligence chief, unlike his predecessor, showed little appetite for political intrigue.
Yet he kept Yermak's team in place. He said in an interview on national television aired on Aug. 28 that he believes in "institutional continuity" and didn't want to disrupt the government's work while new officials learned their roles.
Critics say he wasn't allowed to bring the people he trusted.
Some saw Budanov's appointment as head of the President's Office as either Zelensky's attempt to remove a potential rival or to shape a possible successor.
Budanov has regularly been featured in opinion polls, consistently ranking among the country's most trusted public figures. He has trailed only Zelensky and Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former army chief and now Ukraine's ambassador to the U.K. The latest poll by the Socis research center also placed Budanov behind former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in the potential presidential race.
Fedorov was riding a high wave following his dismissal as defense minister. Nationwide protests to reappoint Fedorov were ongoing for a month.
Observers who spoke to the Kyiv Independent believe the current political crisis and corruption scandal that followed could damage Budanov's reputation and weaken his political standing.
Political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko says Budanov has now become a "hostage of Zelensky," a position that could undermine his chances of pursuing an independent political career.
"This is the main problem and challenge for him," Fesenko told the Kyiv Independent. "(Budanov) will have to decide soon whether he stays on Zelensky's team, risking further reputational damage and potentially legal problems if situations like this continue to arise."
"If he wants to preserve his potential status as an independent political figure, I think he will have to distance himself from Zelensky."
"If Budanov has political ambitions — and he does — he would have been better off staying on as the war hero and building up his popularity," one pro-government lawmaker said on condition of anonymity, echoing the sentiment. "The President's Office has always been a toxic place."
Fesenko says the question now is whether Budanov will face any legal consequences, including actual charges. The case materials suggest he may have asked Mudra to collect money for bail, he says, but "collecting money for bail is not a criminal offense."
"And if it turns out that there was a breach of the law or some illegal schemes involved, then there could be legal risks," he added.
The politics
Since taking office, Budanov has been devoted to peace talks with Russia. He has also taken up efforts to rebury the remains of prominent Ukrainian historical figures and pushed for the creation of the National Pantheon to honor its heroes, past and present.
After joining the President's Office, Budanov soon appeared at an event dedicated to Ukraine's European integration, presenting himself as an opponent of corruption and saying that the President's Office was open to proposals from anti-corruption activists.
"Corruption begins where hands-on management begins," he said in April, after Yermak, who was tainted in controversy, was dismissed.
But the recently published materials alleged that, behind the scenes, corruption didn't die out with Yermak out of office. On the tapes, Mudra allegedly said that an unnamed top official from the President's Office had told her that "corruption shouldn't be fought — it should be controlled."
On domestic political scandals Budanov has always kept his distance, urging unity and saying that wartime infighting weakens Ukraine. Following the scandal, Budanov echoed the same line, saying that "let the court sort it out."
Officials and experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent believe that, if true, the published recordings by anti-corruption institutions could tie Budanov to the existing unpopular system.
"Budanov is, after all, part of the military establishment, which is clearly tied to the political leadership. That system can force everyone to play by its rules, even a war hero," says Olexiy Haran, politics professor at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy and research advisor at the Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
Fesenko argues that Budanov was shaped by a military hierarchy in which orders from above are effectively binding, making refusal a potential breach of discipline.
"Zelensky most likely gave Budanov the order. Budanov had no personal motive to save (an unconnected high-ranking official)," he said.
The President's Office hasn't responded as of publication time.
The future
Budanov's involvement in the scandal has raised a broader question about how Ukrainians tend to balance corruption allegations against those who have a good track record defending the country against Russia. Budanov is perhaps the most prominent Ukrainian military figure who may become embroiled in a corruption scandal.
His record as a military officer shapes how people perceive the allegations against him — with his supporters downplaying the allegations and his critics more condemning him, during multiple interviews with the Kyiv Independent.
"For a significant portion of the population, particularly among the military, the position is unequivocal: 'Don’t touch the war hero,'" Fesenko said.
Commanders of the Christian Corps, a military group fighting under the supervision of Ukraine's military intelligence, have issued a public statement in Budanov's defense. The corps includes several units, including Bratstvo (Brotherhood), Tradition and Order, and Revansh, which grew out of far-right movements.
Commenting on the allegations, they said there had been "an attempt to push a negative narrative" about Budanov, pointing to his record of achievements.
Fesenko said military figures could, both publicly and privately, signal to the country's anti-corruption institutions that there is a red line the bureau should not cross. Crossing it, he believes, could trigger a confrontation.
Haran argues that the military has already crossed the line. Further involvement by military figures in politics or anti-corruption efforts, he says, would be "very dangerous."
"People with military achievements are treated differently," Haran told the Kyiv Independent. "But those achievements should not put them beyond the reach of law enforcement or anti-corruption bodies."

articles.title: EU urges Iran to curb nuclear, missile programs, backs diplomatic efforts
articles.body:
Melike Pala
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
The European Union on Monday urged Iran to curb its nuclear and ballistic missile programs, halt what it described as destabilizing activities and end its military support for Russia.
In a statement issued ahead of the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meetings in Asheville, US, on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, the EU also called on Tehran to cease “violence and repression against its own people.”
The bloc said continued diplomatic efforts were necessary to reach a peace settlement, restore regional stability and ensure “full freedom of navigation and safe transit” through the Strait of Hormuz.
“The EU has adopted extensive sanctions to prevent Iran from exploiting the global economy and financial system to sustain its hostile actions and undermine international security,” the statement said.
The EU added that it remained ready to take further measures when necessary to safeguard its security and interests, including freedom of navigation through the strategic waterway.
It also welcomed efforts aimed at persuading Iran to end what the bloc described as destabilizing activities and engage in peace negotiations “in good faith,” including through additional economic pressure.
The statement specifically cited the US-led Operation Economic Outcast as part of those efforts.
“The EU will continue to work closely with the United States and other G7 and international partners to maintain pressure on Iran and contribute to de-escalation and regional stability,” the statement added.

articles.title: Sen. Ted Cruz says 'unequivocal yes' to Trump’s 'mission accomplished' claim on Iran
articles.body:
United States Senator Ted Cruz backed President Donald Trump’s Truth Social post declaring “mission accomplished” in the war with Iran, while going further by calling for the collapse of the Iranian regime during a Meet the Press interview on Sunday.
Host Kristen Welker asked Cruz whether he agreed with the president’s declaration, noting that the war was entering its sixth month this week despite Trump previously saying it would last only a few weeks.
Cruz responded that he agreed “unequivocally” that the president’s military objectives had been achieved.
According to Cruz, the US has eliminated Iran’s military capabilities and nearly destroyed its supply and manufacturing infrastructure for ballistic missiles and drone programs, as well as its air force, navy, and leadership.
“Their air force is in rubble on the runway. Their navy is sunk and at the bottom of the ocean. Much of their senior leadership has been eliminated. So in terms of military objectives, I think that is correct,” Cruz said.
Cruz also addressed the US blockade of Iran and its objective of imposing economic pressure on the country, claiming that Iran’s economy is in “free fall.”
“Now, if you also look at the objective of imposing economic harm, right now with the blockade that we are holding on Iran, Iran is facing $500 million a day of economic cost. That is enormous cost that is ratcheting up,” Cruz said.
Cruz supports collapsing Iran regime, arming Kurds and protesters
The senator went further, saying he supports a long-term objective of collapsing the Iranian regime and doing so by arming Kurdish forces and protesters.
“Now, I would like to see the longer-term objective be regime collapse,” Cruz said.
“The ayatollah and the mullahs are radical Islamist zealots... The Ayatollah routinely chants, ‘Death to America.’ The Ayatollah... This regime... has been the world’s leading state sponsor of terror for 47 years. So what I’ve been urging is for President Trump and the Trump administration to arm the protesters, the people of Iran. Arm the Kurds and let the protesters remove this regime,” he said.
Welker followed up by asking Cruz why US troops had not returned home if the military objectives had been achieved.
Cruz responded that while there are “occasional skirmishes,” the “active military conflict has reduced significantly,” and said the troops’ current role is focused on enforcing economic pressure through the blockade.
Cruz highlights role of Iranian protesters
Cruz said he believes economic sanctions are a powerful tool, but argued they would be even more effective with support from protesters inside Iran. He also highlighted that the conflict began after the regime killed tens of thousands of protesters.
He reiterated his support for arming protesters, saying: “Frankly, Kristen, it’s not fair to expect some Iranian protester standing there with a rock to stand up against soldiers with machine guns. I believe if we arm the protesters, particularly the Kurds, who had a long history of being effective fighters.”
Cruz said that while the US should not determine who governs Iran, it does have an interest in preventing the country from being ruled by a regime that threatens America.
“It’s not our business to determine who the government of Iran is. But it is our business to say the government of Iran should not be a radical theocrat who hates America and is trying to kill Americans,” he said.
Cruz concluded by praising Trump’s leadership, saying: “And President Trump is acting as a strong commander in chief to keep the American people safe.”

articles.title: Russia’s shadow war on Europe is widening—NATO still sees no attack coming
articles.body:
NATO said on 30 August 2026 it sees no imminent threat of attack from Russia, Reuters reported. Russia is stepping up covert operations across Europe alongside its war on Ukraine, a NATO official said. The statement followed a week of warnings from Western capitals.
Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe has grown steeply since the full-scale invasion, reaching from Molotov cocktails thrown at a French drone plant to severed undersea cables and attacks on railways. Recorded attacks in Europe hit 34 in 2024, nearly triple the 12 counted a year earlier by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, which says Western states have yet to build an effective answer to a campaign pitched below the threshold that would trigger a military response.
Attacks on Ukraine and covert acts in Europe are both rising
Russia is attacking Ukraine harder and running more covert operations in Europe at the same time, the official said.
"Even as the Russians are facing very substantial resistance from Ukraine, they are stepping up attacks on Ukraine as well as hybrid acts in Europe," the official said, adding: "As always, NATO remains vigilant and alert to the variety of threats we face. At this time, we see no imminent threat of attack."
Hybrid acts mean covert moves—sabotage, arson, drone flights—that stop short of open war.
A week of alarms
Three developments that week bore on the same question—whether Russia would strike a NATO country, not only Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on 28 August that Russia is preparing to escalate both in Ukraine and across the region, putting the critical window at seven or eight months.
Days earlier, CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to meet intelligence counterparts. Two people familiar with the meeting told Reuters that Ratcliffe did raise the prospect of Russia acting against a NATO state, though whether the trip had any other aim stayed unclear. One source said several topics came up, including Russia's support for Iran. US President Donald Trump dismissed that reading two days later, saying Russian President Vladimir Putin will not attack NATO territory and that Ratcliffe carried no message.

articles.title: Drone factory supplying Ukraine catches fire in Poland: unknown individual spotted on premises
articles.body:
Drone factory supplying Ukraine catches fire in Poland: unknown individual spotted on premises
A fire broke out overnight at a factory belonging to WB Electronics in Poland, a company that produces drones for the Ukrainian and Polish armies, among others. Shortly before the fire started, surveillance cameras reportedly captured an unknown individual wearing a balaclava on the company's premises.
Source: Onet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The incident occurred at the WB Electronics factory in the town of Skarżysko-Kamienna, halfway between Warsaw and Kraków, which produces military drones for the Polish and Ukrainian armies, as well as flight controllers.
The fire broke out on the night of 30-31 August, 23 minutes after midnight. Simultaneously, the operator of the security firm tasked with monitoring the facility alerted police after sensors were triggered, potentially indicating the intrusion of unauthorised individuals.
Surveillance cameras reportedly captured an unknown individual wearing a balaclava who entered the company's premises over a fence. An abandoned rucksack and a long-sleeved top were subsequently found near the factory.
The Internal Security Agency and military counterintelligence were notified of the incident, and police have opened an investigation.
The fire service said the fire was relatively small and was extinguished within two hours. Internal Security Agency officers then arrived at the scene.
"In the case of fires like this, the special services do what they are supposed to do. We take this situation very seriously… We caution against the temptation to spread any disinformation about this. Internal Security Agency officers are working meticulously to determine whether there are grounds to speak of sabotage," said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister-coordinator for special services.
Background:
- Latvia previously detained three of its citizens on suspicion of arson at a drone factory in neighbouring Estonia.
- According to media reports, Berlin is planning to directly declare Russia responsible for the appearance of a drone containing explosives in Leipzig near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks more drones and air defence from Latvia
articles.body:
Ukraine has asked Latvia to support the rapid delivery of air defence equipment, unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones and additional strike capabilities as Kyiv sets out its current battlefield priorities, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Mykhailo Drapatyi discussed the requirements during a meeting with Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence announced on 29 August.
The Ukrainian side identified four areas as priorities: unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones, what the ministry described as “middle-strike capabilities”, and air defence assets. Khmara also stressed the need for equipment identified as urgent to reach Ukrainian forces as quickly as possible, making delivery times part of the discussions alongside the type of equipment being sought.
Fibre-optic-controlled drones have taken on a growing battlefield role because the control link is carried through a physical fibre rather than relying on a conventional radio connection. The approach can allow operators to retain control in environments where radio-frequency links are heavily disrupted, although the systems bring their own operational limitations.
Unmanned ground vehicles have similarly been employed for an expanding range of battlefield tasks, including logistics and other activities in areas where exposing personnel carries additional risk. Ukraine has increasingly sought to expand the use of uncrewed systems across land, air and maritime operations.
Air defence remains another continuing requirement for Kyiv as Russian forces employ combinations of missiles and uncrewed attack aircraft against targets across Ukraine. The Ukrainian ministry did not identify particular air defence systems being requested from Latvia in its account of the meeting.
Latvia, meanwhile, intends to continue providing security assistance to Ukraine worth at least 0.25% of its gross domestic product each year. Kyiv said it is also looking to Riga to work with other governments and through multinational initiatives to generate further military assistance. The two defence delegations discussed areas beyond the immediate supply of equipment, including rehabilitation for Ukrainian military personnel, training and the development of cyber capabilities.
Ukraine also offered to share operational experience with Latvia. According to the ministry, this could include lessons from multi-domain operations, territorial defence and the construction and development of modern fortifications.
Latvia has been among the NATO members providing sustained military assistance to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: U.S. Army Command Warns Hegseth Against Expanding Operations Against Iran
articles.body:
U.S. military leadership is warning Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against further expanding military operations against Iran.
The Washington Post reports that in a recent classified assessment, U.S. military officials warned that a prolonged large-scale operation in the Middle East could weaken U.S. military capabilities in other regions of the world.
These warnings to Hegseth came from the leaders of the U.S. Army, Navy, and Air Force, as well as four-star commanders responsible for U.S. operations in Europe, Asia, and Latin America. They are contained in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense’s Orders Book (SDOB).
The SDOB is typically published twice a month. The document contains information on the global readiness of U.S. ships, aircraft, personnel, and weapons systems.
The compilation reflects the president’s priorities for the armed forces, as implemented by the secretary of defense, and also includes assessments from senior generals and admirals. Based on these assessments, the Pentagon develops further directives.
According to the document, some U.S. forces deployed to the Middle East are expected to remain in the region through the end of September, while other units will remain through 2027. According to sources familiar with the document, the possibility of further extending the deployment is a cause for concern.
The heads of U.S. European Command, U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, and U.S. Southern Command, as well as the Chief of Naval Operations, oppose such plans.
To support operations in the vicinity of Iran, U.S. geographic combatant commands have been forced to redeploy their ships, aircraft, and other equipment to the region.
This is already limiting the U.S. military’s ability to carry out its missions in other regions and maintain the necessary level of combat readiness.
As previously reported, the Pentagon is preparing at least four options for potentially reducing the U.S. military presence in Europe.
However, European officials remain skeptical about the review and suggest that a decision to reduce the U.S. military presence in Europe may have already been made.
