articles.title: Ex-defence minister Fedorov proposes US creation of "army of drones" in exchange for Patriot interceptors – FT
articles.body:
Ex-defence minister Fedorov offers to help US build "army of drones" in exchange for Patriot interceptors – FT
Former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has said he is ready to help the United States create an "army of drones" in exchange for the supply of Patriot interceptor missiles.
Source: Fedorov in an interview with the Financial Times
Details: Fedorov said he would be "very glad to help America build an army of drones – especially in exchange for Patriot [interceptors] so that we survive this winter".
"I'm ready to make that trade," he said.
Fedorov declined to comment on whether he will meet anyone from US President Donald Trump's administration during his visit to Washington.
According to the FT, citing sources, SpaceX owner Elon Musk previously told Fedorov that he is prepared to allow Ukraine to use drones equipped with Starlink satellite communications beyond its borders to strike targets in Russia. However, according to these sources, Musk said this is a political decision that will have to be made by the White House. Fedorov himself declined to comment on his conversations with Musk.
Speaking about his decision to become an adviser to Italy's defence minister, Fedorov said he would seek similar advisory positions in other partner countries, potentially including France and the US.
He also said he wants to attract American investment to a defence technology fund which, he hopes, will write "a new history" of the war against Russia by creating and managing companies developing new weapons.
Fedorov is seeking backing for the proposed fund from venture capitalists, private investors and US technology companies. He said he was in talks with "a large number" of potential investors interested in Ukrainian innovation.
Fedorov did not provide details about his role in managing the fund or clarify whether he would personally benefit financially from it.
He said Russia is likely to prolong the war and that, if the war continues for another two or three years, the fund will develop cutting-edge "solutions for the battlefield" while giving investors access to the knowledge and experience Ukraine has gained throughout the war.
Background:
- On 22 August, Fedorov said that following his dismissal from government, his future plans include working on a venture fund to attract investment in Ukrainian defence start-ups, setting up a think tank and civic initiatives aimed at a "return to democracy", and lecturing at universities.
- At the time, Fedorov categorically denied plans to seek Donald Trump's backing during his trip to the US but did not rule out meeting billionaire and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
- On 28 August, Fedorov announced that he had accepted an offer from Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto to become his adviser.
- Fedorov's press office stated that his previous position as defence minister does not prevent him from serving as an adviser to the governments of other countries and that he will continue to live and work in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukrainian Influencer Infiltrates Russian Zoom Meeting Covering Drones, Insults Attendees
articles.body:
A popular Ukrainian prankster hacked a video conference for Russian officials discussing chronic problems in national drone production and ended the meeting by demanding that attendees explain why they were so unprofessional and seemingly intent on stealing government money, according to a recording of the Zoom meeting made public on Sunday.
The breach by Evhen Volnov (handle: “Major Chernobaev”) targeted a virtual meeting attended by representatives of the Russian Federation’s Ministry of Industry and Trade and the Russian state air industry agency Rosaviatsia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zoom footage published by Volnov showed 14 Russian officials signed in, including, among others, Rosaviatsia Deputy Head Andrey Potemkin, Evgenia Gvozditsina of the Aviation Register of Russia, and Evgeny Sivaev, deputy director of the drone division at the company Radar MMS.
The Zoom description said the meeting would discuss “the process of certifying developed models of unmanned aviation by organizations and manufacturers.”
Potempkin as chair of the proceedings said that Russian drone manufacturers were underperforming in developing new models of aircraft for his agency’s certification. “We can say that we have room to improve,” Potempkin said, comparing relatively quick Chinese certification of new drones with relatively slow Russian state certification of similar aircraft.
‘They Will Hang Me’: Putin Fears Defeat in Ukraine, Plans to Send 400,000 More Russians to War
Using indirect, bureaucratic language, typical for mid-level Russian officials speaking about an unpleasant fact, he said: “Therefore we must organize our work more responsibly than our colleagues from the Chinese People’s Republic.”
The officials attending the video conference seemed passive. While none interrupted Potempkin’s presentation, most had their video feeds turned off.
Drones have become a war-critical weapon system for Russia, accounting for at least half of all Ukrainian casualties and military equipment losses inflicted by Russian forces. Despite having an economy more than ten times larger than Ukraine’s, Russia likely produces 20-50% fewer military drones by volume. In terms of technology, Ukrainian drone manufacturers have maintained a strong, and at times decisive, advantage over their Russian counterparts since Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine in 2014.
The Ukrainian prankster Volnov hijacked the meeting after Potempkin finished reading off statistics about the relative rates of Russian and Chinese certification of newly-developed drones and opened the floor for discussion.
“Yes, colleagues, there is this question, how is it that Ukrainian engineers assemble effective, combat-capable unmanned air vehicles (UAVs) in the space of three weeks, in primitive conditions, yet Russian aviation, with everyone here sitting at this meeting, billions of rubles spent, and all we have is a little packet of certification documents to show their bosses?”The Russian officials at the meeting did not immediately respond to Volnov’s comments, which under Russia’s wartime laws are not only punishable by more than a decade in prison for the person making them, but can also be incriminating for anyone who intentionally listens to or repeats them.
“How is that on the one hand the enemy (Ukraine) is fighting a war, and meanwhile at the same time you are just siphoning off money from the state budget?” Volnov said.The video showed attendees sitting silently in response to the question. After a brief pause, Potempkin demanded that Volnov identify himself.
“I am Truntek. But can you explain yourself? I mean, I’m sitting here, and all I hear is ‘bla, bla, bla, bla, bla, bla.’”
At the 1:06 mark one attendee uses profanity and another accuses Volnov of being a “provocateur.”
“In my passport it’s written that I’m from the SBU,” Volnov responded, falsely identifying himself as an operator for Ukraine’s national spy agency.
“Thank you for the information. Everything has been recorded. All you participants are recorded. Thank you for the incriminating evidence. And thank you for the interesting and optimistic information.”
Then the video organizer cuts off the conference feed.
Volnov’s commentary accompanying the video said that the meeting had been called to address the fact that Russian drone manufacturers are unable to assemble or certify a single drone unless Beijing supplies the components.
The embarrassing-for-Moscow breach of an official Zoom conference discussing poor drone-certification rates came in the wake of another intrusion publicized by Volkov on Aug. 6. In that incident, he gained access to a closed video conference organized by the Russian Ministry of Defense to discuss the production of anti-drone jamming systems. Representatives of major military contractors, including VoenTorg, VoenTelecom, and OboronLogistics, attended the Zoom meeting, which included at least 25 logins and more than 60 Russian officials.
A cascade of PowerPoint presentations by multiple attendees appeared to show agencies working hard despite limited resources, while arguing that shortcomings in military production were beyond their control. In the video edited by Volnov, balalaika music played in the background and presenters’ remarks were sped up for comedic effect.Volnov disrupted what had until then been a dull, slide-heavy discussion. He pointed out that, despite the efforts of Russian manufacturers of anti-drone jamming systems, thousands of Ukrainian drone strikes continued to hit energy and other critical infrastructure targets across Russia. He then posed a direct question: “Is there any money in the budget for jamming systems at all?”
At least three conference rooms full of attendees were shown picking up papers and walking off-camera, rather than staying and answering Volnov’s question.
“You are all co-conspirators with the regime and you will be held responsible for its crimes. It doesn’t matter what your job is. You know what you are doing and you know that on your hands is the blood of innocent people. Children and women.” Volnov told officials leaving the conference.
In April, per the independent Russian news agency Meduza, Ukrainian operators infiltrated a closed video conference held by Russian army recruiters at Kuban State Agrarian University to drum up volunteers. Volnov on Apr. 4 published a video of an unidentified man calling himself a Ukrainian agent telling potential recruits sitting in a classroom with Russian officers not to sign up.

articles.title: NATO driving the Arctic toward ‘militarization’ – Lavrov (FULL ARTICLE)
articles.body:
Lavrov outlines Arctic ‘challenges and opportunities’ (FULL ARTICLE)
NATO is driving the militarization of the Arctic through intense military preparations that pose a direct threat to Russia’s security and increase the risk of direct armed confrontation, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
However, other than the members of the US-led military bloc, the overwhelming majority of countries are willing to engage with Moscow on equal and mutually beneficial terms, the top diplomat wrote in an article for Arctic.ru published on Monday.
The sweeping article touched on Moscow’s plans to develop Arctic shipping and maritime logistics along its Northern Sea Route, upcoming international cooperation, and the steady erosion of previous guardrails for multilateral collaboration in the region.
Read the full text below:
On August 19, a landmark event took place in Arctic shipping. For the first time, a container ship from China arrived at the port of Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route, a vital part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor. In collaboration with our international partners, this represents the start of a new phase in the development of Russia’s Arctic region, which accounts for at least 10% of the country’s GDP and is home to more than 2.5 million of our citizens. In this regard, I would like to share a number of considerations on how we assess the current state of affairs in the Arctic and how we plan to develop international cooperation there.
Russia and international partners in the Arctic
The Foundations of the Russian State Policy in the Arctic for the Period up to 2035, approved by President Vladimir Putin, focus the efforts of all government bodies on improving the quality of life for the population of the Arctic zone of the Russian Federation, promoting economic growth in its territories, protecting the environment, and fostering mutually beneficial international cooperation. The latter is of particular importance to the Foreign Ministry, which is entrusted with coordinating functions in relations with foreign countries and intergovernmental organizations. And, I would like to emphasize, the whole range of issues relating to the development of the Arctic zone, maritime logistics and the Northern Sea Route plays an important role in the activities of the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation.
Foreign policy priorities at high latitudes have been enshrined in the currently effective Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Russian Federation of March 31, 2023. In the Arctic, Russia is seeking to preserve peace and stability, reduce the level of threats to national security, and create favorable external conditions for the country’s socio-economic development. We are open to interaction with all constructively minded foreign countries displaying reciprocal readiness to put these ideas into practice. There are quite a few such countries. The vast resource, transport, and logistics potential of the Far North, its unique natural and climatic features, long-standing traditions of regional cooperation, and the rich cultural heritage of its indigenous peoples offer broad opportunities for advantageous partnership.
The countries that cooperate closely with us in the Arctic include, first and foremost, China and India. Substantive discussions on Arctic issues take place with Beijing during regular meetings between the heads of government. The specialized bilateral sub-commission on the Northern Sea Route is operational, as are mechanisms for interministerial consultations and scientific exchanges. The results speak for themselves: they include the launch of regular container shipments across Russia’s northern seas, with plans to increase their frequency, and other achievements, including in polar research.
We are engaged in an active dialogue with New Delhi on issues related to high latitudes. In late August, it was discussed at a meeting of the Russian-Indian Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical, and Cultural Cooperation. Indian corporations are involved in developing the resource potential of Russia’s Arctic region. According to some experts, the Arctic could become a major area of cooperation between Russia and India over the next 20 years.
There are prospects for interaction in the Far North with Brazil, Indonesia, Iran and other BRICS countries. We are also ready to develop cooperation with Belarus and other partners and allies in the CIS. South Korea and Singapore should also be mentioned as showing an interest in joint work with Russia in some Arctic projects, notwithstanding their participation in the unfriendly sanction campaign launched by the collective West against our country.
The interest of non-Arctic countries in establishing cooperation with Russia in the High North is reflected in the active participation of foreign guests in symposia and conferences devoted to Arctic issues. Numerous foreign delegations will take part in discussions during special sessions at the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, which opens on September 1 in Vladivostok. Next March, we look forward to welcoming distinguished guests from abroad to the next major international forum of the Russian Arctic, The Arctic – Territory of Dialogue, which will take place in Murmansk.
Challenges affecting international cooperation in the Arctic
Preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation meets the interests of the entire international community, and Russia is undoubtedly interested in this as well. However, there are those who do not share this point of view. How else can one explain the fact that NATO countries, as well as the Alliance as a whole, are driving the region towards militarization and creating hotbeds of international tension there?
In February 2026, NATO launched its Arctic Sentry operation, designed to expand its military presence in the High North. Intensive military preparations are underway in close proximity to our northern borders. NATO is conducting large-scale military exercises involving non-regional countries and introducing new components of its command-and-control system.
Such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security. It also increases the risk of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences.
This deliberate and systematic effort to foster an atmosphere of mistrust in the military sphere is taking place alongside Western attempts to undermine Russia’s legitimate rights in international cooperation through illegitimate financial and economic sanctions targeting legal entities and individuals from countries of the Global Majority involved in joint projects in the Arctic region.
NATO members and other Western countries make no secret of their true motives, openly declaring their intention to turn the Arctic into a new front for opposing the development of Russia and its like-minded partners.
One manifestation of the West’s anti-Russian policy has been the disruption of previously effective mechanisms of multilateral cooperation in the Far North. Some have ceased to exist altogether, while others have largely lost their relevance without Russia’s participation, after Moscow was forced to suspend its engagement with them in response to hostile actions. The Arctic Council, established almost 30 years ago, on September 19, 1996, remains the only functioning intergovernmental organization.
The Council is approaching its anniversary in a shape that is far from ideal. Since March 2022, as a result of actions by its Western member states, its work has effectively been frozen, leaving the organization in a severe crisis. Ministerial meetings and sessions of its key coordinating body, the Senior Arctic Officials, have been suspended, while its capacity to implement projects has been significantly curtailed. The Council’s activities are now largely confined to expert-level contacts and remote meetings of its working bodies.
Russia is ready to resume the full-fledged work of the Arctic Council, provided that all parties engage in good faith and take into account the legitimate interests of every participant. At the same time, we are prepared for the scenario currently being pursued by NATO countries within the organization as they attempt to discuss Arctic issues among themselves, without Russia, thereby effectively discrediting and marginalizing the Arctic Council. Should this scenario materialize, Russia has the territory, logistics, technology, and reliable partners needed to carry out mutually beneficial projects and confidently implement its plans in the Arctic.
The future of international cooperation in the Arctic
A glance at the world map makes it clear that Russia has been, is, and will remain a leading Arctic state. As climate change continues and the polar ice cover recedes, experts predict that the Arctic will become increasingly accessible for transportation and resource development. The region is already playing an increasingly important role in maintaining stable trade links amid more frequent disruptions to global supply chains, particularly in the straits of the world’s oceans that are of systemic importance to the global economy.
The strategic importance of the Arctic to our country’s national interests and security will also continue to grow. We will pursue the comprehensive development of the High North and further expand the infrastructure of Russia’s Arctic zone in accordance with Russian law and the country’s development priorities.
In our economic activities, we will continue to proceed from the understanding that the Arctic maritime areas form an integral part of the World Ocean. The provisions of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establish special rights and responsibilities for coastal states in the Arctic, apply there in full. Commitment to these rights and responsibilities was reaffirmed in the Ilulissat Declaration, adopted in 2008 by the five Arctic coastal states – Russia, Denmark, Canada, Norway, and the United States. At this stage, we see no need to develop new international legal instruments governing economic and other activities in the High North.
Russia’s foreign policy in the Arctic will remain comprehensive and pragmatic. We support the Arctic’s development as an integral part of the broader Eurasian space of security and cooperation.
Our current opponents should have learned the many lessons of history by now and understood that attempts to speak to Russia in the language of sanctions and threats are futile. Unfriendly and hostile actions have been and will continue to be met with an appropriate response, including asymmetric measures. Russia favors constructive dialogue in all regions of the world, but, when necessary, we will defend our national interests by all available means.
As President of Russia Vladimir Putin has repeatedly emphasized, extensive work is underway in the Arctic, and we are open to cooperation with all partners willing to engage on the basis of equality and mutual benefit. Such partners, beyond the circle of NATO countries pursuing Russophobic policies, constitute the overwhelming majority.Promising areas of cooperation include the development of natural resources and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, including its key component, the Northern Sea Route. Priorities also include the development of industrial, transport, and tourism infrastructure.Improving the well-being of people living in the Far North, preserving the Arctic environment, and advancing scientific research will also remain key priorities. In all these areas, we see international cooperation as playing a major role.

articles.title: North Korea denounces upcoming US-South Korea-Japan military drills as 'air espionage'
articles.body:
Riyaz ul Khaliq
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
North Korea on Monday denounced upcoming trilateral military exercises by the US, South Korea and Japan as "air espionage," accusing Washington of reaffirming what it called an unchanging hostile policy threatening its sovereignty and security interests.
Pyongyang's reaction came after the US State Department reiterated Washington's commitment to the "complete denuclearization" of North Korea, state-run KCNA reported, citing a Foreign Ministry statement.
The State Department "openly betrayed its extremely sinister and vicious hostile attempt to tarnish the image of our country and create its internal instability, talking about someone's 'human rights abuses,'" the ministry said.
South Korea, the US and Japan are scheduled to conduct their trilateral "Freedom Edge" military exercise from Sept. 7-11 in waters east and south of South Korea's Jeju Island.
The drills come after the Trump administration earlier this month cut short joint exercises with Seoul in an apparent effort to encourage Pyongyang to resume talks.
"It is pointless to expect any detente in the region, given the grave situation where the US persistent hostile policy toward" North Korea "is evolving in a more dangerous way," the ministry said.
"Our nukes serve as an absolute guarantee for defending its sovereignty," it added.
The ministry said Freedom Edge constituted a "threat to the DPRK and regional countries" and accused the US and its allies of "perpetrating air espionage and other anti-DPRK military provocations one after another," using the acronym for North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The statement came a day after North Korea appointed Kim Song Gi, director of the General Political Bureau of the Korean People's Army, as defense minister, replacing No Kwang Chol.
No was reassigned as vice director of the Munitions Industry Department.

articles.title: US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month, a US official said Sunday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the attack on Larak island killed and wounded several Iranian fighters and civilians, and vowed to punish those responsible.
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month on Sunday, according to a US official, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.
Forces with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to the official who spoke on condition of anonymity, to detail sensitive military movements.
The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
Semi-official news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The IRCG in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots.”
The statement said the attack will “result in punishment of the aggressor.”
The fighting comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure – rather than military action – to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centers on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran.
The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe.
Read moreTrump says Strait of Hormuz demined, warns of ‘zero tolerance’ for new mines
As the conflict grinds on, Trump’s talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he’s “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes.
Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signaled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home.
Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israel campaign has been devastating for Iran’s navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered $270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government’s leadership structure.
But Iran has found leverage through its own strikes in the critical Strait of Hormuz where relatively few vessels carrying oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the vital energy waterway, through which 20% of the world's oil normally flows, effectively controlling much of the traffic in the strait.
Tehran continues to assert that even after it works out a management plan for the strait with Oman, its neighbour on the other side of the waterway, the US can't use it until it fulfils its obligations under the memorandum of understanding (MOU) the countries signed in mid-June.
Trump has repeatedly declared that the “Strait of Hormuz is open,” saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that’s a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that transited daily before the war began.
Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at “reduced levels.”
And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation ((UKMTO) said no casualties or environmental impact had been reported, and cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
The US military said that as of Sunday, it had redirected 83 commercial vessels and disabled three under its blockade of Iranian ports.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernan
articles.body:
Nowhere was the confidence of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, shown as clearly as in his appointment of chancellor. There were weeks of speculation that this appointment was a choice between the energy secretary, Ed Miliband, and the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, with their contrasting political economies.
It has been a hallmark of Burnham’s politics that he and his team do not get involved in briefing wars, so it was only when former defence secretary John Healey appeared in Downing Street together with Mahmood that it was clear that the prime minister had cut the Gordian knot, reassuring the markets with a cool, calm political operator with extensive Treasury experience as chancellor. Healey’s two years in defence meant that he would know both sides of the argument when it came to one of the biggest questions of the forthcoming budget: how to meet the bold new Nato defence spending targets without derailing the social ambitions of the Burnham government.
Just last week, it was revealed that the question of getting the right balance of the competing demands of defence, social care, council housing and devolution would be deferred to a spending review next year, and that this October’s budget would be a low-key, continuity affair. That’s a good thing, because the facts about the Ministry of Defence are stark – the stridency of its claims of underfunding are only matched by its record of overspending. The National Audit Office has a series of reports detailing the failures of the MoD’s control of spending.
When I was a special adviser in the MoD during the Gordon Brown government, there was a saying that if you wanted to know what was going on in procurement you just needed to speak to BAE Systems. It was a sardonic acknowledgment of the extent of producer capture by the UK defence industries. Now, there are more elevated phrases like “sovereign capability” or references to seemingly objective measures like percentages of GDP – “3% by the next parliament and 3.5% by 2035”. But they all mean the same thing: like the Cyclops in The Odyssey, the military industrial complex is hungry.
This is one of the strongest arguments for the appointment of Wes Streeting as defence secretary. He has, it seems, tamed the NHS appetite for overspending. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported last week that “last year the NHS saw no spending top up for frontline services from the Treasury reserve or capital budgets for the first time since 2013-14”.
Of course, geopolitics looms over the defence spending question. The godfather – in all meanings – of the Hague investment plan, which committed the US’s Nato allies to higher defence spending, was President Trump, despite his repeated threats to the territorial integrity of members of that alliance. Keir Starmer decided that a mixture of flattery in the form of a second royal visit, and subservience – embarrassedly picking up the president’s dropped papers – was the right formula. The problem is that going along with a bully just reinforces their behaviour.
The more appropriate political response is being modelled by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney. He sketched out a new emerging world order in a speech at Davos in January, and most Canadians support his stance since his resolute response to US trade talks and Trump’s attempted “renaming” of Lake Ontario. This led Carney to float the possibility of a deepening partnership between Canada and the European Union – an arrangement that could set a precedent for the UK to realign with the EU without rerunning the entire Brexit debate.
Political entrepreneurship on that level is already being demonstrated by Miliband, now foreign secretary, who has chosen to take the UK seat on the World Bank rather than delegating it to a junior minister. That shows an intent to shape rather than respond to the emerging international situation, and should give space for the prime minister to deal with a pressing domestic agenda.
The question that is rarely addressed in the defence debate is what kind of country we are fighting for. With his mantra of “growth in every postcode”, fixing social care, devolving power and building council houses, Burnham has laid out his programme. Simply setting out his stall has greatly increased Labour’s support. Now he has to build that better Britain – a socially democratic one in which defence spending is taken seriously but doesn’t prevent other societal needs from being fulfilled.
Of course, in politics, one of the huge advantages of having a positive vision of what you are for is that you can go negative on your opponents. Here, defence can be a huge wedge for Burnham. On the right, both the Conservative party and Reform UK were so eager to support Trump that they wanted the UK to commit to the quagmire of the Iran war. They should never be allowed to forget that they put US interests above the UK’s. On the centre-left the attack lines are easy, too. The SNP wants to be a member of an imaginary non-nuclear Nato and never address the challenge of Russian infractions into Scottish waters and airspace. Likewise, the Greens are split on whether to be in Nato and have no idea of why the UK should have defence forces.
All in all, defence is returning to the right space in UK politics. Neither an unfeasible demand on resources, nor a neglected backwater, but a positive tool for a progressive government.

articles.title: Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones in July as in June
articles.body:
Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones in July as in June
A Ukrainian military official has said Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones to attack Ukraine in July as it did in June, following a change in its drone attack tactics and increased use of jet-powered UAVs, which are more difficult for the Ukrainian Air Force to shoot down.
Source: Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, in an interview on the national joint 24/7 newscast
Quote: "The enemy has changed the weapons it uses more than its tactics. In other words, it has significantly increased the number of jet-powered [drones – ed.] specifically. This happened... in July. The enemy used five times as many jet-powered UAVs in July as in June. That was the month when the number of these UAVs, along with Banderol missile drones, began to increase significantly."
Details: Ihnat reported that Russia had launched more than 1,500 UAVs on Ukraine over the past four days. Of these, 800 – more than half – were jet-powered.
Ihnat said the Russians have resorted to using jet-powered drones as Ukraine's defence forces were successfully shooting down and jamming large numbers of conventional petrol-powered Shaheds.
"Of course, they did not start using jet-powered UAVs just recently, but they have now increased their use, realising that they cannot be shot down using the conventional methods we already employ against ordinary UAVs," the spokesperson said.
He added that Ukraine's interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is currently lower than for conventional drones, 88-90% of which are shot down.
Ihnat explained that the successful interception of jet-powered drones requires the use of ground-based air defence systems, aviation systems and platforms, fighter jets equipped with air-to-air missiles, and other weapons.

articles.title: Car bomb reportedly targets Dmitry Neelov, Ukraine war crimes suspect linked to Olenivka POW deaths, in occupied Donetsk
articles.body:
Car bomb reportedly targets Dmitry Neelov, Ukraine war crimes suspect linked to Olenivka POW deaths, in occupied Donetsk
A car belonging to Dmitry Neelov — first deputy head of the Olenivka penal colony in the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DNR”) — was blown up in occupied Donetsk overnight on August 28–29, Ukrainian news outlets Censor.NET and Ukrainska Pravda said, citing sources.
The outlets said an explosive device had been planted under the car. Neither said whether Neelov was hurt.
On July 29, 2022, a missile strike hit the penal colony in the village of Olenivka, 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Donetsk, killing 53 Ukrainian prisoners of war and wounding 75 others. Ukraine’s General Staff blamed Russia for the attack; Russia’s Defense Ministry blamed Ukraine.
The colony’s former head, Sergey Yevsyukov, was killed in a car bombing in central Donetsk in December 2024. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) soon said it had detained a Donetsk resident suspected of involvement in the bombing.
Two years after the missile strike, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) named Yevsyukov and his deputy, Dmitry Neelov, as suspects. Ukrainian investigators said the pair had deliberately delayed evacuating wounded Ukrainian prisoners to medical facilities. In spring 2026, the SBU and Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office charged Neelov with war crimes. Ukraine has accused him of torturing, beating, and humiliating Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilians.

articles.title: FACTBOX: 239 drones downed, Ukrainian strikes on homes, logistics center in Yekaterinburg
articles.body:
YEKATERINBURG, August 31. /TASS/. Drones and their debris struck residential buildings and a logistics center in Yekaterinburg. No fatalities were recorded, Sverdlovsk Region Governor Denis Pasler said. According to the latest reports, four people were injured.
Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 239 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Black Sea overnight, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
TASS has compiled the main developments.
Attack scale
- Alert air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 239 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions during the night, the Defense Ministry said.
- According to the ministry, the drones were downed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Samara, Saratov, Tambov, Tula, Moscow, and Krasnodar Regions, as well as the Republic of Crimea and the Black Sea.
- More than 30 Ukrainian drones were destroyed overnight over the Chertkovsky, Sholokhovsky, Tarasovsky, Millerovsky, Verkhnedonskoy and Bokovsky districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 12 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region during the night, Governor Alexander Gusev said on Max.
- Air defenses intercepted six drones over the Oryol Region during the night, Governor Andrey Klichkov said on Max.
Aftermath
- Drones and their debris damaged residential buildings and a logistics center in Yekaterinburg, Sverdlovsk Region Governor Denis Pasler said on Max.
- No fatalities were reported.
- Information about those injured is being clarified.
- Pasler said fires had been reported following the strikes.
- All emergency services are working at the sites.
- An evacuation is underway.
- Residents of the Yekaterinburg building struck by a drone will receive all necessary assistance, Russian Presidential Envoy to the Urals Federal District Artyom Zhoga said on Max.
- He noted an attack on a warehouse of a trading company in the Sverdlovsk Region had been prevented, with drone debris falling near the building.
- Pasler later reported that three multifamily buildings were damaged as a result of the drone attack on Yekaterinburg.
- They will be repaired as soon as possible, the governor said.
- Ukrainian forces attacked the village of Koshlakovo in the Shebekinsky District of the Belgorod Region with a drone. A civilian was injured in the detonation, the regional crisis management center said on Max.
- The man sustained multiple shrapnel wounds to his head, chest, arm and legs.
- He was taken to Shebekino Central District Hospital, where he is receiving medical assistance.
- He will be transferred to Belgorod City Hospital No. 2 for further treatment, the regional crisis management center said.
- A drone attack on a private home in the Graivoronsky District damaged the roof. Windows of an apartment building were also damaged.
- In the Belgorod area, a vehicle was hit by shrapnel, the canopy of a commercial facility was damaged and windows in a private home were shattered.
- The Ukrainian military attacked a commercial facility in the village of Repnoye in the Belgorodsky district with a drone, injuring a 12-year-old girl, the region’s crisis management center reported on Max.
- She was diagnosed with a blast injury and an abrasion on her forearm.
- After receiving medical treatment, the child was sent home.

articles.title: Politico and Welt: Germany plans to blame Russia for the Leipzig airport sabotage attempt and announce new sanctions
articles.body:
Politico and Welt: Germany plans to blame Russia for the Leipzig airport sabotage attempt and announce new sanctions
In the coming days, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz plans to accuse Russia of an attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig airport, where drones with explosives were found, Politico and the German newspaper Welt am Sonntag said, citing sources.
Merz is expected to announce new sanctions against Moscow. The package would combine direct German measures with new EU sanctions being prepared in parallel in Brussels, according to the two outlets.
Expelling individual Russian diplomats or closing the Russian House in Berlin is no longer an adequate response to the Leipzig drone incident, one source said. Tougher steps were needed, the source said — harsher sanctions or even more extensive arms deliveries to Ukraine.
Berlin has also begun preparing for a sharp response from Moscow, according to Politico.
Sources who spoke to Politico described Germany’s upcoming move as a ”Zeitenwende 2.0” — a second turning point, echoing the Zeitenwende, the term former Chancellor Olaf Scholz used after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when he announced an abrupt overhaul of Berlin’s relations with Moscow.
On August 25, Merz said those behind the attempted sabotage in Leipzig would be held accountable, though he leveled no specific accusations. He promised to say more about the investigation’s findings soon. The government had been working with intelligence agencies on “intensive” efforts to identify those responsible, he said.
A drone of unknown origin was found at Leipzig airport overnight into August 5, German media said. It later emerged that multiple drones had been involved in the attempted sabotage. The first drone, discovered beside a Ukrainian Antonov transport plane loaded with ammunition, had explosives and a detonator attached. A second drone apparently collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing and go around because the airport had closed. A third drone did not turn up until 10 days after the incident. Investigators found about 50 grams (1.8 ounces) of explosives nearby.

articles.title: Quick EU help to Ukraine lies in depriving Russia of funding sources - former US special envoy Volker
articles.body:
Ukraine needs urgent assistance in the war unleashed by Russia, and while the European Union lags behind the United States in terms of military aid, it could be doing far more to deprive the aggressor of sources of funding, according to Kurt Volker, a distinguished fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA) and former US special representative for Ukraine negotiations.
"What Europe could really do is make every effort to try to deprive Russia of sources of funding," he said at the "Ukraine as Europe’s Stress Test" discussion panel at the European Forum in Alpbach on Monday, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reported.
Volker noted that Russia can still sell oil and gas to Europe, and that such sales will only end at the end of next year. In addition, Russia can receive payments through the international financial system for the sale of oil and gas.
"There are many third parties outside the US and Europe who are willing to do business with Russia. We need to make it clear to them that they cannot do that and do business with Europe," the former US special representative for Ukraine negotiations said.
"There should be a sense of urgency. There isn’t one, and that effectively means we’re on a train together that’s speeding not toward victory, but toward another option, which is subjugation. And China is watching. Russia is watching, and other potential players are watching," said Yevhen Hlibovytsky, co-founder and CEO of the Frontier Institute, describing the situation.
Volker also agreed with his Ukrainian colleague’s view that Europeans need to change their mentality.
"It all starts with mentality. There needs to be a mentality that Russia needs to be stopped… It’s not enough to say we should help Ukraine, provide assistance, or something like that. This won’t end until Russia is stopped," he explained his view.
According to him, such a change in mentality would also lead to changes in terms of concrete actions - for example, in the military approach, this means providing Taurus missiles and other long-range systems.
The CEPA fellow added that Europe also underestimates the urgency of changes in military approaches - for example, it is rolling out drone technology more slowly than the US, although the US pace in this area is also insufficient.
In Volker’s view, Europe’s position is stronger than that of the US when it comes to motivation and understanding that Ukraine is waging a fundamental fight for freedom against authoritarianism.
"They (the US) perceive this war against Ukraine incorrectly. I’m not sure the American people or Congress do, but the current administration certainly does. They don’t view it in the context of values, so they don’t see it as an attack on us. They view it as a fight between two sides," the former special representative for Ukraine negotiations said.
According to him, as a result, there is no particular sense of urgency from the US administration regarding support for Ukraine or ending the war, and the discussion instead centers on selling American weapons.

articles.title: 96 of 121 Russian drones neutralized; missile did not reach its target
articles.body:
96 of 121 Russian drones neutralized; missile did not reach its target
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched an Kh-59 missile and 121 drones at Ukraine overnight. Air defense shot down or suppressed 96 unmanned aerial vehicles; the missile did not reach its target.
Russia launched a missile and 121 drones at Ukraine overnight, of which 96 were shot down or suppressed; the missile did not reach its target, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Monday, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of August 31 (from 18:00 on August 30), the enemy attacked with one Kh-59 guided air-launched missile from the airspace over the Black Sea, as well as 121 Shahed-type attack UAVs (most of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Kursk, Oryol, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defenses had shot down/suppressed 96 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types in the north, south, east, and center of the country; the Kh-59 guided air-launched missile did not reach its target. Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 11 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed targets (debris) at 8 locations
The attack is ongoing; about ten enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: CIA-backed investor helped top German drones firm break into US
articles.body:
German drone maker Quantum Systems gained an early foothold in the United States with help from CIA-linked investor In-Q-Tel (IQT), its co-CEO said, highlighting how US capital and networks continue to shape Europe's emerging defense companies.
Sven Kruck told Reuters that US investors, including IQT, helped open doors in Washington and win work with the Central Intelligence Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
The comments, reported here for the first time, underscore the importance of US investors and contacts to some European defense startups even as governments across the continent push for greater independence from Washington.
"It made it easier to get started in the US with clients CIA and FBI," said Kruck, whose firm sells reconnaissance, attack and interceptor drones to countries including Ukraine and Germany.
"There were routes that opened up. That's how we found the way to the USA. We were stronger in the US early on, where the German customer was much weaker."
Berlin is seeking to reduce its dependence on Washington after President Donald Trump threatened to abandon NATO, the alliance underpinning Europe's defense against Russia.
But rebuilding Germany's long-neglected military without access to US capital and defense markets is a major challenge.
Kruck said business generated from a reconnaissance contract with US intelligence agencies was modest but helped establish Quantum's credibility. The company is now one of Europe's biggest defense startups, valued at around $8 billion.
Like other defense companies, Quantum cannot sell technology developed in the US to other countries without US approval.
IQT, established by intelligence officials, grows reach
The case also underscores the growing reach of IQT, the venture capital firm established by intelligence officials to identify and invest in technologies relevant to US national security.
IQT, whose name is a nod to James Bond's gadget maker Q, owns stakes in several companies, including German defense firm Stark, and is increasingly focusing on Europe as the continent ramps up military spending.
While IQT's investments are typically small, often less than $3 million, one person with knowledge of its operations said its value lies in connecting companies with US defense buyers, the sector's top spenders.
"Europe's deep-tech ecosystem is a critical source of mission-relevant innovation," said Jennifer Nelson, executive vice president international at IQT, responding to Reuters' questions.
"Germany is a particularly important innovation partner and strategic ally," she said, calling it a "cornerstone of Europe's defense ecosystem."
The venture firm, which invests in technologies ranging from cybersecurity and energy to satellites, has backed startups including data analytics giant Palantir Technologies and Anduril, one of the biggest military technology and drone firms.
"IQT continues to expand investments in German dual-use innovators ... so allied government teams can evaluate and adopt breakthrough capabilities faster," said Nelson.
Pervasive US influence
As Europe seeks to reduce its dependence on US military power, IQT's growing presence in the region has prompted concerns that strategically important new technologies could become increasingly tied to US interests.
Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, chair of the European Parliament's security and defense committee, said IQT should be viewed differently from a conventional investor because of its links to US intelligence agencies.
"In-Q-Tel is not a purely financial investor but has a mandate to secure access to the best technologies for the US intelligence services," said Strack-Zimmermann.
"There can be strategic influence beyond the business with the United States through investment stakes, observation rights, development and license deals as well as the access to government contracts."
Earlier this year, CIA Director John Ratcliffe said it was "optimizing our approach to working with the private sector." The CIA declined to comment.
Germany's defense ministry said it took investor influence in the defense sector seriously and that shareholders should not interfere with a company's operations, technology or research.
Kruck's comments shed light on the close links that continue to bind Europe's defense sector to the US, even as governments strive to build up domestic military capabilities.
"Every investor ... has a network behind it and, logically, you try to use this," Kruck said, adding that other investors had also helped the company.
"At the end of the day, your products have to be convincing. But for sure, American investors ... know the administration that rules and make it possible to open up communication."
Kruck added, however, that IQT had not sent him a "proactive email" in the past two years.
He also pointed to Washington's requirement that foreign defense suppliers establish local operations in the US. "That is why we have factories in the USA and staff there," he said.
European lawmakers have argued the region needs to do more to channel funding into startups. Europe has no equivalent of IQT.

articles.title: Trump posts AI videos of key Iranian oil hub ‘being blown to smithereens’
articles.body:
Trump posts AI videos of key Iranian oil hub ‘being blown to smithereens’
US President Donald Trump has published AI-generated clips showing a missile attack on Iran’s Kharg Island oil hub amid a new escalation between Washington and Tehran.
US and Iranian forces earlier exchanged strikes for the first time since late July. On Sunday, the US Central Command said it had targeted two Iranian launchers on Larak Island, near the narrowest point of the Strait of Hormuz, which it claimed were preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the waterway, accounting for some 20% of global crude oil trade. According to Tehran, the bombing killed several Iranian soldiers and civilians.
Iran retaliated early on Monday, with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) saying its drones and missiles had inflicted “significant damage” on the US military’s King Hussein and Al-Azraq air bases in Jordan.
Following the strikes, oil prices went up in early trading in Asia, with WTI futures growing by 2.47% to $85.46 per barrel and Brent futures climbing by 2.71% to $90.49 per barrel.
Trump did not issue any immediate statements on the escalation on his Truth Social platform, instead posting two short AI-generated videos of multiple missiles striking oil facilities on an island and causing huge explosions.
“Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!” the caption to one of the videos read.
When you CANT Win The Real War so you use AI to COPE
Trump posted this video with the caption: Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!
President DJT
THEN he posted it AGAIN without the caption. This is just sad pic.twitter.com/4JbFOxiHkX
The head of the National Iranian Oil Company, Hamid Bovard, ridiculed Trump for posting the clips, saying that his “tweets are laughable and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate.”
The energy hub hasn’t been attacked, with routine oil operations continuing there, Bovard said, as cited by Nournews.
According to Reuters, there was no evidence of any strikes being carried out against Kharg Island.
Located around 25 km (15 miles) off Iran’s Gulf coast, Kharg Island handles around 90% of the country’s crude exports, serving as the primary outlet for its oil revenue. The coral outcrop, often referred to by the public as the “forbidden island” because of the tight security, also hosts a major oil storage facility.
The US struck military sites on Kharg Island several times after the start of the conflict in late February, but refrained from targeting energy infrastructure. Trump also mulled a ground operation to seize the oil hub, saying it could be carried out by US forces or by “other people.” However, those plans never materialized.
Tehran has warned repeatedly that it will set the whole oil and gas infrastructure of the US allies in the Gulf States “on fire” if energy facilities on Kharg island are hit or an attempt to capture it is made.

articles.title: "It is a moment of extreme urgency": US senator urges House to approve Russia sanctions bill
articles.body:
"It is a moment of extreme urgency": US senator urges House to approve Russia sanctions bill
US Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut has urged the House of Representatives to support a Senate-passed bill imposing sanctions on Russia, describing the situation in the war in Ukraine as a "moment of extreme urgency".
Source: Blumenthal in an interview with CBS News
Quote: "It is a moment of extreme urgency, for the reason that Putin may try to escalate, but also because Putin is on his heels economically.
And this kind of sanctions bill, throttling the flow of revenue to his war machine could undercut completely his ability to wage this brutal, murderous war."
Details: The US Senate passed the bill by a wide bipartisan majority before breaking for its August recess. The initiative emerged after the sudden death of Senator Lindsey Graham, who had long advocated the measures alongside Blumenthal. The bill has now moved to the House of Representatives, which is due to return to work this week after a five-week recess. However, its prospects in the lower chamber remain uncertain.
The bill, known as the The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, would allow the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas, except for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia while also taking steps to reduce those imports. Some Democrats in the House, however, have raised concerns about giving the president additional powers.
Asked about possible opposition from Democrats, Blumenthal defended the bill, saying it was the "result of painstaking, sometimes painful, negotiations" with the US Trade Representative, the White House and lawmakers from both parties.
"It passed the Senate 86 to 11 – not many measures doing that kind of successful passage these days," Blumenthal said.
He highlighted the additional powers the bill would give the president to "impose scorching sanctions on the oligarchs" and financial institutions, as well as measures to "crack down on the shadow fleet" and the power to impose tariffs, "narrowly constrained" to the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Blumenthal said the sanctions bill could weaken Russian leader Vladimir Putin's position.
Quote: "His economy is on the verge of major crisis.
He has a deficit looming of US$125 billion, 5% of his GDP, an interest rate of 14% on his national debt."
Details: Blumenthal expressed great hope that the sanctions bill would receive enough support from Democrats to pass the House. He added that during his visit to Ukraine last week, he urged President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to meet with members of Congress, as the Ukrainian leader had done in the Senate.
Previously: Zelenskyy met with US senators from both parties – Richard Blumenthal and James Lankford – in Kyiv on 23 August.
Read also: This time could be different for Russia sanctions
Background: The US imposed sanctions on a number of entities within the Russian Defence Ministry as well as two Russian companies and five Russian nationals at the beginning of August.

articles.title: Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
articles.body:
Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
Iraq is committed to a full withdrawal of US-led coalition forces by the end of September, UK-based Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat reported on Saturday, citing an Iraqi official.
US forces have been in the country for 23 years since the 2003 invasion and subsequent smaller-scale operations against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS).
Reports that US and other foreign troops could remain after September “contradict what was agreed upon between the previous Iraqi government and the US administration,” Asharq Al-Awsat cited the official as saying.
The comments followed media reports suggesting that Washington was only planning a drawdown, rather than a full withdraw by the end of the September deadline.
“This is a transition of the Coalition’s military mission to a more traditional bilateral security partnership,” Iraqi news outlet Shafaq News reported, citing an anonymous US official.
Earlier this month, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s office stated that the September 30 deadline would be “the fixed and final date” for the pullout of international coalition forces.
US President Donald Trump has previously backed reducing the US military presence in Iraq, reaffirming a withdrawal plan originally agreed in 2024 under the Biden administration. During a meeting with al-Zaidi this summer, Trump said the two countries were developing a relationship “where we don’t need the military” in Iraq.
Washington’s presence in the region has taken a significant hit during the Iran war, as Tehran has damaged or outright destroyed key US radar, communications, and other military infrastructure at bases in Gulf nations.
During the conflict, US military infrastructure in the region also faced attacks by pro-Iranian armed groups in Iraq operating outside Baghdad’s direct control.
The Pentagon is now considering whether to reduce the US military footprint in the Gulf after the Iran war ends, The Washington Post reported earlier in August, citing anonymous officials.
US allies in the Gulf have also reportedly expressed frustration over what they see as a lack of proper consultation before the US-Israeli attack on Iran, which led to bases on their territories being targeted. Regional powers have since moved to diversify their security partnerships, with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, already dubbed by commentators an ‘Islamic NATO,’ early this month.

articles.title: Why Japan’s hypersonic and underwater weapon plans might worry China
articles.body:
Why Japan’s hypersonic and underwater weapon plans might worry China
Beijing has hit out at Tokyo’s moves to arm submarine drones with long-range missiles and test hypersonic weapons in Australia
China’s defence ministry spokesman Zhang Xiaogang highlighted the two initiatives on Thursday, saying Japan had “openly expanded its military arsenal”.
Zhang said the “dangerous” moves had a “striking resemblance” to Japan’s pre-World War II militarisation, though he did not explain why these particular weapon programmes could pose challenges for the PLA.
Japan has rapidly expanded its long-range strike capabilities since adopting a “counterstrike capability” in its 2022 security strategy. Under the policy, Tokyo says it could strike military targets in an adversary’s territory for self-defence following an armed attack, while pre-emptive strikes remain prohibited.

articles.title: "Italy ‘recruits’ Fedorov" — Italy’s top media outlets ran headlines about the former defense minister beginning work for another country
articles.body:
"Italy ‘recruits’ Fedorov" — Italy’s top media outlets ran headlines about the former defense minister beginning work for another country
Kyiv • UNN
Mykhailo Fedorov will advise Italy’s defense minister pro bono on drones and air defense. In Ukraine, there are concerns about a leak of military technologies.
Italian media published articles with headlines stating that Italy is “recruiting” former Ukrainian Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The articles appeared after Fedorov announced that he had become an adviser to Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto on defence issues, UNN reports.
According to Italian media reports, Fedorov decided to cooperate with Italy, providing it with his expertise.
“It is no coincidence that the main topics of his meeting with Minister Guido Crosetto were drones, air defence and so-called “unmanned” systems—remotely controlled or autonomous vehicles or devices,” Italy’s leading news agency ANSA writes.
The agency reports that, announcing his new position, Fedorov specified that “Ukraine’s experience could become the foundation for a new European defence model”.
“We must be “able to quickly test and implement new solutions, combining technology with reliable production capabilities. Minister Crosetto expressed his satisfaction: I am glad that Mykhailo Fedorov agreed to offer me his services,” ANSA quotes Italy’s Defence Minister.
Fedorov, for his part, stressed that “Ukraine and our team “have experience that we are ready to share”.
“In this position, I will help Italy implement modern technologies of warfare, strengthen its defence sector and adapt to new global security challenges,” Italy’s national news agency Adnkronos quotes Fedorov as saying.
The influential British publication the Financial Times, for its part, writes that Ukrainian MPs, veterans and civil society leaders, including many who supported Fedorov after his dismissal, were outraged by the news of his trip abroad.
“Many questioned his motives when, on Friday, after a visit to Rome, he announced that he would work as an unpaid adviser to Italy’s defence minister. Oleksii Honcharenko, an opposition MP who chairs the parliamentary investigative committee, wrote that Fedorov’s role in Italy could pose “a threat of leakage of knowledge about our advanced military technologies”, the Financial Times wrote.
As is known, the Law of Ukraine “On State Secrets” establishes a special procedure for transferring classified information to a foreign state or international organisation—on the basis of an international treaty or another state decision provided for by law. Such actions carried out privately are illegal.

articles.title: Russia’s Putin and China’s Xi to Attend Summit in Kyrgyzstan
articles.body:
Russia’s Vladimir Putin, China’s Xi Jinping and more than a dozen other leaders will gather in Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a regional bloc that seeks to be a counterinfluence to the West.
The group, which is celebrating its 25-year anniversary, brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Arriving in Bishkek on Sunday, Xi hailed what he described as a “golden period” in relations with Central Asian Kyrgyzstan, as China deepens its influence in the historically Russia-dominated region.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India’s Narendra Modi and Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdogan is also expected to attend, though his country is not a formal member.
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran’s Pezeshkian and China’s Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
How Russia’s Cultural Projects Conceal Their Human Atrocities
Russia and Iran – among the most sanctioned states in the world – have massively deepened their military and economic ties since Moscow invaded Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA’s director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues, but has gained momentum in recent years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 “dialogue partners”, including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states”.
But Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation”, referring to US-Chinese tensions.
- Real and trade wars -
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars – the Ukraine and Iran conflicts – or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation and maritime transport, aiming to cripple Tehran’s economy.
Washington has also threatened Iran’s allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it will “firmly defend” its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces “economic difficulties”.
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.
Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran “believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions”.
But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as “in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties”.
While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia – a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia – while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.
